An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). Furthermore, when combining this result with the $B^0_s$ mixing rate, a quantity known as $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ was determined to have an absolute value less than 0.065, considering a 0.036-day inverse time-scale. Additionally, the ratio of this parameter to the $B^0_s$ decay rate into two muons, $\Delta\Gamma_{s}/\Gamma_{s}^{0s}$, was found to be less than 0.034, providing the most restrictive upper limit to date on this measure. Moreover, the total decay rate of the $B^0_s$ meson was measured to be $\Gamma_{B^0_s}$ = 0.617 ± 0.003 (statistical) ± 0.001 (systematic) × 10^12 sec^-1. All of these results were more precise and/or more constraining than previous findings.

Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. We developed an energy-dependent thesis according to which the origin of these anisotropy patterns lies in the excess cosmic ray arrival patterns, resulting from quadrupolar anisotropy existing at source locations, shaped by global cosmic magnetic field patterns, specifically across the Energetic Particle Channel towards the observer. We validated this hypothesis through numerical simulation, and found that it effectively explains our observations, and that it relies moderately on the characteristics of the global cosmic magnetic field, resembling an " clover-leaf" structure, with an index of 0.55 ± 0.15 for its energy dependence. We also found supporting evidence for an anisotropy pattern existing at energy levels as low as 20 EeV, but it lacks sufficient statistical significance. We developed an event stream table that includes the most energetic cosmic ray events detected to date, along with 31 newly identified extremely energetic cosmic ray events detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory, with energies above 55 EeV, and magnetic horizontal interference angles ranging from 19.5 to 176.9, reflecting various cosmic magnetic field paths towards the observer. We propose that the extreme energy of these cosmic rays can be explained by Stratton's theoretical model, with further investigation required to understand the particle composition and arrival directions within this energy range. We also set robust limits on the flux and anisotropy of cosmic rays with energies above 20 EeVC, below existing general limits. In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the detection of tumor cells within whole-slide images. By simulating a FL environment and applying data protection measures, we trained and evaluated several deep learning models using a simulated client-server framework that reflected real-world conditions found in a cancer research setting. Our findings indicated that federated learning can efficiently train high-quality image analysis models, even when processing and analyzing digital microscope images, which typically consist of large, high-resolution images known as "slides." Furthermore, our results demonstrated that using a combination of data compression techniques and carefully selected training samples from client devices can prevent data breaches and minimize the loss of accuracy due to data protection, thereby enabling secure and reliable learning from distributed, protected data sets. We also examined the influence of client devices with varying capacities on the performance of federated learning and discovered that strong client devices can significantly accelerate training processes and produce more accurate outcomes, which could be critical factors in certain applications involving image analysis, particularly those involving the diagnosis of cancer from digitized tissue samples. In such cases, the best approaches may involve developing personalized diagnosis tools capable of detecting rare types of tumors. Overall, our study provides a comprehensive framework and set of experiments that can serve as a foundation for further research and development in the field of federated learning, particularly in the analysis of digitized tissue samples, which can play a key role in advancing the diagnosis and treatment of cancer. In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal distortions in the transmission path, significantly hindering the accuracy of received data. To counter this effect, a vortex mode photonic crystal fiber is proposed as an optical regeneration device.  This fiber's unique properties allow it to isolate the desired signal from interfering signals with differing wavelengths. Additionally, the FDTD method shows that a 1km long fiber can accurately receive 72Gbit/s data signals at various data modulation patterns.  Field tests reveal that this method can significantly reduce errors in data reception, even over long distances.  Furthermore, this technique may also have potential applications in other underwater communication channels.  Finally, this research is discussed in the context of the current state and future prospects of high-speed underwater communications.

Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. We've applied this technique to two fundamental time-series tasks: time-series classification and forecasting. Our experiments show that it produces TCN classifiers that outperform the current state-of-the-art, delivering a 125x performance improvement across 25 datasets in just 0.01s of inference time. For time-series forecasting, it led to a 15% improvement in Mean Absolute Error (MAE) without the use of external data or task-specific architectures. Our approach and code are openly accessible, enabling widespread integration into resource-constrained devices. These devices can now efficiently handle complex time-series data, enabling real-time forecasting and classification capabilities. This breakthrough also paves the way for more complex TCN applications in such devices. Furthermore, our weight-pruning framework can be adapted for use in other convolutional networks, making it a versatile technique with considerable potential. Its concurrent weight-pruning capability can be adapted for other deep learning models, making it a versatile technique with considerable potential. Its ability to optimize dilation factors can be applied to any iteration-based deep learning model. This breaks new ground in the field and may lead to improved efficiency and performance in various machine learning applications. This model is now available on the CompactTCN GitHub page. We further demonstrate that the finite-dimensional Hamiltonian and Jordan algebras are nilpotent. Lastly, our research identifies a particular condition under which the finite-dimensional Motzkin algebra becomes nilpotent. This condition can be utilized to determine the nilpotency of these algebras in certain specific situations. Our study draws from known examples and novel constructions of algebras with specific properties. We also explore related open questions in this field. Our work is also based on our paper titled "Finite-dimensional Lie, Zinbiel, Hamilton, Jordan and Motzkin algebras are nilpotent" which is currently undergoing review. It is worth noting that the terms 'Lie', 'Zinbiel', 'Hamilton', 'Jordan' and 'Motzkin' algebras refer to types of mathematical algebras used in geometry and abstract algebra. Our research finds that certain finite-dimensional versions of these algebras have unique properties such as being nilpotent or solvable. Our study also explores new constructions of these algebras and their subalgebras. It shows that our results cover all possible finite-dimensional Lie, Zinbiel, Hamilton, Jordan and Motzkin algebras. Our paper provides detailed proofs of our research findings along with related discussions. It also presents several open questions for further research in this field. Our study can serve as a basis for a broader investigation of non-associative algebras and their representations. It can also be used as a foundation for a deeper analysis of the nilpotency and solvability characteristics of these algebras. Our research can be applied in various scientific disciplines such as physics, computer science, biology, economics and mathematics itself. This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. Our research includes an examination of various loss functions related to these data sets. All necessary R code and data sets are available online for replication purposes. Our study provides a framework for flexible modeling of time series data and is suitable for researchers interested in count-based time series forecasting. This research is published in the journal Econometrics. Corresponding authors are responsible for making the associated code and data sets accessible at https://doi.org/10.56832/2023.arXiv.220705186 for replication purposes. Code is also accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/aleixtarrés/TV-PARX.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on local object features. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/. We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The findings showed a moderate metal content and the absence of an internal variation in metal abundance. Tononzintla 2 displayed an increased presence of alpha-enrichment which aligns with patterns observed in other rich-metallic galactic clusters. A nitrogen spread was discovered in Tononzintla 2 with multiple nitrogen-rich stars residing within it, significantly above average levels for this region, suggesting a multi-generational population within the cluster that consists of first-generation nitrogen-abundance members. A [Ce/Fe] spread was identified and found to correlate with nitrogen, suggesting a relatively minor, s-process enriched population within the cluster which was probably the result of smaller low-mass Asymptotic Giant Branch stars. A radial velocity mean of -178.6 km/s and minimal velocity dispersion of 2.99 km/s was discovered for the cluster, indicative of typical globular cluster features, including an eccentric orbit. The lack of straggling stars at the high metal content end of the distribution function suggests the cluster may have experienced a loss of more metal-enriched members due to tidal interactions with the galaxy's central region. The estimated age of the cluster ranges from 13.1 to 14.6 billion years, making it one of the oldest detected galaxy clusters and requiring multiple generations of stars within it, a phenomenon that is rare and needing further study to understand its full implications. The cluster's multiple nitrogen-abundance generations, a [Ce/Fe] spread and a possible small s-process population make Tononzintla 2 an especially fascinating and yielding target for research in the far future. The findings provided in this article are the result of a broader investigation aimed at analyzing 15 California-plateau globular clusters that were observed by APOGEE-2 and are scheduled for publication in a separate article. The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, representing an impressive compilation of research and offering a diverse range of opportunities for statistical exploration in the field of theorem proving. Despite the numerous contributions made so far, the ever-expanding nature of the archive still poses certain challenges: locating specific content has become increasingly difficult, making it essential to prioritize reuse and clarity of comprehension. In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to create an area around the optimal value where the non-convex function can be expressed with a local log-Sobolev inequality, given that the optimization method with proper initialization and growth conditions is used. We specifically show that for a wide range of non-convex functions, including those that can be defined through the exponential function and for various common regularization methods, such as L1 and L2, we can find a local convex region near the optimal value. We also provide an inequality that measures the size of this local convex region in terms of the log-Sobolev constant, and establish the relationships between the log-Sobolev constant and other measures, such as the Poincare constant, the spectral gap, and the total variation bound, which can be obtained through recent results on optimization methods. Moreover, we apply our findings to show the local convexity for two specific functions: one is the empirical risk function under uniform loss, the other is the negative log-likelihood function under Poisson distribution. Our results can be seen as an extension of the existing results, and provide an alternative way to establish the local convexity, which can be useful for deviating from the current methods. This report outlines a deep learning approach known as the Electron Correlation
Potential Neural Network (eCPNN), which can learn simplified potential functions
that accurately capture the intricate instantaneous relationships among electrons
within complex multi-electron atomic systems. Trained in an unsupervised manner,
eCPNN models effectively convey the substantial amount of data obtained from highly
accurate configuration interaction approaches, such as CI+HF, which takes into account
every possible electronic configuration and their relative energies. Once trained,
these eCPNN models can predict various atomic properties with high precision, such
as total energies, electron correlation energies, static polarizabilities, and energy
margins, even when confronted with unfamiliar states of the atom. To further its
applicability, the eCPNN framework has been integrated with the Hamiltonian neural
network, which iteratively improves the potential functions it learns through the
application of existing quantum mechanics. By doing so, the accuracy of predictions for
total energies is significantly enhanced for all atoms in the second and third periods. 
The approach highlights the potential of hybrid quantum-classical approaches to accelerate
the precise calculation of complex multi-electron atomic systems. The eCPNN model is
also available upon request.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. Bond-based Peridynamics, despite its modeling restrictions, has become a widely-used approach in numerical simulations because of its ease of implementation and intuitive connection to real-world physics. This paper delves into the aspects of bond-based peridynamic models, providing a thorough examination of the theory and its numerical representations. Various bond-based PD integral kernels have been presented along with their distinguishing characteristics, leading to discussions on their implications and common traits. A closer examination was conducted on the role of non-locality in determining motion, the interplay between kernel structure and material non-penetration, as well as the influence of PD kernel non-linearity on predicting fracture development. Finally, an exploration is initiated on adapting BB-PD to model fluids within the context of fading memory materials, suggesting directions for enhanced understanding of fluid dynamics through peridynamics. This comprehensive exploration aims to contribute to the advancement of bond-based peridynamics, especially its potential applications in solving fluid mechanics problems. This potential is illustrated through a simple experiment involving a fading memory material, with simulation results comparing favorably with actual experiments. This analysis and associated discussions and potential research ideas are presented in the context of the motion of a PD particle over various surfaces, revealing valuable insights into the capabilities and limitations of bond-based peridynamics. This paper is intended for early-career professionals in mechanics, physics, and related fields, aiming to provide an in-depth examination of BB-PD that is both thoroughly referenced and easily accessible. This paper is accompanied by publicly available code to facilitate replication of numerical experiments mentioned within the text. This code can also serve as a starting point for further developing numerical solutions within the context of bond-based peridynamics. Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Furthermore, research found that an optimal method could be identified that boasts extremely low bias in comparison to other alternatives. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no decrease in computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps without compromising conformational exploration. Ultimately, the most efficient method demonstrated enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 25% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least a factor of ten in configurational average errors in solvent simulations with larger time steps. The newly developed impulse approximation was found to be highly compatible with energy minimization and molecular dynamics simulations, leading to enhanced molecular sampling. As a result, the method is expected to contribute meaningfully to the further improvement of molecular dynamics simulations. Ultimately, the most efficient method is anticipated to become the new standard for molecular dynamics simulations. As an open-source implementation, the Python module ``piMM`` is available for download at https://git.tuebingen.mpg.de/MBE/piMM.git or can be installed via ``pip install piMM``. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through analyses of a social network and a citation network. The additional data required to extend current multi-layer network analyses to networks with separate layers is also illustrated through the examination of an economic multiplex. The potential applications of this approach are vast and could be applied to any research that relies on multi-layer network data, such as networked contagion, spread of opinion, and node classification. This approach is also compatible with current multi-layer network generation models. The corresponding source code is available at https://github/multileyeigencentrality. We tackle the issue of non-blind deblurring and demosaicking on noisy raw images using a learning-based approach tailored to handle these images directly, with an innovative new component that simultaneously demosaicks and deblurs them in an interpretable way. To train this model, we utilize real-world camera data transformed into raw images through a realistic process, mimicking real-world camera functions. By doing so, we demonstrate the advantages of our single-stage model over traditional approaches combining demosaicking and deblurring modules, according to objective performance metrics. Additionally, our method is capable of removing a camera's intrinsic blurring effect, which effectively enables deblurring of sharper images from actual pictures. Visual comparisons also reveal that our method produces visually pleasing and realistic images. To facilitate further research, we are releasing both the trained model and the real-world camera data used to train it. This data consists of 20,000 raw images, along with their transformed forms, which until now have not been available as part of any deep learning training datasets. This dataset is particularly noteworthy because it is the first to include demosaicked and blured versions of raw images, in addition to actual pictures taken with a camera. This dataset can be accessed through the following link: https://github.com/cg1176/camera-raw-dataset. For more information and code, please visit https://cg1176.github.io/projects/raw-image-processing/. Our approach has been compared to the current state-of-the-art methods, along with the code and metrics employed, which can also be found at the aforementioned link. Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture. This involves multiplying the wave function by a symmetry-breaking 
factor. As a result, we derive a new potential that mimics the behavior of the Dirac equation 
within the de Sitter spacetime. We find that this potential leads to an eigenvalue equation 
whose solutions correlate with the energy levels of the harmonic oscillator. We predict that 
this new potential could be useful in modeling atomic physics phenomena that exhibit 
symmetry breaking.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. Moreover, our research offers a more comprehensive understanding of the water-entry process by analyzing the relationships between velocities, pressures, and the resulting surface seal patterns. High-speed cameras and high-resolution radiography were used to high-resolve the 1-to-100 km/s water-entry regime, a speed range unique to this work. The discovered pressure-induced effects also have implications for understanding similar phenomena in water-entry interactions, including those involving ellipsoidal and disc-shaped bodies. In cases where the pinched-off cavity forms a concave shape, as seen with mid-range speed sphere entries, it is possible for the surface of the cavity to retain rippling patterns until the secondary pinch-off stage, a phenomenon that could result in the partial or complete breaking of the pinched-off cavity surface when the sphere slows down enough for the secondary pinch-off to occur. In conclusion, this study provides a detailed, experimentally supported analysis of the surface-seal regime in water-entry interactions, involving both pressurized and non-penetrating pinched-off cavities, and involving all possible speed ranges for both supercritical and subcritical flow conditions. A well-known hypothesis posits that gravity at a quantum level must be devoid of universal symmetries. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and their connection to the shape of Calabi-Yau three-fold manifolds used in their construction. Generalized $\theta$-terms were found to break many of these symmetries. The results revealed that a number of the theories evolve through phase transitions, resulting in the generation of matter particles and the expulsion of universal symmetries. The theories' ability to support topological strings and $\alpha'$-corrections was also determined. The findings facilitated the creation of supersymmetric QCD-like theories, along with theories analogous to the standard model, QCD, or a "QCD-like" little string theory. The studies also led to the discovery that most of the constructed theories possess an age-related problem, with an inevitable cosmological coproduction of matter and dark energy. The possibility of employing these theories to address the cosmological dark matter and dark energy enigmas is also being explored. The complete set of generalized $\theta$-term couplings is defined by a set of modular functions, presented here for the first time. The general $\alpha'$-expanded type IIB action, encompassing all generalized $\theta$-terms, is also provided. The studies were also facilitated by an innovative, automated method for computing three-dimensional supersymmetric effective actions. A collection of the newly derived four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective actions, including $\alpha'$-expanded expressions, is appended for reference. Mobile device owners frequently require running sensitive security applications alongside unverified, potentially malicious software, which necessitates reliance on device hardware and system software to safely isolate threats. 

This often misplaced trust is the foundation on which our objective is built – namely to minimize the reliance on device hardware and software components for users to withstand cyber threats. 

We introduce an innovative multi-domain hardware setup consisting of isolated sections, where programs are partitioned statically to prevent malicious interaction. 

A few key hardware components with proven security functionality are integrated to grant secure temporary access to processing resources and external input/output interfaces simultaneously.

To manage these hardware components, we introduce OctopOS, a unique OS comprising several secure subsystems working together in distrust. 

We showcase a functioning prototype, incorporating our hardware and software, utilizing a combined CPU-FPGA board with an acceptable additional hardware expense in comparison to existing SoCs. 

We observe substantial reduction in trust requirements for security applications using our device, delivering better security performance compared to standard security architectures, with little performance impact for non-security programs, matching legacy system speeds. 

We also demonstrate successful execution of security-critical applications despite malware present on iOS and Android, with proper security reinitializations following threat containment. 

Our approach's effectiveness is further highlighted by an evaluation of well-known security applications, demonstrating our method's scalability and operational efficiency. 

Our research offers an innovative concept for a multi-domain hardware platform, with OctopOS providing an operating framework that optimizes hardware security functionality for maximum effectiveness. 
Our study's design and functioning prototype has given rise to several potential pathways for expansion and enhancement, with numerous security applications just waiting to be explored and developed.

We uncover an unselectable version of the box game paradox, featuring players making remarkably accurate predictions of unknown real numbers without access to relevant information. Additionally, our analysis confirms the requirement of choice in solving the classic problem and examines alternative configurations of the game. Finally, we explore connections to other mathematical puzzles involving accumulation points and conditional probability. This additional material is provided as an appendix to our existing article on the box game paradox.

A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication technology. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. Notably, this breakthrough facilitates the creation of dark states within the quantum dot without relying on an external magnetic field and allows for the emission of N-phonon bundles even in a system with losses, transforming it into an efficient phonon gun. Furthermore, this innovation creates opportunities for developing accurate phonon counters and accurate frequencyometers. Moreover, researchers propose the possibility of developing timeometers and meters for time based on the duration of phonon pulses produced by traveling photons. Finally, potential applications of this multi-phonon physics, encompassing phonon guns, counters, and meters, are also explored across various fields such as quantum communication, metrology, and the study of fundamental phenomena in physics. Ultimately, this groundbreaking research is positioned to push the boundaries of current knowledge and spark a new era in multi-phonon physics and physics research. Furthermore, this method displays superior performance compared to existing methods when assessing compound compounds composed of more complex structures. Additionally, the study validates the effectiveness of its depolymerization strategy by accurately reconstructing the original polymer from its predicted structure. The framework's potential to contribute positively to the field of drug discovery is also highlighted. The source code for this project is available online.

Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. Our focus is on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta schemes, highlighting their applications to a case study related to the ventilator shortage during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our approach was to convert the continuous time domain problem into a discrete time optimal control problem using different numerical schemes, resulting in acceptable solutions with fewer transcriptions than expected. Our primary method of comparison was the simultaneous direct approach versus the indirect approach. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks and dilated convolution layers to prioritize specific features and patterns. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. Additionally, the evaluation of different extraction tasks reveals that the proposed approach achieves superior performance over linear models and adapts better to new data. To facilitate future research, this study has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/Global-NER. Code has been optimized and a new paper outlining improvements has been published at https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.01799 for neural models and https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.01800 for statistical models. Consequently, the proposed holistic model has been successfully applied to three additional extraction tasks with promising results.}

We develop and test an innovative RSSI-based location finding method suitable for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) networks. To counteract interference between different technologies operating in the same frequency range, we design and execute a new method for calculating the distance between nodes. The aim of this approach is to minimize the average error in location estimation, and when compared to ideal, interference-free results, we have achieved a level of accuracy of less than half a metre using actual hardware. Additionally, we investigate the impact of using this new distance calculation method on location estimation and compare it with existing techniques. To provide context, the methodology we use to counteract interference can also be applied to other location detection systems. Further, we explore the possibilities of further improving location estimation by taking into account the height of nodes within outdoor scenarios. To validate our approach, a test network consisting of one mobile and multiple static 802.15.4 (ZigBee) nodes was developed and used to gather and analyze data at both an indoor and outdoor location. The data collected was used to calculate location estimation methods, including one proposed method where we estimate the distance between nodes using the minimum mean squared error (MMSE). Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications, promoting greater understanding and more effective communication across language barriers. This study serves as a comprehensive survey, covering prominent NLP studies involving code-mixing and presenting potential avenues for further research in this area. The related model architectures, along with relevant datasets and resources, are detailed in Table 1. These advancements, combined with recommended future directions, aim to contribute positively to the development of more effective NLP applications, particularly those involving code-mixing, and pave the way for overcoming language-related barriers.

Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, this paper focuses on developing a robust training and evaluation framework that utilizes high-quality descriptions alongside the primary goal of improving the performance of these systems. Initially, a metric is proposed to evaluate this quality by measuring the diversity and relevance of these descriptions. Subsequently, a training approach is presented that incorporates two objectives: producing relevant descriptions and maintaining visual consistency. These goals are achieved via an iterative process employing contrastive learning and a decoder objective. To ensure the integrity of the evaluation process, the training dataset and evaluation dataset are treated as separate entities to prevent data contamination. Consequently, this method yields superior performance compared to existing approaches, as validated by both theoretical and practical analyses. Experimental results across four datasets confirm that this proposed framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art automatic image description models, which are renowned for their impressive performance. Notably, when using the MS-COCO dataset, 35.95% of accurate descriptions were obtained without aid of external models, surpassing non-iterative baselines by >10%. Moreover, when using real-world datasets along with the MS-COCO dataset, this method yielded 31.39% accurate descriptions without the aid of external models. Overall, this proposed framework provides a robust foundation for developing automatic image description systems and showcases the importance of high-quality descriptions in this domain. It is available online at https://github.com/ziangun/AIEvaluate.

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. However, only areas experiencing increased population sorting and cultural drift have seen an uptick in misinformation dissemination. These findings have implications for the development and targeting of effective misinformation mitigation strategies. We propose a potential approach, based on existing research, to estimate the misinformation dissemination risk in each population segment. This method could be utilized within platforms' existing evaluation frameworks, helping to prioritize population segments for intervention. Additionally, we suggest possible intervention strategies for various scenarios, such as increasing user engagement or altering news recommendation algorithms to tackle the spread of misinformation.... The emergence of large language models like BERT has significantly facilitated the study of misinformation dissemination. However, their deployment on large-scale datasets, crucial for understanding phenomena at the population level, is often hindered by their substantial size and computational cost. We introduce a method that leverages a pre-trained language model on a downsampled subset of the large dataset to study the behavior of the remaining, unsampled population. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by analyzing the circulation of news, including misinformation, in different states, and validate its consistency with existing findings obtained using larger models. The proposed method offers a practical solution for researchers to explore the population-level phenomena on large datasets, aided by the flexibility to incorporate additional data. It is available online at https://github.com/ajtjj/bertrank.

We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called HALFADO. HALFADO uses a limited number of human judgments to effectively identify and report anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams. Implementing a precise detection system is crucial, as inaccurate detection can lead to undue attention being given to normal occurrences, thereby wasting valuable time and resources. Unfortunately, developing such a reliable system involves a significant upfront investment of time and money due to the extensive labeling required. As a result, researchers have explored the possibilities of creating good-enough detection systems using minimal human input, focusing on datasets that can learn from themselves with a little bit of guidance. Such systems have the potential to revolutionize the way we approach data validation, especially in applications like online review platforms, social media, and real-time sensor data streams. In such scenarios, a good-enough detection system can reduce the burden of validation by minimizing the number of human judgments required to validate data. Specifically, we demonstrate the capabilities of semi-supervised algorithms in modeling their own understanding of normal behavior from just a few examples, combined with a small amount of labeled data. We also show that these algorithms can detect anomalies in a real-world sensor data stream stream, an online review platform, and a scientific dataset. Finally, we highlight several directions for future research in this area. This work leverages prior research on context-free grammars, neural networks, and conformance checking, and is accompanied by a publicly accessible toolkit that includes the algorithms, data sets, and a graphical user interface. This toolkit can be found at https://r3d3.github.io/halfado/. HALFADO has the potential to make a significant impact on various applications that involve validating large amounts of high-frequency data in real-time. While there are several well-established validation methods that can be applied to these applications, they often struggle with scalability, real-time validation, or both. HALFADO overcomes these limitations, making it an invaluable resource for researchers and practitioners working with online data streams. Despite its numerous benefits, the use of HALFADO is hindered by a lack of relevant reference applications. To address this issue, we have created over 200 formal specifications and corresponding data instances, along with additional data instances that have been generated randomly to simulate real-world data streams. These data sets and formal specifications can be used as labeled and unlabeled training, testing, and validation sets for evaluating and comparing the effectiveness of anomaly detection algorithms. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. Furthermore, our findings suggest that low-frequency tone variations can be distinguished from speech duration and may offer additional robotic learning opportunities. Previous studies have demonstrated that Translation Memory (TM) can enhance Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Unlike existing approaches which rely on bilingual corpora for TM and employ source-side similarity searches, our proposed framework leverages monolingual data and retrieves memories in a cross-lingual manner. Notably, our framework offers two significant advantages: firstly, it enables vast amounts of monolingual data to be incorporated into TM; secondly, both the memory retriever and the NMT model can be jointly optimized for translation objectives. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves substantial gains in performance and outperforms TM-augmented NMT baselines even when utilizing bilingual TM. Furthermore, our model's capacity to tap into monolingual data allows it to excel in low-resource and domain adaptation scenarios. Researchers have suggested that specific patterns in the Cosmic Microwave Background, namely low-variance circles and Hawking points, could provide evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model. These patterns are predicted to originate from previous black hole mergers and evaporation events. We analyzed the Planck and WMAP data using a machine learning tool called HawkingNet, and initially found potential anomalies resembling low-variance circles and Hawking points. However, these anomalies were later removed, and upon re-examination, we found no statistically significant evidence supporting the existence of low-variance circles or Hawking points. Our analysis does indicate the presence of local non-Gaussian fluctuations in the CMB, suggesting that the real sky may differ from theoretical predictions. Moreover, we discovered a potential circular pattern at a 2 standard deviation confidence level, which warrants further investigation. In contrast, our findings contradict earlier studies claiming the detection of low-variance circles and Hawking points. Our analysis demonstrates the importance of verifying previously reported findings through re-analysis. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The comprehensive analyses cover model comparisons, in-depth dataset analyses, and practical scalability assessments, thereby providing trustworthy evidence for the efficacy of MSDCR. In particular, MSDCR achieves a notable improvement of up to 25.67% in Mean Average Precision (MAP) over the strongest baseline on one of the tested datasets. The outstanding performance of MSDCR is attributed to its ability to extract a user's complete preference profile, encompassing both specific and general aspect preferences, which is critically important for accurately recommending items across multiple sparse domains. In the future, future research within the MSDCR framework can be explored to allow for the incorporation of side information in cross-domain recommendation scenarios. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. This study's outcomes highlight the complexity of accurately analyzing MRI data in large, multi-center datasets and stress the importance of thoroughly evaluating any quality control pipeline using diverse, independently collected datasets. The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Moreover, we establish a connection between the standard ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, and the descent set of Bn. Our approach is distinct from the known relation between the length and descent set, which is established via the permutation representation of Bn. Instead, our analysis draws from the underlying geometry of the Coxeter system, which gives a more general understanding of how the order of generating sequences relates to the group's structure. We also explore the concept of ordered generating sequences within the direct product of finite classical Coxeter systems. Lastly, our results encompass the special case of Sn, which offers a generalized framework of earlier findings by R. Shwartz. We believe our approach and related discussions about the standard ordered generating sequences of Bn will contribute meaningfully to further research within this area.

The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Furthermore, a comparison between bulk and interface-based experiments revealed that while the latter provides a substantial increase in optical transition rates, it also comes with elevated levels of spectral diffusion. Nonetheless, our study provides a significant breakthrough in the evolution of silicon quantum communication devices and photon-spin interfaces, enabling the efficient, controllable, and reliable operation of such devices. This investigation is grounded in an innovative algebraic framework for generating functions and symbolic evaluation functions, allowing us to derive $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$. Our findings demonstrate intriguing connections with circulant matrices and Galois fields, while showcasing the potential for $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$ to be applied in computationally efficient contexts. Additionally, we establish a governing equation for $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$ and confirm its connection to the classical Bernoulli polynomial, enabling us to collect explicit formulas for $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$ up to $k = 6$. Moreover, we clarify the relationship between $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$ and its counterparts, including Euler and Bernoulli polynomials and hypergeometric types. The high activity levels of M dwarfs present a significant challenge for discovering exoplanets, as their stellar activity masks the signals from these celestial bodies. This problem requires an effective method for filtering out the stellar activity from the data sets, especially when searching for habitable Earth-like planets. To achieve this goal, we conducted an analysis on how to optimise the line lists used for least-squares deconvolution to minimize the dispersion in RV data sets and thereby eliminate the stellar activity noise. Our research employs optical observations of the M dwarfs EV Lac, AD Leo and DS Leo to compare two approaches to selecting line lists, one based on line properties and the other using a randomised algorithm. The results show that the latter yields a significant >50% improvement in RV RMS reduction regardless of the activity level of the star. This new approach not only enhances the sensitivity of planet detection, but also allows the construction of line lists tailored to detect the stellar rotation period. Moreover, we were able to successfully recover the signals from synthetic planets despite the presence of moderate and high activity levels. This new approach enables a critical 3sigma confidence level to be achieved in at least 30% of cases when searching for long-period planets. This research provides a crucial step in realising the full scientific potential of large spectroscopic surveys of M dwarfs. This could potentially lead to the discovery of habitable exoplanets similar to Earth, provided that sufficient field stars can be studied in depth. This goal becomes feasible thanks to the recent upgrade of APOGEE to include more than 1,600 M dwarfs in its final data set, a significant number of which will undergo follow-up radial velocity observations. This research paper proposes a pair of methods for designing a flexible and efficient data collection process in Wireless Sensor Networks, ensuring high reliability and performance. Firstly, a link quality estimation technique is utilized, enabling swift computation of link quality between nodes. Secondly, a hierarchical sector-based system is established to organize and coordinate nodes within each sector to minimize interference and improve data transmission. The effectiveness of these methods was demonstrated through a protocol, called HBCP, developed and evaluated in a simulated environment utilizing TinyOS and TelosB devices. The outcome of the evaluation revealed that HBCP can achieve very high reliability levels, particularly in large-scale networks and networks prone to bottlenecks. Furthermore, HBCP proves capable of adapting to varying application requirements and network sizes. An analytical model was also developed to explain the reliability performance of HBCP. The results of the evaluation indicated that HBCP's reliability performance can range from 96.6% in small networks to as high as 99.9% in larger networks. Additionally, HBCP's ability to adapt to different quality requirements was validated through testing of various sector sizes. The outcome of these tests revealed that HBCP can efficiently adapt to requirements as tight as 0.1% and as loose as 30%. The outcome of these tests was used to validate the proposed analytical model. The outcome of these tests revealed that the model's average deviation from the actual outcome was less than 5%. The proposed link quality estimation methods and sector-based hierarchy have significant potential for use in other ad hoc networks. The source code of HBCP has been made publicly available to facilitate further research and development. The code is accessible upon request from the paper's authors. For our task that considers context, a suitable object detector is needed.
Different object detectors exploit scene context for recognition in varying ways.
This study categorizes object detectors into 3 groups based on context usage:
one that doesn't use context by isolating the input, another that uses partial
context by isolating part of the feature map, and one that uses full context
without isolation.
Our evaluation method assesses the effect of context for each deep detector
category systematically. A specially designed dataset is created to test the
effect of context for deep detectors. The impact of removing the background
context and foreground objects on the MS COCO is also examined.
It is shown that both two-stage and single-stage object detectors can make use
of the context due to their extensive receptive field.
Thus, selecting the best object detector for a particular application depends
on the specific context in question. 

This research leads to several important conclusions that can benefit the
development of object detectors:
1. Context, whether foreground or background, can significantly aid object
recognition and thus it's essential to incorporate it into the detection
process.
2. Since most deep detectors have an extensive receptive field, they can
effectively make use of the provided context.
3. The effect of the background and foreground objects on the detection
process varies widely.

on the specific context in question.

detection process with respect to deep detectors is also included.
An evaluation metric, named context effect metric, is proposed to assess the
effect of context on the detection process.

The main objective of this paper is to investigate multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations that are given by the system of equations where $m\left(\sum^k_{j=1}\|u_j\|^2\right)\Delta u_i=\frac{f_i(x,u_1,\ldots,u_k)}{|x|^\beta}+\varepsilon h_i(x)$ holds for $i=1,\ldots,k$, within the bounded domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where $x$ contains the origin with smooth boundary, and for a certain condition $\beta\in [0,2)$; here $m$ denotes a function that belongs to Kirchhoff type, $f_i$ behave like $e^{\beta s^2}$, and there is a function $h_i\in \left(\big(H^1_0(\Omega)\big)^*,\|\cdot\|_*\right)$. By making use of a singular Trudinger-Moser inequality for a small positive value $\varepsilon$ and variational methods, we are able to establish sufficient conditions for a multiplicity of the system's solutions given the given conditions. Additionally, we are able to demonstrate the existence of a positive solution for the system of equations when $\varepsilon$ equals zero, provided that the system satisfies certain conditions, with multiple solution possibilities depending on the conditions of $f_1,\ldots,f_k$. Furthermore, we are able to prove that when $\varepsilon$ equals zero, a minimization problem related to the system's solution has multiple solution possibilities, and we are able to provide a condition under which the system's solution has a property related to symmetry. This research is an extension of the work found in a specific paper.

These vectors must adhere to either the stochastic covering property (SCP) or the strong Rayleigh property (SRP). Our findings concerning SCP measures yield new subgaussian inequalities of a bounded-difference type, surpassing earlier results by Pemantle and Peres and extending analogous outcomes for matrix-valued settings as seen in recent estimates by Aoun, Banna, and Youssef. For functions under SRP we establish stronger inequalities of a Bernstein-type for matrix-valued functions, thereby broadening earlier general bounds for linear combinations of positive definite matrices due to Kyng and Song.

Furthermore, we investigate the unique case where we condition on Bernoulli random variables with independent outcomes for their sum. In doing so, we establish sharpened estimates resulting in specifically tailored log-Sobolev inequalities, as well as Talagrand's convex distance inequality, with concentration inequalities for convex functions, polynomials, and matrix-valued functions as direct consequences. These generalised inequalities encompass results for uniform distributions over discrete slices of the cube, extensively explored in numerous studies. The current approach builds upon recent outcomes from Hermon and Salez as well as on a broader framework involving modified log-Sobolev inequalities within various contexts. A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques can make incompatible donations compatible, but they also introduce the risk of delaying necessary medications to the patient, which in turn increases the likelihood of rejection complications, including severe conditions like thrombotic microangiopathy and vascular injuries. Our research aims to develop a method that can identify the most valuable incompatible donations, taking into consideration various patient and donor factors, such as the level of incompatibility and the delay required for kidney transplants. By leveraging a multi-objective optimization approach and a kidney transplant network in the United States, we demonstrated the effectiveness of our method in identifying the most compatible donations and providing valuable insights for medical practitioners to make informed decisions. Moreover, our approach can be adapted to accommodate different criteria and priorities held by individual transplant centers. By bridging the gap between medical expertise and computational optimization, our solution can be modified to solve a wide range of donation acceptance problems, thus addressing one of the significant challenges facing the kidney transplant community today. Additionally, our study includes a critical evaluation of various acceptance strategies, including solutions proposed by the kidney transplant community, and compares their value based on the likelihood of graft survival and function. All necessary data and code are available online for replication purposes. 

Keywords: kidney transplantation, incompatible donations, acceptance strategies, multi-objective optimization, computational medicine, operations research, transplantation logistics.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems. 
An analysis of our proposed methods' performance is provided, including numerical and asymptotic results. 
Our findings can be extended to other multi-band communication systems. 
Examples of such systems include SISO-/MISO-FCBC and SISO-/MISO-FCI systems. 
As far as we know, this is the first time these optimisation problems have been studied in multi-band wideband waveforming contexts. 
The proposed methods address previous research limitations and address the core challenges of multi-band wideband waveforming. 
The derived algorithms' asymptotic performance is comparable to that of existing state-of-the-art algorithms. 
The proposed methods' efficiency is demonstrated via numerical simulations and the asymptotic analysis is validated via additional simulations. 
The impact of different communication system configurations and channel conditions on performance is also explored. 
The resulting performance insights are relevant to various high-speed communication systems, including those based on SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM technologies. 
The study of fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems enables us to obtain closed-loop wideband waveforming strategies that account for potential interference and channel knowledge at both the transmitter and receiver ends. 
The ability to formulate and solve such problems opens up avenues for further research in this context. 
The problems and methods discussed here can be expanded to consider additional factors, such as the impact of subbands on system performance and their influence on optimisation results. 
The ability to design efficient algorithms that tackle complex communication systems challenges also highlights the importance of collaborative research between mathematicians and engineers. 
The ability to model and solve such problems also highlights the potential for applications in other multi-band communication systems, such as those involving co-operative communication and/or interference. 
The methods discussed here are relevant to various high-speed communication systems, including those based on SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM technologies, and the study of such systems is ongoing.

In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This research addresses long-unmet challenges and the achieved achievements are anticipated to make meaningful inroads in addressing broader learning challenges in multiagent settings. The developed algorithms are backed by extensive numerical experiments, including results involving up to 6 players in a general game setting, with further research streams identified for further exploration. Establishing the electronic and superconducting gap structure of iron-based superconductors requires in-depth microscopic understanding. Even with extensively studied samples like (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$, there has been significant controversy over the initial structure of these materials' band structures and superconducting gap distributions. Our team resolves this by employing high-resolution and high-momentum-resolution ARPES on (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ utilizing both He lamps and laser sources. We have accurately mapped the band structure and superconducting gap distribution around the entire Brillouin zone, revealing an unusual 'flat band' feature at the center of the zone and an anisotropic s$_{+-}$-wave gap distribution across the remaining area. We further demonstrate that the proposed model distinguishes between hole and electron bands on opposite sides of the Brillouin zone center. Notably, our results are consistent across all measured bands, providing a foundation for understanding the mechanism behind superconductivity in these materials. We also establish that the superconducting gap distribution is directly proportional to the self-correlation of the electron condensation distribution, as predicted by theory. Lastly, our findings provide an opportunity for further investigation into the material's spin excitation and electron correlation properties.

We have conducted an in-depth examination of the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ using $^8$Li and $^{63}$Ni NMR in LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices with varying bilayer thickness. Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in electron correlation strength and is unaffected by LaNiO$_3$ thin film stress. Additionally, we found that the fast-recovering component is influenced by the LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness and has its spin-lattice relaxation enhanced when the volume of the recovery time is considered. This phenomenon is attributed to a mixture of two metallic states, one with fast spin-lattice relaxation and the other with slower recovery, that coexist within the same material. These two components coalesce into a single metallic state in bulk LaNiO$_3$. Our findings offer new insights into the electronic structure of LaNiO$_3$ and provide a framework for comparing other complex metals. Our research showcases the capability of LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices as a powerful tool for studying the fundamental characteristics of correlated metals.
