We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether it was covered in a hard or soft coating. Notably, the anisotropy increased dramatically when the cylinder was moved quickly through the granular layer, especially when its length was much greater than its width. This is not what we might expect, given that the drag experienced by a solid moving through a fluid typically becomes less dependent on its shape as the speed at which it moves increases. Additionally, we found that the drag experienced by the cylinder when it was moving quickly through the granular layer was highly accelerated and contained more of the grains' kinetic energy than it does when moved more slowly. This, along with other factors, causes the drag experienced by the cylinder to drop more sharply as its speed increases when it is moving more quickly. Furthermore, the speed at which the cylinder experiences the greatest drag experienced was similar to the speed at which the greatest anisotropy occurs. We propose that the drag experienced by an object moving through a granular layer is the result of a combination of friction and the breaking of bonds between the grains, and that the most anisotropic objects will be those with the longest dimensions compared to the distance between the grains. This theory is supported by computer simulations of objects moving through different types of granular materials. We also found that the long axis of an object will often become aligned with the direction of the greatest resistance it experiences as it moves through a granular layer, likely due to a combination of factors including the object becoming aligned with the path of the least resistance and the direction of the greatest anisotropy. This alignment can occur quickly enough to allow the object to adjust its path in response to changes in the direction of the greatest resistance it experiences. Additionally, we found that the drag experienced by an object moving through a granular layer will often depend on the speed at which it breaks through the 'loose surface layer' that forms on top of the granular material. Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings support the idea that outflows play a critical role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe. More specifically, we found that in regions of low to moderate star formation within our observed galaxy, outflows are in a state of stagnation, while in more actively starbursting regions, outflows are accelerated and interact with dense gas within the galaxy, giving us a deeper understanding of outflow dynamics and how they shape the formation of galaxies. Furthermore, our research suggests that outflows from galaxies with high rates of star formation can suppress the formation of low-mass stars, consistent with previous findings, and that outflows are likely the origin of heavy elements found in gas within the galaxy's central region. By comparing our observations to theoretical models, we found that outflows from galaxies with high rates of star formation can lead to the buildup of massive stars at the galaxy's center, causing outflows that contain heavy elements and low-mass star formation, resulting in the formation of low-mass, starburst galaxies throughout the universe. These galaxies can then merge with more massive, less actively starbursting galaxies, such as the Milky Way, containing heavy element enriched gas formed as a result of the absorption of these low-mass galaxies. This provides a possible explanation for the universal presence of heavy elements within galaxies across the universe. However, more observational and theoretical studies are needed to validate our findings and outflow regulations across various types of galaxies throughout the universe. Our research also highlights the importance of observing galaxies during periods of low to moderate star formation, as well as during mergers and starbursts, to gain a deeper understanding of how outflows are formed, what role they play in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, and how they contribute to the buildup of heavy elements within galaxies throughout the universe. This, in turn, can lead to a better comprehension of how galaxies, including our own, acquired their heavy element enrichment.

Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO), a technique that rapidly converges to optimal configurations by exploiting expert-provided contextual information about the system's structure. Despite its effectiveness, the SBO approach has limited adoption due to the complexity involved in building probabilistic models. To address this issue, we introduce BoAnon, an SBO framework that enables the discovery of system structures from logs, allowing for the incorporation of expert knowledge. By combining this learned structure with expert-provided performance models and dependency information, BoAnon generates a probabilistic graph model. This model accelerates the optimization process, allowing BoAnon to identify efficient configurations significantly faster than existing methods. Through evaluation of a hardware architecture search problem, BoAnon demonstrates a notable improvement in energy-latency objectives, achieving a 5-7x factor improvement over the default architecture. The innovative approach of BoAnon, based on its contextual structure learning pipeline, now makes SBO applicable to various computer system optimization challenges. This technique is open to further research, with potential areas of enhancement identified, such as the incorporation of multiple objectives within the performance models. Furthermore, BoAnon's context structure learning has implications for other design spaces, and the framework's code is openly available at https://github.com/parrot-ai/boanonsbo.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. Yet, initial geometry's influence on $v_2$ and $v_3$ diverged at higher centrality levels, with $v_3$ exhibiting sensitivity to initial conditions beyond that of $v_2$. This divergence is attributed to initial triaxial geometry found in central, high-collision-energy collisions. This study provides a deeper understanding of the connections and distinctions between triangular and elliptical flow within heavy ion collisions.

Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable for single-machine operations.  To address these challenges, our proposed DistQualityAssessment is an open-source, cluster-enabled implementation designed for comprehensive quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets, leveraging the processing capabilities of Apache Spark to distribute quality metrics computation.  This innovative, distributed in-memory approach allows for flexible metric extension via a provided quality assessment pattern and, through seamless integration with the SANSA framework, has been successfully applied in at least three external use cases, showcasing its superiority over existing methodologies. When working with data generated by random processes, an appropriate model is often employed for subsequent statistical analysis, but the standard method of maximum likelihood estimation is vulnerable to model imperfections and data contamination. As alternative methods without assumptions about a specific model typically lose efficiency, this paper introduces a robust procedure for estimating parameters in discrete data sets based on a well-known distance measure. Specifically, this method defines and evaluates minimum density power divergence estimators for independent increments and Markov processes, proving its consistency and providing distributional results in the context of dependent stochastic processes, ultimately showing the method's advantages in comparison to traditional maximum likelihood estimation for common processes like Poisson processes, Brownian motion with a drift and autoregressive models. The method's performance is also demonstrated through simulations of AR models and time series. Furthermore, the paper addresses the challenging issue of specifying a model for complex data sets by suggesting the use of a two-step procedure: first estimating process parameters independently for different components or different groups of data, and then using these estimates as starting points for further analysis within a more comprehensive model. The paper's methods are applied to real data sets involving cancer incidence rates and Internet traffic. The implementation of the proposed methods is available in R. The paper also raises thought-provoking questions about the role of modeling in the analysis of complex data sets. The results presented are the basis for an ongoing research project. The authors invite contributions to this research project. The project's code is available at https://github.com/krzysztofbreuls/robust-processes. The project's PDF report can be found at https://krzysztofbreuls.github.io/files/2019-12-20-robust-processes.pdf. This study presents temperature maps for electrons within one kiloparsec of three high-brightness Seyfert galaxies. The findings from Gemini's GMOS-IFU data, acquired at a spatial resolution of 110-280 parsecs, reveal temperature variations between 8000 to >30000 Kelvin. We discovered temperature ranges in these galaxies are significantly influenced by gas outflows producing shocks, particularly in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348, while photoionization processes fit the results for Mrk 607. The orientation of these shocks in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348 appears to be perpendicular to the axis of ionization, suggesting the potential for shock ionization to be observed more easily when obscured by a dusty torus. This implies that narrow ionization cones can coexist with wider shock patterns. The ability to produce such shock patterns likely depends on the mass loss rate of the galaxy's supermassive black hole, which can help clarify the relationship between the central black hole and its host galaxy. This may also influence the shape of the galaxy's narrow ionization cone. The variation in electron temperatures observed in these galaxies highlights the importance of resolving ionization regions on a parsec-scale level. This could involve using optical recoils as an indicator to study the interactions between black holes and their host galaxies. This research demonstrates the capability of using optical recoils as an analyzer of black hole mergers and their interactions with their surroundings, which could provide unique insights into the properties of these events. This study's innovative analysis of electron temperatures maps a new path for studying the relationships between black holes and their host galaxies, which could be expanded to other galaxies through better data resolution. This potential growth is illustrated by Mrk 79, which shows a temperature pattern resembling that produced by an accretion disk with a white dwarf-like component. This finding suggests that high-brightness Seyfert galaxies can serve as a bridge between studying the physics of white dwarfs and studying the relationships between black holes and their host galaxies. This study's findings also imply that wide shock patterns in ionization regions of active galaxies can provide valuable information about the mass loss rates of black holes and their interactions with their surrounding galaxies. This research's analysis of electron temperatures maps a new way of studying black hole mergers, particularly those with neutron star or black hole components, which often produce distinctive shock patterns visible from a great distance. As IoT systems shift towards Edge computing and less reliable infrastructure closer to users, the complex environments of IoT pose significant challenges for software developers when testing their applications. Although various testing tools are available for IoT, several issues persist, such as the absence of advanced features for logical dependencies, fault injection, and multi-platform testing. To address these shortcomings, we have developed Frisbee, a framework for the automated testing of IoT applications. By utilizing Kubernetes and virtual testbeds, Frisbee speeds up the testing process by streamlining the setup of distributed virtual environments and enabling complex 'what-if' scenario simulations. Furthermore, Frisbee includes an innovative approach called TaintProp, which enables the analysis of proprietary protocols employed by IoT devices through a novel application of a method called SMT. We have successfully applied Frisbee to test the reliability of an open-source Home Automation system and have made its source code freely accessible on GitHub. We have also contributed a new, publicly accessible IoT testing benchmark, called BBQ, to facilitate collaborative innovation in this area. BBQ comprises a set of standardized protocols, software components, and functional testing scenarios that can be used to compare the performance and effectiveness of various IoT testing solutions. We have already used BBQ to conduct a comparative analysis of Frisbee's performance against two other popular IoT testing tools, Kite and TOAST. Our study has shown that Frisbee outperforms these tools by a margin of at least 2-3 times in terms of performance and efficiency. We are committed to enhancing BBQ as a benchmark through regular contributions and encourage other researchers and developers to join us in this endeavor. We have already made initial improvements to Frisbee's performance, supported by BBQ, and have made its source code freely available on GitHub at the URL mentioned above. We are confident that Frisbee has the potential to become a leading open-source framework for the automated testing of IoT applications. We look forward to collaborating with software developers and researchers who can contribute to its growth and help us address its current limitations. The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely neutral B meson mixing and CP violation, as well as in rare electroweak processes occurring in suppressed B-meson decays. This study concentrates on recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration, encompassing evaluations of rare occurrences like $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays and the determination of CP-violating processes in $B^0_s \to J/\psi\phi$. Additionally, it compares these results with other relevant experiments, encompassing those carried out at the BaBar, Belle, and LHCb experiments under operation at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN). Furthermore, it places these findings within the context of various theoretical constraints and predictions derived from lattice QCD computations, as well as on the prospects for furthering our understanding of these phenomena as a part of future LHC runs with increased luminosity, specifically with the LHC at 14 TeV and an cumulative luminosity exposure of 300 inverse femtobarns available for study. As a result of such research, with its scheduled completion around 2040, there will be detailed investigations of several aspects, including but not limited to, the precise validation of certain theoretical predictions, such as but not limited to, top-quark mediated corrections and charm-quark contributions, as well as further exploration of the $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ decay and potentially even rare leptonic decays of both the $B^0$ and $B^0_s$ mesons. Consequently, with these results at hand, we will be in a better position to deepen our understanding of the matter-antimatter asymmetry present in the universe. 

This analysis will be presented with the latest findings available from March 2021 and will encompass various recent research results available in scientific literature up to March 2021.

The creation of realistic traffic scenarios through automation is the primary focus.
Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions, ultimately resulting in a gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones. As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. To mitigate this limitation, we propose SceneGen, a traffic scenario model that utilizes neural networks to bypass reliance on predefined rules. SceneGen is particularly adept at inserting a variety of virtual characters into the environment and accurately modeling their sizes, positions, and speeds. Through extensive testing on two large datasets derived from real-world traffic, we demonstrate SceneGen's capacity to accurately replicate the distributions seen in real traffic scenarios. Furthermore, when combined with sensor simulation, SceneGen is shown to be an effective means of training perception models capable of performing well in real traffic scenarios. The trained models achieve high accuracy levels on multiple evaluation metrics, including a notable 99.5% accuracy in detecting virtual characters of varying sizes. Ultimately, SceneGen represents a significant advancement in traffic scenario modeling, bridging the gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones and enabling the reliable use of simulation-based training methods for self-driving vehicles. This methodology is now widely adopted as the industry standard.

On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation. We establish the relationship between these periodic measures and the Kac-Wilson susceptibility, obtaining an explicit formula for the latter as a sum of justifiable roots for a related polynomial. We further demonstrate that the largest justifiable root corresponds to a unique periodic measure, defining a special two-state translation dynamic on the Ising lattice that can be used to bound the original dynamic's mixing time. This new dynamic outperforms the current best-known bound for the mixing time of the Ising model on a Cayley tree from [Diaz, Krivelevich, and Tsfasil, 2019]. Additionally, we show that this new dynamic achieves its fastest mixing time at a temperature that is critically high. Furthermore, we establish that the algebraic rotation number of the two-state translation dynamic is rational and provide an explicit formula for it. We also prove that the mixing time of this new dynamic is precisely equal to its rotation number multiplied by the dynamical system's period. This represents the first confirmed instance of a dynamically defined, strictly periodic mixing time on an infinitely extended, non-transient graph. This development paves the way for further exploration of dynamically defined mixing times and their connection to matrix semigroups. We conclude by discussing potential applications to other statistical mechanics models. We determine the new periodic measures to be exactly the invariant measures of a subsemigroup within the full symmetry group of the Ising lattice, generated by the product of any two adjacent dynamic shifts. We establish the outcome of any interaction between the dynamic and an independent, randomly chosen edge walk on the Cayley tree. We precisely define the dynamic for the one-dimensional Heisenberg chain and obtain an explicit formula for the algebraic rotation number of this dynamic. We outline how this new dynamic may lead to fresh bounds on the mixing time of this model. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Furthermore, by incorporating this new iteration within the context of conservative and admissible element-based formulations, it provides a framework encompassing element-wise preservation and consistent approximations. Specifically, the proposed approach is applied to an elastic mechanics problem and a Navier-Stokes problem, involving both structured and unstructured meshes – with the latter showcasing the success of this approach in preventing artificial compression for fluids. All numerical simulations were implemented using the $FiniteElasticity$ and $FiniteFluids$ packages on GitHub, with further details on algorithmic theory and numerical results available in this repository. The algorithmic theory is also validated through comparison with totalistic relaxation schemes. Additionally, this research introduces the concept of admissible iterative methods as a superclass for all element-wise preservation algorithms, and explores potential extensions to multi-dimensional systems and rigorous analysis. Ultimately, this work provides a foundation for further investigation into admissible iterative methods within the context of computational continuum mechanics. Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects, which isn't aligned with either human vision or the disparities seen in stereo images. As a result, the task of three-dimensional detection has been slow to progress. To accelerate progress and make autonomous vehicles safer, we've created a new evaluation benchmark called Best-Far-Scene, which includes a method for accurately annotating distant objects and introduces metric learning algorithms tailored to far-field detection challenges. We've also designed a novel evaluation protocol that compares performance at different distance ranges. To give itself the best possible chance of success, one of the three autonomous methods that took part in the evaluation used the benchmark's training data, which was created by combining the datasets captured by seven different lidar sensors in urban and highway scenes. The results show that even the best autonomous methods struggle with far-field detection, with an average mean aperture error of just 6.2 degrees up to 50m and 14.4 degrees up to 70m. To accelerate the development of safer autonomous vehicles, we've made Best-Far-Scene and the methods it uses to annotate distant objects open-source, along with the code for the two metric learning algorithms that it includes. We also plan to expand the dataset to include more varied highway scenes. The paper that outlines these methods and results has been accepted for presentation at CVPR 2020. Chemical reactions can be comprehensively understood through a primary analytical tool called the potential energy surface (PES) which maps the relationships between molecular nuclei and their energy levels. Nevertheless, this tool becomes impractically challenging to utilize because identifying a substantial number of ground states across various configurations of molecular nuclei is extremely difficult. Moreover, there is significant variability in the methods used to create PESs at the nuclear and chemical levels. To address this issue, researchers have proposed the use of entropy-weighted calculations to generate PESs, especially for complex nuclear systems and molecules. These proposed methods involve generating adiabatic surfaces under constraints, adjusting the spin and alignment of excited states, and employing time-dependent density functional theory. Examples of such applications include studies of diatomic molecular systems consisting of heavy elements, complex nuclear systems consisting of three or more particles, and catenated molecular systems consisting of multiple atomic nuclei linked end-to-end. Researchers have particularly highlighted the significance of global adiabatic surfaces in understanding nuclear reactions and predicting reaction paths. Additionally, they have emphasized the potential of adiabatic surfaces to clarify the dynamics of nuclear inductions and excitations encountered during deepening entering states and returning states. Moreover, with the development of new generation four-dimensional microscopes, researchers anticipate the direct observation of rotating molecular systems consisting of three or more particles. Consequently, there is a growing need to investigate adiabatic surfaces of these complex molecular systems consisting of multiple atomic nuclei. Researchers have initially explored such studies at the chemical level with research on the molecular systems consisting of two atomic nuclei, specifically studying diatomic molecular systems consisting of heavy elements such as actinides and superheavy elements and complex nuclear systems consisting of three or more particles such as polyatomic molecules consisting of carbon, oxygen, and other elements. Nevertheless, there is significant variability in the methods used to create PESs at the nuclear and chemical levels. While nuclear PESs are created through the application of constraint calculations and rotating finite amplitude ground states, researchers have utilized a range of methods including density functional theory and strong coupling theory to create PESs at the chemical level. In this review, we provide an overview of the methods used to create adiabatic surfaces and associated reaction paths in nuclear and chemical systems, with a focus on complex molecular systems consisting of multiple atomic nuclei. We primarily highlight research on diatomic molecular systems consisting of heavy elements, complex nuclear systems consisting of three or four particles and catenated molecular systems consisting of two, three, or four atomic nuclei.

Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. Formulas for point-wise energy functions can facilitate the creation of real-world training datasets, allowing for semi-supervised training across all points within a given scene. Such formulations have been developed for synthetic datasets, but they fail to account for the discrepancies that arise when adapting them to real-world data. On the other hand, developing robust algorithms for solving these point-wise energy functions is also crucial. A novel method called SelfSupFlow is introduced, involving a end-to-end neural network that uses a bilateral refinement module to enhance motion vector estimation. This new method is designed to work in conjunction with the widely used geometric consistency constraint, resulting in an adaptable system suitable for various scene flow datasets, including the challenging KITTI2012 dataset that features multiple objects in complex global motions. Notably, this method demonstrates its strength in accurately estimating mid-flight trajectories in such scenarios. To leverage its potential, a new real-world dataset called Dynamic3D is created, comprising annotated LiDAR datasets from various global movements and complex environments, along with a dataset that includes only partial trajectories. This dataset serves as the perfect testing ground for the newly developed point-wise energy function formulas, which can now be adapted to real-world data thanks to the training of the SelfSupFlow algorithm. Specifically, three key contributions are made: (1) a study on scene flow estimation is conducted using the SelfSupFlow algorithm, which is used to demonstrate the efficacy of a particular bilateral refinement module across multiple datasets; (2) a set of formulas for point-wise energy functions is explored and adapted for use with real-world data, resulting in improved results when compared to previous formulations; (3) the creation of the Dynamic3D dataset, which includes datasets from various global movements and complex environments, along with only partial trajectories, facilitating the development of robust algorithms for scene flow estimation. Ultimately, this research is aimed at paving the way for the development of scene flow datasets that can be used for real-world training purposes. Alongside the presentation of this novel method, a study on scene flow estimation is conducted, along with an extensive evaluation of the SelfSupFlow algorithm on multiple datasets, showcasing its versatility and robustness. A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. This research also introduces the spider graph, a new infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs, tailored to have a specific interaction with the papillon family. This interaction enables the creation of infinite families of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs from the papillon graphs. This phenomenon holds the potential to lead to significant breakthroughs in future research. Our work may be a foundation for extensive investigations into the fields of even-2-factorability, papillon graphs, spider graphs and their combinations, and the related properties of cubic graphs. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, low-cost hardware and software components, Timeloops features a simple, efficient design comprising just over 300 lines of code per language implementation, with notable benefits including: (a) programs with reliable security can be quickly developed, (b) existing programs requiring system call filtering support only need to be modified slightly, and (c) a program's secure functionality cannot be subverted even when it encounters exceptions or security vulnerabilities and is subject to malicious data input. Timeloops can also prevent data leaks resulting from system calls like read and write. Furthermore, Timeloops introduces a novel technique called the'monotonic stack' for automatically analyzing and limiting the program access to the system calls it should be allowed to make, with a range of applications, including the creation of firewalls for operating systems and the development of secure languages. Ultimately, Timeloops demonstrates the feasibility and effectiveness of combining program verification techniques with program development tools to ensure the security of programs, particularly those with dynamic behavior, through a process dubbed'verified, exception-safe' development. This approach is now being adopted by companies like Google, Amazon, and Microsoft. To facilitate further research and development, the Timeloops project includes fully functional implementations of system call filters for Python, PHP, and JavaScript, with all source code and program examples freely accessible at https://timeloops.cs.berkeley.edu/. In addition, the project includes a range of system call APIs, program verification tools, and a tutorial on how to design and implement your own secure programs using this technology. The project also includes two real-world use cases, with one of these use cases representing a widely used web application. The project is now being maintained on GitHub at https://github.com/google/timeloops. This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes an interior degenerate diffusion component. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system in its entirety, and subsequently deriving a relevant observability inequality, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a localized control action capable of driving the population towards extinction within a finite time frame. Our approach builds upon a recent breakthrough by Frassino and Raiata, which enables us to extend the concept of null controllability to more complex systems involving interior degenerate diffusion. We also obtain an optimal localization measure for the control via a mathematical optimization problem. Notably, our results can be applied to a specific population growth model, which involves a logistic type reaction term and was first analyzed by Bouhadoile in 1970. His analysis revealed an interesting phenomenon, which is characterized by the presence of a stable equilibrium state and a destabilized eigenmode when the equilibrium state is locally asymptotically stable. By demonstrating the exact controllability of this system, our study provides a theoretical framework that can be employed to develop a feedback control system, which can be derived through a standard optimization approach. However, such an approach would result in a nonlinear state-constrained optimal control problem, which is notoriously challenging to solve computationally. Nonetheless, our results can be used as a stepping stone for exploring more advanced numerical methods, which can efficiently solve complex nonlinear optimal control problems. Ultimately, our work has the potential to contribute to a better understanding of how adaptive management strategies, which account for spatial heterogeneities and diffusion processes, can be designed and analyzed computationally. To this end, our research involves a multidisciplinary investigation, which combines mathematical analysis, computational modeling, and applied analysis to address fundamental questions of controllability, observability, and identifiability in complex systems. Although our specific findings are focused on a population growth model, our study has broader implications for the analysis and design of adaptive management policies in the presence of spatially distributed processes and diffusion. Moreover, our results can be extended to other partial differential equation systems, which exhibit similar characteristics. Lastly, our research has the potential to lay the groundwork for more comprehensive investigations of adaptive management systems, which can handle multiple state variables and nonlinear interactions, thus making it suitable for a wide range of scientific and engineering applications.

The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in pivotal situations. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. To address this need, we propose a novel way to describe the game's state and a batch reinforcement learning method to train a strategic policy network. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields. Ultimately, both single-frequency and multi-frequency joint inversion methods are proposed to combine the advantages of different frequency wavefield reconstructions and models, and the results from numerical experiments conducted on synthetic and real data demonstrate the effectiveness of these new methods.  The implementation of these methods is also made publicly available under the PyGWITools repository on GitHub.  Future research directions are also discussed, including building an ES-WRI method that combines the advantages of both methods, and challenging the storage requirement challenge directly.

We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary X-ray pulsar IGR J19294+1816 during its Type-I outburst in October 2019. Timing and spectral data from the decline phase of the outburst revealed the spin period to be 12.485 seconds, with significant spectral features. A Quasi Periodic Oscillation was observed at a frequency of 0.032 Hz and an RMS amplitude of 18%. Our joint spectral analysis detected Cyclotron Resonant Scattering and an Iron emission line at 42.7 keV and 6.4 keV respectively, further highlighting the complex nature of this intermediate spin pulsar's behavior during its 2019 outburst. Comparison with historical data shows the pulsar's spin period is increasing at a rate of 1.6 x 10^-3 seconds per day. Additionally, a phase residual analysis revealed the pulsar's orbital period to be 19.962 days, with a significant decrease in its orbital decay rate at 1.8 x 10^-12 days. These findings enhance our understanding of the pulsar's behavior and its binary system's characteristics. Moreover, they emphasize the significance of regular space-based monitoring to capture the full spectral and temporal spectrum of high-energy transient sources. Lastly, the detection of an Alfv\'en wave-like phenomenon in the pulsar's light curve during this outburst provides valuable insights into the study of transient X-ray pulsars and their possible connections to other transient sources observed during outbursts of Advection-Driven X-ray Transients. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain evaluation tasks prove more manageable for certain sophisticated architectures to grasp than others and, interestingly, that RNN-based architectures outperform Transformer models in these evaluation tasks despite underperforming them in standard text generation metrics. This suggests that encoder representations holding important contextual information may become difficult for some models to capture due to their focus on maintaining and generating contextual information rather than being forced to produce meaningful text during evaluation. Additionally, it can offer practical guidance in tuning these models for improved performance.

Q-ball studies in a single symmetry theory are common, yet the field can be more expansive, allowing for the examination of theories featuring multiple symmetries in a more general context. In this paper, we explore this broader scenario, analyzing both the standard and advanced limits within this theoretical framework and identifying essential conditions for existence in the more complex scenarios. Additionally, we identify a previously unexamined Q-ball state, which we term 'cored', and demonstrate that it could possess stability under specific conditions; a more detailed investigation into its implications will be addressed in a subsequent study. 

In the context of a complex Q-ball theory, we identify both the necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of both standard and advanced Q-balls, and further establish that these conditions are consistent with current experimental limitations as illustrated in Figure 1. Our research to identify Q-ball states within a complex theory framework was conducted within the scope of a larger investigation into its cosmological implications, specifically within the scalar-driven inflation model. 

It is worth noting that, to facilitate the understanding of complex Q-ball dynamics, we developed the Vector Field Effective Theory (VET), allowing for the analysis of Q-ball studies through the effective action of a complex scalar field. Using VET, we defined the effective potential of a complex scalar field at its minimum energy state, derived both the standard and advanced Q-ball masses, and established the viability criteria for both. 

Furthermore, our research involving the effective action of a complex scalar field highlighted the significance of the 'flat direction' in Q-ball studies, an aspect that has been misinterpreted in earlier studies. We also established that the mass of a standard Q-ball is directly proportional to the symmetry breaking scale of the theory, whereas the mass of an advanced Q-ball is influenced by both the symmetry breaking scale and the potential energy of the flat direction. 

In line with our research within the Vector Field Effective Theory (VET), we developed a single-step formula to calculate the mass of both standard and advanced Q-balls, which can be further extended to cover those found within a complex theory framework, such as the 'cored' Q-ball state. Our study provides a foundation for a deeper investigation into the implications of 'cored' Q-balls within the scalar-driven inflation model. 

In addition, our research involving the Vector Field Effective Theory (VET) enabled us to establish that the creation of standard and advanced Q-balls can occur through the gravitational process known as the collapse of massive stars, which results in the formation of a black hole

This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, or whose
status remains unclear. These difficult cases are scrutinized, along with
suggested categorizations, to better understand the challenges faced. We
conclude that pre-trained contextual language models frequently confuse shifts
in word meanings and contextual fluctuations due to their reliance on
distributional properties. Moreover, they often blend the grammatical and
semantics components of words, differing from issues seen with static
embeddings. We propose multiple possible avenues for resolving these issues
in the future. Additionally, we introduce an additional corpus with
annotated semantic shift data for the English vocabulary from 1990 to 2005,
alongside the previously established corpus covering the period 1952-1990. 
This expanded corpus provides 1,115 newly validated semantic shift instances. 
The combined corpus now comprises 1,517 validated instances of language
change, along with the levels of change or uncertainty for each word. 
The corpus is accessible via the Semantic Shifts Corpus webpage. 
Our top-performing ensemble method, comprising a contextualized language model
and a static word2vec model, achieves the best previous study's accuracy level
of 68% and the previously mentioned challenging case analysis accuracy of
76%.

A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms governing
the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system. Moreover, we propose that this approach to studying
retinal IKNM can serve as a model for analyzing the dynamics of other IKNM-employing neuroepithelia. Additionally, we
observe that the diffusion rate of nuclei in the zebrafish retina corresponds with the speed of retinal neuroblast production. 
This finding leads us to argue that the interaction between the pace of cell fate commitment and the rate of cell migration
may play a significant role in the development of various neural tissues. We conclude by discussing how our discoveries
in this zebrafish retina system relate to broader, biologically relevant themes and open research questions. 
This work is represented by an accompanying video, which showcases our imaging results and related analysis at multiple scales, from the broader retinal perspective to the closer, migrating cell nucleus perspective. This study offers a comprehensive, dynamically imaged exploration of the retinal IKNM system and its behavior during initial development.

In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be reconstructed from coded and noisy versions. Real-world codes, such as those used in video (e.g. H.264) and sensor arrays, exhibit non-trivial structures that complicate this process. This paper addresses the challenge of developing highly codeword-readable patterns, suitable for such applications, by exploring code constructions that balance two key properties: ease of image reconstruction from coded data and minimal overlap with each other. Specifically, three code patterns are investigated: those with specific symmetry groups, used in video compression, and two new approaches: one based on algebraic theory and the other on rotational symmetries. Experiments validate our codes' superiority over currently used codes and the important role of code structure in the reconstruction process. Moreover, this work provides the foundation for further research into real-world code applications. the concept of an "exceptional" van Hove singularity, where a strong 
electron interaction fragments a continuous Fermi surface into disjoint regions. 
We identify this singularity with the merging of two separated Fermi surface 
segments, and demonstrate that it is close to a van Hove singularity, 
reaching it by adjusting a material parameter affecting its dispersion. 
We assert that, in the broader family of cuprate materials, 
the onset of pseudogap is attainable solely through inducing this exceptional 
van Hove singularity, and that this results in a distinct Lifshitz 
transition distinguished by heightened heat capacity and a nematic susceptibility, 
both consistent with empirical observations. 
We further illustrate that this concept may be applicable to other electron 
systems with complex Fermi surfaces, such as the heavy-fermion material CeCu$_2$Si$_2$. 
In these cases, intense electron interactions may give rise to the prevalence of 
van Hove singularities, creating multiple critical points that can be crossed 
by adjusting the material's volume, allowing for a continuous variation of 
its physical properties without a phase transition. 
Our study emphasizes that the interplay between electron interactions and 
band structure topology holds significant implications for the behavior of these 
materials, and that a thorough understanding of this relationship is 
essential for pinpointing the underlying physics governing their transition 
states.

and we propose that the onset of pseudogap in cuprates can be described 
exclusively through the induction of this exceptional van Hove singularity.

experimentally identifying this singularity in laboratory measurements.

This paper details a specialized apparatus built for use in Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory in Hong Kong. The laboratory is uniquely situated to study spallation neutrons produced by cosmic-ray muons with 611 meters of water equivalent in depth. The apparatus consists of six layers of horizontal plastic-scintillator detectors that pinpoint the direction and location of incoming muons. However, its all-star surveys sometimes produce false positives among the detected exoplanets, which can be dispelled through follow-up radial velocity surveys from the ground. This study assesses the consistency between radial velocity measurements derived from spectral analyses and the signals detected by TESS, which can validate the existence of these newly discovered exoplanets. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in three asteroids and found that the YORP acceleration in all ten detected cases was positive, accelerating their rotations. Furthermore, incorporating solar precession into their algorithm revealed evidence of this phenomenon in the data obtained for Geographos, which may be a crucial feature that needs further explanation. Ultimately, the longest duration observed for the YORP acceleration in this study was approximately six and a half years, which may indicate that the YORP effect has acceleration limits due to its own consequences on an asteroid's shape and rotation. While more research is needed to validate these findings, they contribute significantly to the understanding of how the YORP effect shapes the rotational dynamics of small asteroids. Political discussions on social media generate a high volume of online content, with people expressing varying opinions through posts that often receive low levels of engagement due to the anonymity of the internet. Despite this challenge, social media platforms remain a rich source of potentially influential information. To tackle this issue, we propose a method to enhance the visibility of unpopular online posts by identifying under-posted comments related to political discussions on Twitter. Our proposed algorithm leverages a two-staged approach to tackle this problem. Initially, we develop a method to pinpoint unengaged comments that have a strong chance of becoming popular, based on their similarity to already popular posts. Next, we utilize a collaborative filtering technique to identify similar user behavior and rank the comments accordingly. Our results show that our algorithm outperforms existing methods, with the top-ranked comment from our results matching the top-ranked comment from the baseline method over 70% of the time. Furthermore, we observe that the majority of the top-ranked comments identified by our algorithm have indeed gained more attention on Twitter. Additionally, we explore the implementation feasibility of this algorithm with real-world data, utilizing Twitter's API to retrieve additional data related to the top-ranked comments. Our findings provide valuable insights into developing low-latency, real-time recommendation systems for enhancing the visibility of online content on social media platforms. Moreover, our study offers a unique perspective on analyzing unseen content on Twitter, with our proposed algorithm available as an open-source project on GitHub. Lastly, our investigation raises thought-provoking questions on further optimizing search engines to increase the visibility of less popular online content.

This finding is accompanied by a demonstration that such a subgroup, whose action is not highly transitive, may indeed be topologically compact. Furthermore, we establish that the compact-open topology's inherited subgroups share compactness properties with those of point-wise convergence. A key component of our proof involves establishing an isomorphism between a certain group of continuous functions and a new group of boundary-fixing homeomorphisms, which enables us to leverage compactness within the surface's interior to prove our desired results. This construction leverages the surface's ability to be cut into rectangles, along with properties of the free group on two generators. Precise stellar characteristics are vital for both astrophysics and exoplanetary science, particularly when studying M-dwarfs. Researchers have developed numerous empirical relations that can utilize easily accessible observations to estimate stellar properties. However, these relations are often presented in a non-linear format, which is not suitable for Bayesian modeling. A novel Bayesian approach has been developed to consistently and simultaneously apply multiple empirical calibrations to accurately determine the mass, luminosity, size, and surface temperature of a typical M-dwarf. This new framework incorporates a mass-radius relation for M-dwarfs with a scatter of just 3.1% at fixed mass. The researchers also established the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Sample (MUSS), and applied their method to obtain consistent stellar parameters for these low-mass stars. The MUSS targets are of interest primarily due to their potential to host exoplanets or serve as benchmarks for stellar activity across different wavelengths. Using the field MUSS stars, a mass range for low-mass stars in the solar neighborhood was defined through a process involving Gaussian Process regression. The resulting data show a distinct feature - a turn-on point - around 0.4 to 0.5 solar masses, which indicates a sharp increase in the cooling rate of M-dwarfs. No evidence was found for a significant scattering or scattering scatter in the mass range above 0.5 solar masses. Rather, the ratio of radius to mass for M-dwarfs follows a smooth, linear curve across the range from 0.1 to 0.5 solar masses. Above this point, the ratio increases more steeply with mass. The researchers anticipate that this new method and the MUSS sample will be valuable resources for interpreting future observations with spectrographs like ESPS and TESS. The study is also expected to lay the groundwork for a revised mass range for low-mass stars in the solar neighborhood, one that is defined empirically rather than arbitrarily. The researchers hope that their framework will be used widely and consider it a important step towards developing a robust, theoretically-based mass range that is based directly on the properties of the stars themselves. Confining modes at the edge, known as line waves, can propagate on the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic interfaces that maintain mirror symmetry properties.
Studies have previously analyzed line waves in theory and in practice, revealing their occurrence at both microwave and terahertz frequencies.
It has also been demonstrated that these waves can occur when there's a sudden change from a negative to a positive symmetric resistance and uniform surface reactance present.
Characteristics of line waves include highly confineable mode propagation, polarization that remains constant, and quadratic relationships between edge wave velocity and size and surface impedance.
A new study proposes a graphene patch structure, showing that the line waves produced can operate in the x-band frequency range.
In addition, the proposed design demonstrates the capability to tune the line waves' velocity in the x-band frequency range and the ability to control the direction of line waves using negative refractive index.
The proposed structure also exhibits the ability to tune the line waves' velocity in the x-band frequency range and change the direction of line waves using negative refractive index.
This could lead to the development of very small, tunable devices like filters, antennas, and sensors. 
Both theoretical and practical investigations have verified the existence of line waves on the proposed structure, confirming its capability to function as a reliable platform for investigating the phenomena of line waves.

Our investigation aims to quantify the increased difficulty of answering complex database queries that incorporate self-joins, including how self-joins affect the time and space required to enumerate results. To assess this, we developed a framework to measure the complexity of conjunctive queries based on the number of self-joins and the level of nesting, as well as a framework to measure the complexity of query answers based on the number of possible solutions and the time and space required to find them. Our study specifically examines three types of recursive queries: tree-like queries, circular queries, and queries with nested recursion. Our findings indicate that even simple recursive queries can have computationally expensive answers, while more complex queries can have answers that can be computed efficiently using an optimized enumeration method. This research has the potential to contribute to several fields by improving query optimization techniques, enabling the efficient processing of queries in relational databases, and addressing the challenges associated with the increasing size and complexity of modern databases. Additionally, our techniques may be applied to solve problems of computational saturation and space-time tradeoffs that arise in the enumeration of query answers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, a more nuanced concept related to continuous functions is explored and related to its computable counterpart. This research provides a foundation for studying functions with respect to their ability to efficiently process infinite strings with an order, and its principles can be adapted for application in other contexts involving sequences along a one-dimensional timeline. A key feature of these models is then shown to be equivalent to a concept called strong continuity, a more rigorous version of continuous functions. To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control. We've demonstrated the efficacy of our method by applying it to a scenario involving the coexistence of multiple agents subject to worst-case interactions and by comparing it to alternative methods. Our algorithm forms the basis for an efficient implementation of a popular multi-agent motion planning algorithm, allowing it to handle significantly more agents than previously possible. We've verified the performance of our method with several test scenarios, including a large-scale simulation involving over 500 agents. Our implementation is now available online as an open-source tool.

Multi-Layer Perceptrons are particularly effective at generating accurate
low-dimensional representations of data, such as images, shapes and light
fields. Despite advancements using periodic activations or positional
encodings, they have historically been tailored to process a single signal
and sacrificed some degree of generality. We introduce an innovative new
approach to representation learning that not only generalizes well to multiple
signals, but outperforms the competition in fidelity. We utilize a unique
two-part neural network design, where a synthesis network produces the output
given a point in space (like a pixel's position) and a modulation network uses a
given input's specific latent code to control the activation of this synthesis
network's periodic elements. We also develop an innovative local-function
approach to representation. It divides the input domain into uniform squares,
and each one has a unique encoded code. Then, at inference time, a highly
realistic representation of the given input is produced by either learning
or inferring the entire codebook. Our method produces general representations
for data, such as videos, shapes and images, outperforming previous methods.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs. Furthermore, our extended theory of quantized relational Hoare logic enables the derivation of quantized Hoare triples which can be used to verify the performance of programs relative to one another, expressed as quantized relational specifications. We have successfully applied our methodology to a range of case studies, including the evaluation of (1) the overall performance of programs across different inputs, (2) the efficient execution of programs with respect to various performance metrics, and (3) the comparison of programs implemented through different circuits. Moreover, our approach has enabled us to identify instances of suboptimal program performance, as identified through the verification of quantized relational specifications. We have further developed a novel tool, called QRL-Expectation-Checker, tailored to checking the expectations incorporated into quantized relational Hoare triples. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach by successfully verifying the efficient execution of multiple quantum programs using this tool. Our research is poised to contribute significantly to the development of efficient quantum compilers, particularly in ensuring that compiled programs operate efficiently relative to their inputs and outputs. Additionally, our approach has implications for the verification of other relational Hoare logic theories, enabling the verification of programs' performance relative to their inputs and outputs. We have publicly released our extension of the quantum relational Hoare logic theory, along with the associated QRL-Expectation-Checker tool, on GitHub, along with the source code for our case studies, including the efficient execution of the Shor's algorithm and the quantum simulator for Grover's algorithm. The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. This effect should be given considerable consideration in traditional epidemiological modeling, which requires reliable estimates of critical parameters such as $R_0$. We illustrate in this report that the effective $R_0$ value in scenarios featuring a super-spreader event is significantly elevated, with an order of magnitude equivalent to several hundred, which is indicative of a very brief period of rapid transmission during such events. A simulation involving a well-mixed space aligns with these findings and contributes valuable insights to modeling infectious transmission dynamics within enclosed environments. These environments diverge significantly from the parameters typically modeled in a standard SIR scenario. The proposed model also yields expressions that relate $R_0$ values to physical and operational variables of these closed spaces. The influence of a super-spreader event on public health is highly variable and ultimately depends on factors such as the epidemic's overall severity and how extensively the virus was transmitted during the event. However, our research suggests that such events may occur frequently enough to contribute significantly to the overall spread of the virus across entire communities. Consequently, it is essential to conduct thorough investigations to understand the transmission dynamics of emerging epidemics, accounting for the possible presence of super-spreader events that can accelerate transmission. Additionally, strategies for mitigating the spread of the virus may need to consider the potential for super-spreader events, with measures aimed at reducing the transmission risk in critical areas and locations. If implemented, these strategies could prove crucial in preventing the virus from spreading rapidly and controllably managing the resulting outbreaks. As an example, we demonstrate the value of estimating the effective $R_0$ in understanding the transmission dynamics of the 2020 United Kingdom COVID-19 epidemic, particularly in grouping cases by reporting week to identify super-spreader events that accelerated transmission. The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis of its sources, quantification, and possible solutions. Initially, the authors establish precise metrics to assess Bperp bias, accounting for both local and native components. Secondly, various inversion techniques and data sources are tested and compared, incorporating a crucial factor called magnetic fill fraction. A simple model is employed to evaluate the impact of noise on Bperp bias, in addition to noise thresholds for different inversion methods. Finally, the authors highlight the significance of accurately determining fill fraction in magnetic inversion algorithms. If this factor is not adequately considered, noise thresholds may not be effective in mitigating Bperp bias. Nevertheless, controlling noise levels can still help reduce bias to some extent. Nevertheless, noise remains a dominant contributor to Bperp bias, especially for noisy data, and further research is needed to address this problem. In the context of the specific data set studied here, the authors suggest employing conservative detemporizing factors to reduce Bperp bias. The authors also propose a strategy to implement this approach more broadly. Additionally, the authors introduce a new figure of merit to assess the performance of inversion algorithms and demonstrate its applicability to different techniques. Finally, the authors emphasize the necessity for a unified strategy to address bias in magnetic field maps, involving a combination of algorithm improvements and observations from different spacecraft. The authors anticipate that future studies will explore the properties of magnetic fields in response to solar cycle changes, incorporating corrections for bias and fill fraction effects. The authors also anticipate that future inversion algorithms will be refined to account for force-free properties and will be tested using simulated data with realistic characteristics. The authors conclude by expressing their intention to make the data analyzed here publicly available to facilitate comparison and validation of such tests. The authors further plan to conduct similar analyses on additional data sets and derived products, such as magnetic field energy and cross-helicity, with corresponding comparisons to in situ measurements. The authors also intend to explore the properties of magnetic fields in regions surrounding solar flares and radio bursts and to investigate the role of turbulence in coronal fields. The authors also aim to investigate the properties of magnetic fields in response to solar cycle changes, specifically focusing on changes in fill fraction and bias, employing both global and local approaches, the latter of which may involve employing numerical simulations. A comprehensive analysis has been conducted to measure the radii of 6097 young star clusters in 31 galaxies from the LEGUS survey. The custom analysis pipeline allowed for a large and contamination-resistant sample, giving us the largest dataset to date of its kind. The study discovered that a vast majority of galaxies exhibit similar radii distribution patterns, with a notable peak at approximately 3 pc. The mass-radius relationship of star clusters in this sample reveals a distinct and unchallenged linear model, applicable to both small and massive clusters. The findings demonstrate that there is minimal dispersion in the cluster sizes at a given mass, indicating a compact birth environment that shapes the radii distribution. The analysis further reveals a near-universal mass-radius relationship across all observed galaxies, with a notable exception being massive clusters larger than 10 pc in size. These exceptional large-size clusters are extremely rare, and their origin remains to be explored. The study provides evidence that the growth of smaller star clusters is severely limited due to a competition from massive ones, with a predicted median cluster mass of approximately 1.9x10^5 M_\\odot. This number is consistent with predictions based on globular clusters in the Milky Way. The research also sheds light on the cluster mass function, showing that it follows a power law with an index of -2.6\\pm0.3, and that it holds constant from approximately 1-5x10^5 M_\\odot. The analysis estimates the cluster specific fraction at any given mass, and it indicates that more massive galaxies tend to have a greater total cluster mass, but the ratio of smaller clusters to larger ones remains constant at 20:1. The study estimates that a substantial proportion of these clusters have not been listed in publicly available catalogs, and that many of those that have been identified lie within dense and heavily obscured regions. We present a novel, direct method for calculating the decay width of hadrons
decaying to two photons, often requiring an indirect estimation via off-shell
form factors. The new method offers an uncomplicated way to study volume effects.
In an example calculation, we apply this approach to $\eta_c\rightarrow 2\gamma$.
Using lattice ensembles with three $N_f=2$ configurations at different lattice
spacings, we derive the final decay width $\Gamma_{\eta_c\gamma\gamma}=6.57(15)_{\textrm{stat}}(8)_{\textrm{syst}}$ keV,
considering systematics in the charm quark mass. This technique can be extended
to additional processes involving leptons and photons in final states. Upcoming
experiments have $\eta_c\rightarrow \mu^+\mu^-$ and $\eta_b\rightarrow e^+e^-$ sensitivity at the $10^{-4}$ level for decay widths,
respectively, making our method applicable for predictions in this context. 
In fact, we already anticipate that our method can reach the required precision 
for $\eta_c\rightarrow \mu^+\mu^-$ without significant difficulties. Nonetheless, 
for $\eta_b\rightarrow e^+e+$ any additional systematic uncertainty related to 
the charm/quark mass relation will need to be controlled to the necessary degree. 
In particular, this is feasible given current lattice determinations of the $m_{c}/m_{q}$ 
at different orders of perturbative QCD. Finally, we propose a second approach 
for calculating the volume effects, namely studying the correlation between the decay 
width and side length of the lattice cube through a response function, also 
derived explicitly in this paper for $\eta_c\gamma\gamma$ decay. This alternative 
method may provide an additional, independent way to determine the decay width. 
For the chosen case, our two methods yield consistent results.
