A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by designing a straightforward transformation with negligible additional computational overhead. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large "size" problems efficiently. We further illustrate the feasibility of this approach by incorporating it into a parallel tempering Monte Carlo simulation, demonstrating its effectiveness through simultaneous exponentiation of multiple benchmark models, including the Euler equation and a heavy-fermion model. Our method has been found to exhibit robust performance on both GPU and TPU devices. Our code is openly accessible on the NeuralTP GitHub repository.

This paper examines the relationship between integers that are y-friable (or y-smooth) and the Dickman function. By assuming the Riemann Hypothesis (RH), we had a previous estimate of the count of y-friable integers up to x in terms of the Dickman function but it was limited to integers y greater than or equal to $(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$ due to previous work by Hildebrand and Saias. Without making any assumptions, we derive a more general formula that gives the count of y-friable integers for the larger range of $y \ge (1+\varepsilon)\log x$. This formula reveals a pattern that follows $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ times correction factors. The correction factors consider the influences of zeta zeros and prime powers. By having this more general formula, we resolve two long-standing conjectures of Hildebrand and Pomerance. 

Hildebrand initially hypothesized that once $y$ is smaller than $(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$, the count of y-friable integers would no longer follow the estimated $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ pattern, which we confirm to be true. 

As for Pomerance, he posed the question whether $\Psi(x,y) \ge x \rho(\log x/ \log y)$ would always hold for any y such that $x/2 \ge y \ge 2$, even under the condition where RH is true. We prove that in cases where RH is true and for sufficiently large $x$ except for very small values close to the critical value, $x/2 \ge y \ge 2$ and that it fails infinitely many times when RH is not true. 

Our new estimates and our derivation for the count of y-friable integers for any y such that $x/2 \ge y \ge 2$ also raises questions as to whether this relationship might hold only when $y$ is far away from $x$. In fact, under the condition where RH is true and for sufficiently large $x$ and no matter how closely $y$ may be to $x$, it will always be the case that $\Psi(x,y) \ge x \rho(\log x/ \log y)$, which we confirm to be true.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in this field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. This code is compatible with popular deep learning frameworks, such as TensorFlow and PyTorch. The code can be found at the address provided in the paper. The paper's findings suggest that private deep learning models can achieve up to 80% of the accuracy of their public counterparts, and that the algorithms used can find optimal hyperparameters within a factor of two of the optimal value in a search space with 1000 possible solutions. The paper's results demonstrate the efficiency of the algorithms, with training and tuning times similar to those of the grid search method. The paper's methods can be applied to various applications of private deep learning, and provides a framework for developing more advanced algorithms that can handle more complex scenarios. The paper's code is available at https://github.com/ghulamdaiv/privatednn on GitHub. The code has been successfully run on Linux and Windows operating systems, and is compatible with various private learning APIs, including IBM's DL/WS and Google's TensorFlow Private Learning. The code can be used as a starting point for developing more advanced algorithms for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, and can be extended to handle other types of models, such as residual networks and dense networks. The code provides a generalized framework that can be applied to various datasets, and can be used to tune hyperparameters such as learning rate, batch size, and number of iterations. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection. When the set S has just two elements, we demonstrate that the homeomorphism type of this boolean complex corresponds to a double triangle complex. Additionally, we establish a connection between the number of spheres and the structure of W's subgroups generated by long cycles, providing upper bounds on the number of spheres based on the number of generators in S. Finally, we provide lower and upper estimates for the number of spheres as the dimension |S| increases. These results are further substantiated by concrete examples and calculations for finite Coxeter groups, hyperplane systems, and the symmetric group S_n, where n is at least 4.

The Euclid satellite, set to launch in 2022, will significantly influence future cosmological research with its Visible and Near Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer instruments. The authors of this study analyzed how correlated readout noise affects in-flight measurements for the NISP detectors and proposed an analytical method for noise covariance matrices. Through experimental data analysis, a 1/f-like noise model was fitted to the NISP engineering detectors and their noise characteristics were determined, allowing for more accurate flux measurements via maximum likelihood estimation. It was found that using this approach, a four-fold decrease in measurement bias compared to the white noise model was possible. The authors conclude that even with the white noise model, negligible bias on NISP's in-flight measurements will be maintained, meeting Euclid's processing baseline requirements. However, further in-depth testing with full-field data is still needed to validate these findings before actual in-flight operations. 

This study's key contributions include:
* An overview of the correlated readout noise effect on in-flight measurements for the NISP detectors
* Proposal of an analytical method for covariance matrices of discrete data sets
* Determination of the noise characteristics of the NISP engineering detectors via 1/f-like noise model fitting
* Assessment of two flux measurement strategies (white noise model, maximum likelihood estimation) for their bias and variance
* Analysis of in-flight measurement biases with the considered strategies
* Assessment of these biases against Euclid's processing baseline requirements
* Proposal for further testing with full-field data to validate these findings during in-flight operations. 

This study has a direct relevance to the development of NISP's in-flight measurement processing, its results however have broader implications on the processing of data from other instruments with similar noise characteristics.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Our study provides insights necessary for designing and evaluating counter-measures against the spread of online rumors, particularly during public health crises. Additionally, it paves the way for applications in related areas of social media propagation, such as virus diffusion and reputation propagation. To facilitate replication and advancement of our study, we made the dataset and methods publicly accessible. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically by analyzing the maximum brightness of their hydrogen lines. Researchers have developed a method to calculate the absolute magnitude of these nebulae and, using a statistical analysis, have established a precise linear relationship with their observed brightness. To apply this technique effectively, it is crucial to have an accurate measurement of the nebular absolute magnitude, which can be determined through a method called metal abundance calibration. However, this calibration method relies on the characteristics of nebular absolute magnitudes being independent, randomly distributed. Researchers have discovered that the nebular absolute magnitudes follow a linear relationship with a certain property called the central density and are planning to use this finding for improved calibration. Additionally, they have found that the maximum brightness of the hydrogen line in planetary nebulae is affected by the nebula's shape, specifically its expansion velocity and size, which influence each other and the spectrum's line shape. To apply this technique effectively across various galaxies, it needs to be tested for any systematic errors that might be present in the data. Researchers have discovered a linear relationship between the maximum brightness of the hydrogen line in planetary nebulae and their absolute magnitude, specifically at a certain energy, and are planning to use this finding for improved calibration. Moreover, they have found that the maximum brightness of the hydrogen line in planetary nebulae is affected by the nebula's metal abundance and is planning to use this finding for improved calibration. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations. Additionally, LifeStream facilitates efficient analysis of multiple datasets combined, reducing the total execution time by $2.5\times$ compared to processing each dataset individually. We highlight the capabilities of LifeStream by demonstrating its capability to estimate $50$ vital sign parameters for surgical planning, showcasing its effectiveness in real-world applications. A stabilizable boundary feedback controller is designed for the Navier-Stokes equations using a linear control scheme with an oblique boundary orientation. Specifically, we develop a control method that utilizes a single component of the velocity field to achieve asymptotic stabilization. Employing an oblique boundary orientation enables us to establish the exact controllability of the underlying algebraic operator associated with the Navier-Stokes equations. No assumptions about the stability of the underlying Navier-Stokes flow are made; rather, we leverage an oblique boundary orientation to ensure the invertibility of the operator associated with the Navier-Stokes equations at the boundary. Ultimately, we demonstrate that a linear control scheme with an oblique boundary orientation can asymptotically stabilize the Navier-Stokes equations, and this stabilization occurs within a finite-dimensional subspace defined by the eigenfunctions associated with the underlying algebraic operator. Notably, we find that the asymptotic stabilization rate is directly proportional to the square of the smallest eigenvalue associated with the damped boundary feedback controller. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings numerically using a one-dimensional channel with an oblique boundary orientation. This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model utilizes a unique decomposition approach to the deformation gradient and applies the Coleman--Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle to material modeling. The resulting model includes suitable Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential assumptions, which enables simulation of crystalline region formation, degradation, and temperature changes during cyclic loading tests. Numerical implementation based on the finite element method provides the basis for numerical solutions, which include simulations of material sample microstructure and temperature evolution. Numerical results validate the proposed model's ability to model the effects of crystalline regions on polymer mechanical and thermal properties. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis. 

This computation is relevant to current experimental research on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ and related materials and can facilitate further theoretical and experimental investigation of the interplay between topology and superconductivity. 

We also demonstrate that in the doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$, the nematic superconductivity can be induced by competing pair-pair interactions which result from competing pair-breaking and pairing instabilities triggered by its unique Fermi surface with point nodal structures. 

By computing the pair-pair interaction diagrams, we show that the electron-electron interaction in the doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ exhibits competing pair-breaking and pairing instabilities and that the magnitude of these interactions depends directly on the average angle of the electron trajectories around the point nodal structures. 

This specific angle-dependent interaction drives a long-range nematic order in the superconducting phase and gives rise to a non-trivial response of the superconducting order parameter to a transverse applied magnetic field.

One significant issue in Imitation Learning (IL) is that obtaining perfect optimal demonstrations from a teacher is a challenging task due to the complexities involved, especially in robotics. Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple state actions at once. To overcome these difficulties, researchers propose an alternative where the teacher can provide corrective feedback in the form of preferences or rewards instead of demonstrations. However, existing algorithms are designed to work with specific types of noisy feedback, limiting their application across various teachers and tasks. To tackle this problem, we suggest a different approach, one where we model a variety of feedback types as different loss functions. Using this approach, we can leverage any online learning algorithm to minimize the combined losses and learn from a diversity of weakly correlated feedback. Our proposed method can handle different forms of feedback by treating the teacher's cost function as latent. By applying a general corrective feedback meta-algorithm that unifies prior work, we can achieve similar regret bounds regardless of the type of feedback. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by successfully learning to perform a complex household navigation task on a robotic platform using a variety of noisy feedback. Our approach can also be used to incorporate additional sources of supervision, such as reward signals. This allows us to achieve even better performance by treating the external signal as another form of corrective feedback. Overall, our approach provides a versatile solution for IL problems involving difficult or costly demonstrations, a common scenario in robotics and other complex, real-world learning environments. Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion's accuracy is verified through Monte Carlo simulation, demonstrating close alignment with theoretically determined delay periods, especially in scenarios with low Doppler shift. The theoretical approach facilitates easy customization of conventional differential detection schemes. As an example, the performance of three specific CPM schemes is enhanced using this method. As expected, the gain achieved is proportional to the delay period and signal-to-noise ratio, thus presenting an efficient method for the performance improvement of conventional differential detection. Nonetheless, this approach's effectiveness may be limited in scenarios with significant Doppler shift due to CPM scheme characteristics.

Initially calculated using correlators of quantum field stress-energy tensors, the issue will now be re-examined using quantum thermodynamics. This is accomplished by determining the thermodynamic quantities known as heat capacity and compressibility in complex quantum systems across various spacetime settings, which directly shows the relationship between these quantities and the stress-energy tensor's fluctuations relative to the mean. This connection is derived from the principle of on-shell first-law of thermodynamics. New insights are gained into well-known spacetime settings, including those in black hole, cosmic string, and Einstein universe backgrounds. In these settings, the dimensionless ratio of temperature squared to the mean energy density is found to be a constant, indicating that quantum field thermodynamics is invariant across these backgrounds. Current deep learning techniques used for removing rain from images have achieved notable success in processing artificially created rainy images.  Nonetheless, their effectiveness drastically drops when confronted with genuine rainy conditions, primarily because they often employ highly simplified models of rain which contrast with the complex real rain scenarios.  This study posits that rain simulation and elimination are mutually interconnected and hence need to be inextricably linked.  To accomplish this, a joint approach to learning real rain simulation and elimination within an integrated disentangled image transformation framework is proposed.  A proposed model involves bidirectional translation of disentangled images in two directions: the translation of real rain images into clear backgrounds, coupled with synthetic rain images.  Moreover, enforcing a strategy that decomposes rain images into clear backgrounds and rain elements aids the translation of these components.  This method is further enhanced with the inclusion of disentanglement strategy using losses like cycle consistency loss and adversarial loss for both real and synthetic rain images.  A complementary entanglement strategy that is symmetrically applied is also included to aid rain simulation.  Comprehensive experiments conducted on datasets of artificial and actual rainy conditions demonstrate the superiority of this approach over other techniques.  The code is available for review at https://github.com/ZsongZhao/DisRain.  Besides, the model for generating clear images from real rain images, as well as rain images from clear ones, can be accessed at https://zhongzheng2020.github.io/DisRain_Tools/.  This study's outstanding performance has the potential to contribute meaningfully to various computer vision applications like deblurring, derusting, and image enhancement where realistic data is difficult to manipulate.  Moreover, the introduction of a variety of rain types that can be generated from the proposed model will provide new opportunities for other computer vision tasks like object detection and tracking from rainy conditions.  In order to achieve this, a comprehensive set of 20 rain types was created from clear images and made publicly available at https://zhongzheng2020.github.io/DisRain_Tools/. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks. Notably, our approach demonstrates complementary benefits when combined with other popular human feedback methods. A crucial aspect of our work involves addressing the private data collection challenges associated with labeling, by implementing a private region-masking technique, allowing multiple users to contribute to the same dataset, without compromising individual annotations. This approach not only accelerates learning, but also makes it more scalable, as multiple distinct datasets can be combined, even when labeled under different configuration settings. In experiments, we demonstrate significant improvements in learning performance, with notable gains in tasks involving delicate agent control. Additionally, our method proves robust across various evaluation metrics, including learning efficiency and the quality of its finest-tuned policy outcomes. Our code, a user-friendly labeling interface, along with detailed instruction guides, are available online at our project website. Our work represents a crucial step forward in the development of more effective human feedback strategies, enabling the broader adoption of reward learning techniques, even when aided by a single skilled human labeler. This allows multiple distinct datasets to be created, thereby enabling the aggregation of multiple independent data collections, without compromising individual annotations, which can be publicly shared, thereby accelerating learning and empowering multi-agent learning applications. We discuss recent research findings regarding model companions in set theory within the context of ongoing debates in the philosophy of mathematics. Initially, we explore how the concept of model companions is affected by the signature, before specifically examining the dependence of model companions in set theory. Our analysis indicates that the most intrinsic model companions for set theory correspond to $H_{\kappa^+}$ theories, as the infinite cardinal $\kappa$ varies. Furthermore, we highlight that the Continuum problem has a singular solution of $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_2$, which aligns with some model companion of enriched set theory containing large cardinal axioms. This model-theoretic framework is justified by a maximality concept reminiscent of Hilbert's axiom of completeness. Additionally, we establish that the axioms of ZFC are deducible from the theory of any model companion of set theory containing the axiom of infinity. Lastly, three conjectures related to this project are formulated. One of these conjectures posits that the theory of any model companion of systems of rich sets equates to the theory of some $H_{\kappa^+}$ system of sets. Another conjecture proposes that the maximality of model companions for set theory is synonymous to the axiom of choice within the context of family complete theories. The third conjecture hypothesizes that the number of model companions for set theory over the axioms of ZFC equals the number of $H_{\kappa^+}$ theories over ZFC, as the infinite cardinal $\kappa$ varies. These findings and associated discussions contribute to an ongoing project aimed at integrating analytical philosophy of mathematics and set-theoretic model theory. This project involves several key components, including the examination of prominent open problems in set theory and the examination of core mathematical theories beyond set theory within the context of model theory. One such example is the investigation of stability in the context of the theory of the integers. Another example is the examination of the computability of models of a theory of a countable structure, a topic that has already given rise to several research findings. Any further research conducted within this project's framework is open to discussion and potential contribution. This study establishes conditions and proof of existence for a modified Branson-Paneitz equation under Navier boundary conditions on a finite region of n-dimensional Euclidean space. Researchers Branson and Paneitz initially developed the equation as a generalization of the Branson-Paneitz equation, and Cazacu and Oniciuc subsequently obtained the corresponding existence theorem for Navier boundary conditions in the entire n-dimensional Euclidean space. However, equations defined within a bounded domain require additional analysis. This paper provides the necessary framework and proof of existence within such domains, leveraging the Branson-Paneitz operator's properties and Navier boundary conditions, in addition to regulating the nonlinearity, thus ensuring the existence of weak solutions and a priori estimates for both the strong and weak solutions. This analysis is realized through a minimization problem and compactness methods, supported by the Sobolev inequality, Frechet differentiability of the Branson-Paneitz operator, and Navier boundary conditions, which, in combination with the Branson-Paneitz operator's properties, facilitate effective handling of boundary conditions within the finite domain. This research is further substantiated by a local existence and uniqueness result of a strong solution, derived from a regularity approach, in addition to establishing the uniform bounds and limit equation. This is followed by an analysis of the new equation's solutions within the context of the original Branson-Paneitz equation, including both strong and weak solutions, and an examination of the solutions' invariance properties, supported by an explicit example, in addition to an implicit argument, both highlighting the role of Navier boundary conditions in maintaining the solutions' symmetry properties. Evaluating a person's risk of drug abuse is crucial, and online surveys have proven effective for gathering relevant data. The data collection process included a comprehensive range of characteristics, including personality traits, impulsivity levels, and sensation seeking tendencies. The data set analyzed substance consumption patterns for 18 different central nervous system-altering substances. The research revealed that certain substances are frequently consumed in clusters, characterized by strong correlations, known as "pleiades." Notable clusters were identified around the substances ecstasy, heroin, and benzodiazepines. By exploring various classification methods and features, a leading approach was identified to predict whether an individual consumes a particular substance based on consumption status for all 18 substances. The best-performing algorithm revealed that certain characteristics are predictive of drug consumption, and among those, some were associated with an increased risk of consumption and others with an escalated risk of misuse. The research demonstrated that drugs can be classified into categories based on consumption patterns and proposed a thorough classification system to categorize individuals into four profiles according to their substance consumption patterns. The proposed system is hoped will contribute to the development of targeted online prevention strategies. The code and data used in the research are available for replication and further development. The approach presented can be applied to predicting consumption of other substances as well. The study's limitations highlight potential improvements, including the collection of more recent data and conducting replication studies. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.  Our work paves the way for further advancements in areas of machine intelligence that have struggled with this type of reasoning and lays the foundation for more sophisticated development of this kind of knowledge.  This knowledge can be augmented with data from human perceptions, encouraging a path of research that involves a dataset of this nature being used to explain underlying mechanisms of human thought.  This explanation can be gained through human interactions guided by these patterns of thought and the outcomes of machine learning models operating within these contexts.  This collaborative approach could accelerate the development of machine intelligence by providing a foundational framework of everyday commonsense knowledge and facilitate a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms of human intelligence.  This atlas, a representative cross-section of this kind of knowledge, is now available at https://wiki.mit.edu/2020/03/23/atomic.html. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. From this analysis, we are able to extract broader insights into the convergence rates of $k_n$, particularly in relation to the scaling requirements for its square or the logarithm of the number of observations. Finally, this research is complemented by a discussion of its broader implications within the context of exchangeable systems. The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet a detailed analysis with current spectroscopic methods has been lacking, especially concerning its atmospheric features, which display unusual properties and contradict earlier estimates of the dwarf's mass and orbit, requiring further examination due to their implications for intermediate population object formation processes. With a distance of tens of astronomical units from its host star, GJ 229B exists near the boundary between the planetary and stellar domains, offering an opportunity for its atmospheric analysis to shed light on formation mechanisms. By utilizing the open-source APOLLO code for a thorough spectral analysis across 0.5-5.1 ${\rm \mu m}$, we derived a precise mass estimate of $41.6\pm3.3\, M_J$ and an accurate temperature assessment of $869_{-7}^{+5}$ K that corresponds with evolutionary models, indicating the system to be older than 1 billion years, and also identified high CO molecular abundance replicating earlier observations, which provide implications for this object's formation and evolution, further contributing to the knowledge of analyzing brown dwarfs and planets through new-generation telescopes. Furthermore, a re-examination of existing near-infrared data revealed a possible seasonal change in the object's activity level, thus necessitating additional surveillance to comprehend its rotational period and the phenomenon of intermediate population object formation. Additionally, a possible cometary activity on 2M 22244485-3923374, a recently discovered tidal debris object, suggests that more research is needed to distinguish between stellar, planetary, and cometary activity, necessitating a re-examination of existing data in this domain. Lastly, a thorough analysis of GJ 8815B, a previously underanalyzed T-dwarf, yielded an accurate mass measurement of $35.2\pm2.8\, M_J$ that corresponds with its host star's age, also exhibiting a wide orbital distance of approximately 9 astronomical units, thus providing further insights into intermediate population object formation processes within 10-30 astronomical units. 

This study's findings will significantly contribute to the ongoing analysis of medium population object formation processes with the aid of current and future high-resolution, high-sensitivity spectroscopic methods on telescopes like JWST, a vital component for comprehending the complex formation mechanisms of intermediate population objects, a crucial aspect of our understanding of the solar system.

Our study offers an explanation of the structural properties of a thermal medium like quark-gluon plasma, using the framework of electron scattering via virtual photons on this medium. In particular, we investigate deep-inelastic scattering processes and derive moment sum rules from structure functions. These sum rules can be expressed as the thermal expectation values of twist-two operators, and such calculations are feasible using lattice QCD for a small set of initial moments. We discuss how lattice simulations can determine the functional form of these structure functions, using a parametric model as a basis for interpretation. By analyzing the moments of structure functions in different kinematic regimes, we can extract the kinematic dependence, either following Bjorken scaling in one regime, or modified by virtual masses and chemical potentials in another. Two potential DIS regimes on quark-gluon plasma are considered: (1) a high-energy limit characterized by large virtual momenta, where perturbative QCD applies, and (2) a low-energy limit where thermal mass and color charge dominate. For the former case, calculations are supported by lattice simulations, whereas in the latter, we model the kinematic dependence using the hard thermal loop approximation. In this way, we can determine the functional form of structure functions, and thus gain a deeper understanding of quark and gluon distributions within the quark-gluon plasma. Furthermore, this analysis provides a framework for interpreting experimental data from heavy ion experiments at various collision energies. In this sense, studying the quark-gluon plasma through deep-inelastic scattering off this medium offers a multidisciplinary approach, involving the interplay of lattice QCD, perturbative QCD, and experimental input from particle colliders. This approach paves the way for a comprehensive exploration of the fundamental properties of strong-interaction matter at extreme conditions. In its most general form, this research enables the study of how heavy ion collisions interact with the internal structure of the quark-gluon plasma, allowing for the diagnosis of the plasma's kinematic conditions and its fundamental properties through various DIS processes, from low to very high energies. In this sense, electron-or photon-probe interactions can serve as a set of diagnostic tools for understanding the internal structure and kinematics of the quark-gluon plasma created in heavy ion collisions. This note outlines the algorithm devised by J. M. Eisenlohr and S. L. Farris to
systematically generate all fully transitive polyhedra in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space. Furthermore, this algorithm is employed to construct a novel polyhedron within three-dimensional Euclidean space. Fully transitive polyhedra are geometric structures that exhibit complete rotational symmetry while occupying a specific volume in $d$-dimensional space. In other words, any rotation within a specific dimension will modify the appearance of the polyhedron in a consistent manner. This concept was initially explored in one-dimensional space by Eisenlohr and Farris, who developed an algorithm to identify all fully transitive polyhedra in any given dimension. This algorithm is now an essential tool in constructing sophisticated geometric Transitive Polyhedra Conjectures. In this update, we build upon the algorithm to demonstrate its effectiveness and introduce three-dimensional torus polyhedra – a groundbreaking achievement that marks the first time such structures have been created. We also present an intriguing Geometric Transitive Polyhedra Conjecture related to these innovative constructions. This conjecture positions these innovative constructions as critical components in the comprehensive classification of all fully transitive polyhedra within three-dimensional Euclidean space. This update also provides an overview of the algorithm, featuring a set of fundamental properties that define fully transitive polyhedra and detailing the key components involved in its implementation. In addition, we present several examples derived from this algorithm, featuring various fully transitive polyhedra constructed in five-dimensional Euclidean space. These examples showcase the algorithm's versatility and its potential to contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex geometry involved. This understanding is pivotal in addressing more intricate questions related to the topology of these structures. This update is intended to serve as a preliminary step towards formulating mathematical proofs related to these novel constructions and the proposed Geometric Transitive Polyhedra Conjectures. This is achievable through the application of topological techniques, assuming the validity of certain geometric principles. This update is accompanied by an interactive three-dimensional visualization, featuring an animated rotation of a novel fully transitive polyhedron constructed through this algorithm. This visualization is embedded within an online companion site, along with additional resources and a downloadable three-dimensional file. This file enables users to explore the polyhedron in real-time using any compatible three-dimensional viewer. Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly optimal $0.5^n$ success probability for cloning is attainable. Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks against specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

  - Applications to Copy Protection: We've discovered that strong forms of unclonable encryption can lead to enhanced security, specifically copy-protection for unlearnable functions. We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. We believe our approach provides a valuable framework for the training of neural networks that is robust to input variations. This work was motivated by the widespread adoption of neural networks in safety-critical applications where model performance is crucial across different input parameters and often model reliability is equally as important as performance.

Sequential neural network models are highly versatile in addressing NLP tasks.
Their sequential design leads to fundamental questions regarding their capacity
to learn complex language hierarchies and grammatical patterns naturally
occurring in human language.
As a case study, we investigate the performance of sequential CNNs and RNNs
in developing an intuitive understanding of Basque grammar, specifically
agreement between adjectives and nouns.
Our analysis indicates that the ease with which these networks learned this
grammar depended greatly on the complexity of the sequence and the type of
sequence encountered.
Comparing the networks' performance on Basque and English reveals that they
experienced significant difficulty learning this pattern in sequences lacking
natural hierarchical structure, i.e., phrasal contexts, whereas they demonstrated
considerable aptitude in sequence contexts both with inherent structure,
i.e., clausal contexts, and without it, i.e., pseudosentences.
Furthermore, our experiments disclosed that the networks' ability to grasp this
grammar was heavily influenced by their internal sequence design.
Ultimately, our research proposes a possible explanation for the ability of
these sequential networks to acquire a deep understanding of language patterns
and suggests that they may be better suited to modeling shallow, lexical
grammar. 
In addition, our study reveals that these neural networks can acquire a
deeper understanding of language with complex hierarchies, as illustrated
by their performance in contexts requiring the derivation of combined
lexical and structural meanings. 
As such, they possess significant value as tools for exploring the
intersection of NLP and the study of human language structure, as well as
theoretical linguistics. 
In order to facilitate further research along these lines, we are
publishing a trained model with agreement prediction capabilities on both
English and Basque, along with a public dataset in the latter language. 
This model and dataset can be downloaded from the following address:
https://github.com/joosb/basque-agreement. 
In addition, all of our code, including the neural network models and
data preprocessing software, is also available from this location. 
We are confident that this research will help to stimulate more general
investigations into the potential applications of NLP in the study of
human language structure, as well as theoretical linguistics. 
As such, we invite linguists with expertise in the analysis of human language
structure to collaborate with us in order to provide their insights and
interpretations of our research findings.

To tackle this issue, we propose an innovative approach where an initial statistical model of game performance identifies specific settings that mirror players' typical behavior, even in the face of diminished control. This approach is exemplified through a practical application involving upper limb rehabilitation and a specially designed controller modifiable to accommodate different rehabilitation scenarios. Collaborative sessions between occupational therapists and game developers resulted in the creation of two engaging rehabilitation games, with one being used in a actual upper limb rehabilitation study at a hospital. Our research demonstrates that our method not only maintains the enjoyment aspect of games but also provides valuable performance insights for rehabilitation professionals, offering a promising solution for creating this type of interactive therapy solutions. Additionally, our approach can be adapted to address other challenges related to the coexistence of gaming and analytical objectives. By open-sharing the underlying code used in our research, we aim to contribute to the advancement of this specific class of interactive systems. Our research offers a variational approximation, drawing from the Ambrosio-Tortorelli model, to quantify brittle fracture energies in complex, piecewise-rigid structures, applicable to both nonlinear and linearised elasticity frameworks. We demonstrate the precision of this approximation by comparing it to a more precise recent model developed by Fratke, Kuwert, and Savin. Additionally, we investigate its performance with different approximation parameters and find that it efficiently captures the optimal configuration and associated energy for any given domain by minimizing the sum of a stiffness term and a surface-based damage term. This minimization process is robust to both small and large values of the approximation parameters, with optimal configurations obtained through the combination of pure elasticity and surface-based damage, reflecting the structure's inherent stiffness and vulnerability to surface flaws. As the approximation becomes even more precise, we find that it converges to the actual energy by exploring both theoretical and numerical insights. Our study is particularly relevant to analysing the long-term evolution of plates affected by gravitational forces and the approximation can be adapted to account for non-uniform fracture energies along boundaries. This new model provides a useful tool for approximating brittle fracture energies and may be extended to model damage in structures influenced by gravity or where fractures vary significantly. This model also highlights the role of surface-based damage in approximating complex fracture energies and can be used to analyse optimal configurations and associated energies within both linearised and highly non-linear elasticity frameworks. It can also be employed to both numerical and analytical assessments of complex, piecewise-rigid structures, leading to new avenues for research in both theoretical and practical applications. We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. Additionally, this code can be adapted to facilitate more comprehensive searches for vector leptoquarks, even in scenarios beyond our current understanding. Furthermore, this code is part of a broader framework that can simulate multiple types of vector leptoquarks and provide valuable insights to enhance ongoing and future searches for these exotic particles at the LHC. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. Furthermore, compared to existing deep learning techniques, it demonstrates superior performance in out-of-distribution robustness along with better overall performance. This new framework's ability to handle OOD data is a significant breakthrough, given its potential to counteract various forms of data variability, such as different scanners, institutions, or protocols. Consequently, this model represents a crucial milestone in developing practical deep learning PET image enhancement solutions for real-world applications. Nonetheless, this model's performance can be further improved through the incorporation of additional relevant data. This model's code and data are available online. This work is part of a larger initiative that combines deep learning and maximum likelihood framework for robust medical image analysis, emphasizing the importance of addressing OOD data to achieve Analytic Medical Image Computing. The issue of tailoring news to individuals' interests while respecting their data remains unresolved. Growing worries about over-collected data and its unintended use have motivated our research on balancing personalization and privacy. Our experience creating personalized content platforms that protect users' confidentiality has sparked an investigation into users' attitudes towards these topics. A conducted survey revealed the opinions of various age groups regarding personalization and privacy. In this research, we are sharing our key discoveries with publishers and the community to inform the design and development of next-generation news recommender systems, which should prioritize the human user and achieve a harmonious balance between personalization and privacy. This research has already influenced the development of several ongoing projects in our community. We are continuing this research by examining user behavior in response to our previously designed systems, which have resulted in several notable observations, for example, users' tendency to trade off privacy for high-quality personalized recommendations. This has sparked several thought-provoking research questions, such as whether users' willingness to share data for personalized content varies depending on the type of content, and whether they distinguish between online and offline data collection. These questions represent a crucial step in designing effective, privacy-respecting news recommender systems that can demonstrate a notable improvement over conventional approaches like popularity-based recommendations, thus enhancing the reading experience for both existing and new users. This goal is also supported by emerging technologies, such as the integration of AI, voice assistants, and wearable devices, which provide numerous opportunities and challenges for the community to explore and address in the context of personalization and privacy. In this research, we are sharing our initial, ongoing research with the community and encouraging collaboration to design, develop, and evaluate innovative, privacy-aware news recommender systems, which can provide a better reading experience for both existing and new users, and serve as a benchmark for conducting similar research in other domains. This benchmark, along with the data and software associated with this research, are available at https://github.com/ayush0808/portalresearch for the community to build upon and expand our work. This research is an initiative of the MediaWiki Hackathon 2019, organized by the Wikimedia Foundation. It is also part of the Wikipedia Recommender Systems Research Portal, which aims to aggregate and present the most notable research on Wikipedia recommender systems, and facilitate replication and advancement of such research. This portal is designed to address the difficulty many researchers face in finding and accessing existing Wikipedia recommender systems research, which is often scattered across various domains and cannot be replicated due to a lack of publicly available data

The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations and renders existing operator growth studies accessible and understandable. We also propose a novel framework that distills the operator growth phenomenon into an intrinsic property of the Lie algebra at hand, even as we acknowledge the existing pathway to comprehend this phenomenon through the study of operator growth within distinct quantum systems. Lastly, our work paves the way for further cross-disciplinary exploration at the intersection of Lie groups, quantum information theory, and quantum physics, especially in the areas of quantum thermodynamics, quantum chaos, and quantum gravity, among others. Network-based services provide significant income to service operators, which they regulate through agreements on performance. Ensuring these agreements are being met necessitates the monitoring of service standards. A method to accomplish this involves deploying active measurement tools, which send test traffic and gauge performance. Nonetheless, these tools demand substantial resources and often fail to cover the whole network. Human administrators decide what parts to measure, which proves inefficient and unresponsive to rapidly changing network conditions. This article discusses the advantages of employing peer-to-peer (P2P) technology to enhance the detection of SLA breaches. Initially, we explore the principles of steering the location of performance monitoring within a network through optimization. The goal is to minimize the distance between the points where the SLA is being flouted and those where performance is being measured. Achieving this requires no prior understanding of network topology. We examine three methods for achieving this goal, which involve solving complex mathematical problems. We then examine the effectiveness of these approaches in a demo involving a video streaming service. The results indicate that P2P-based performance monitoring can locate SLA breaches within a 10-fold range of the actual location and outperform conventional methods by at least an order of magnitude. This technique can monitor for SLA breaches in real-time, reduce the resources needed for performance monitoring by at least an order of magnitude, and enable the efficient detection of breaches in larger networks. This innovation has the potential to give network-based services the ability to adapt to changing network conditions and operate efficiently in dynamic environments. This approach can also facilitate the adoption of pay-per-use charging models that compensate users financially for any adverse effect caused by their data usage. Ultimately, this technique can empower network-based services to make autonomous, efficient, and adaptive decisions that ensure they meet their SLA agreements and operate efficiently in dynamic networks. This can be accomplished without requiring extensive expertise in network management. This approach can also serve as a model for other applications involving large-scale, distributed systems. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully designing the filling pattern may offer a powerful beam loss mitigation tool, particularly in multi-pass energy recovery linacs where return beams from different passes can interact with each other. Also, this paper introduces a new concept called the beam-RF interaction phase depolarization factor that can be used to assess filling pattern effects on beam breakup instability and suggests that careful design of filling patterns may also provide opportunities to increase the maximum beam current by reducing beam-beam effects in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. To determine the parameters for neutrino oscillation, cutting-edge experiments employing long-baseline neutrino detection systems rely heavily on the development of detailed models describing the interactions between neutrinos and atomic nuclei. The intricacy of these models is significant, partly because existing detectors have been incapable of observing final state neutrons, which has led to significant systematic uncertainties. The implementation of 3D scintillator tracking technology in next-generation long-baseline neutrino experiments has improved detection capabilities by enabling event-by-event measurement of neutron kinetic energy resulting from neutrino interactions, thus providing valuable information for refining neutrino interaction models and reconstructing neutrino energies. Prototypes of these detectors have undergone neutron irradiation at the LANL beamline in both 2019 and 2020. The primary goal was to demonstrate the ability of neutron detection by comparing the total cross-sectional area of neutrons and scintillator interaction at 98-688 MeV, which was measured at 0.36±0.05 barn, in accordance with established external measurement standards. The most notable outcome was the observation of neutrino-induced events exhibiting multiple neutron tracks, stemming from the conversion of neutral kaons created within the detector, which can be used as a potential event signature for future long-baseline neutrino experiments utilizing 3D tracking technology. The event reconstruction techniques employed a GEANT4-based simulator and resulted in an accuracy of 12.5 cm for both neutron track length and interaction position. The implementation of these innovations has the potential to enhance neutrino cross-section and interaction process research, in addition to refining neutrino energy reconstruction, which is critical for understanding neutrino oscillation behaviors in long-baseline experiments. The developed detection technique is also capable of addressing other complex neutrino research challenges. The comprehensive analysis of the data collected at the LANL beamline in 2019-2020 demonstrates the capability of contemporary solid-scintillator detection systems to provide event-by-event measurement of neutron kinetic energy resulting from neutrino interactions, which can be used to derive neutrino energies through refinement of interaction models. The outcome of this research will be incorporated into the design and development of novel detection systems employed in long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiments, including DUNE. In the case of the cooler protoplanetary discs and moderate temperatures, grains likely only hold one water layer. Since this water layer would evaporate in the warmer sections of the discs as dust moves inward, we decided to examine how two alternative methods for dust preparation affect tensile strength, which involved letting the grains dry in the air (resulting in dry samples) or baking them into airless environments (yielding super-dry samples) as an attempt to mimic how things might appear in the cooler sections of the protoplanetary discs. Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) is a localized adaptation of the traditional Fisher Discriminant Analysis, widely employed for supervised dimensionality reduction techniques. The LFDA R package allows users to execute various LFDA methodologies like Kernel Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis and Semi-Supervised Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis. The package also facilitates dimensionality reduction result visualization, utilizing 3D (rgl) and 2D (ggplot2) tools from the RGL and GGplot2 packages respectively. Moreover, it includes a method for constructing local discriminant analysis graphs based on reduced data dimensions. This package can be utilized from the command line through the RcmdrExpress interface for interactive data analysis guidance. 

The LFDA package is openly accessible on CRAN (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/LFDA/index.html) along with comprehensive documentation, including a guide for users and developers on GitHub (https://github.com/pcalon/LFDA/tree/main/man). The package's capabilities are showcased with a cancer cell classification example, demonstrating its dimensionality reduction capabilities. The code is openly accessible on GitHub (https://github.com/pcalon/LFDA/tree/main/vignettes) for the Cancer cell classification example. 

The LFDA package is collaboratively maintained by Pedro Calonje and Vinicius Zinnio Scarpino. Users can contribute to the package by visiting GitHub (https://github.com/pcalon/LFDA).

- Generalized Robust Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (GRLFA)

Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, and we provide evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm, demonstrating its effectiveness. The code for our research is available online. Despite its versatility, our method still faces performance bottlenecks, and possible paths for optimization are also discussed. EKMP has the potential to contribute significantly to the advancement of robot learning, and we believe it offers a suitable answer to one of the fundamental questions in the field. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. In such a case, rapidity evolution parameters entered the equations as in traditional BFKL approach, with additional constraint that the CEV's discontinuity along the rapidity axis matches the corresponding part of the six-gluon amplitude. Since the latter is known, the CEV's discontinuity along the rapidity axis can be determined for all helicity configurations, which is the central finding of this work. A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Furthermore, we established that Rashba coupling's favorable impact on superconductivity originates from a spin-flip driven enhancement of the likelihood of a pair of electrons traveling in reverse time-states. Our analysis also predicts that under suitable Rashba coupling and Zeeman field conditions, the superconducting state exhibits topologically non-trivial characteristics, as confirmed through inspection of the interacting model's Fermi surface. Lastly, we explored the influence of Rashba coupling on superconductivity in relation to the BCS-BCS phase transition and discovered that it accelerates this transition when subjected to a Zeeman field. Our study provides new insights into the interconnections between Rashba coupling, Zeeman field, superconductivity, and topological properties in attractive Hubbard models.

Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. Through this approach, researchers may be better equipped to design and predict the microstructure of block copolymer blends, including the formation of cylindrical brushes on cylinders with various diameters and the generation of spherical brushes on spheres. By incorporating these considerations, scientists can develop more accurate predictions for the morphology of block copolymer melts, including cases involving highly elongated brushes found on the interfaces of nanoparticles and certain types of amphiphilic block copolymer surfaces. This research may ultimately facilitate the development of methods for manufacturing materials with tailored structure and function, based on the precise design of brush geometry. In line with this goal, we present a case study analyzing the brush morphology on the surface of a nickel nanodot covered in graffed polymers, comparing our theoretical predictions to experimental data obtained via atomic force microscopy and scanning small-angle x-ray scattering. By mastering the geometry of block copolymer brushes, scientists may be able to control their micellization and packing, leading the way for innovative materials applications driven by surface confinement. In these materials, brushes function as structural elements with various roles - e.g., as links between corralled domains, as parts of the corralled domains themselves or as free standing blocks that interact with surrounding brushes. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. Some well-known graphs like a complete graph, star graph, and cycle graph are investigated for their beta_k when k ranges from 1 to 4. Additionally, the relationship between beta_1 and beta_2 of any graph is examined, as well as the connection between a graph's metric dimension and its beta_k when k is greater than the graph's diameter. Finally, the paper concludes by presenting some open research questions related to identifying sets and metric dimension. These questions ask about specific graphs, particular classes of graphs, and general theoretical graph concepts. Some of these questions have already been answered either partially or in full by new results presented at the end of the paper. These new findings also include identifying sets of power-free graphs, some category 1 graphs, and a few others. The paper's authors would like to offer a large sum of money to anyone who can find a smallest identifying set of size 3 or less in the graph known as Mycological Tree. Another challenge is presented by a new technique to determine the minimum identifying set of a graph when the identifying set is capped at some number k. This technique can determine the minimum identifying set of any graph in at most (1/2)(1-k)^3 times the number of points in the graph, when k is greater than 0 and less than 1.
