Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. Furthermore, this method allows for more flexible and efficient mapping of the sky, which could lead to new scientific discoveries. To facilitate replication and further development, the team openly shared their code and examples at the Zooniverse Forum.

Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a numerical value that captures the degree to which the effectiveness of a combinatorial optimization algorithm relies on the structure of that game. We found that some games exhibit strong dependence on this metric as it is in relation to the worst-case approximation ratio in questions of combinatorial optimization. We also found instances of games with polarized outcomes in relation to this metric, with some games resulting in very good quality approximations and some leading to poor quality approximations. We present multiple examples of real-world applications for our model, including issues related to resource allocation, flow control, and data privacy, among others. We further developed a general method for converting induced weighted combinatorial optimization games into their corresponding single-agent combinatorial optimization problems, achieving efficient $2$-approximation in specific optimization tasks, and also discussed the specific challenges and opportunities related to fairness in such multi-agent systems. We implemented a suite of scalable algorithms publically accessible via an online tool that allows users to upload and solve specific combinatorial optimization problems. We conducted extensive numerical experiments covering over 200,000 solving sessions on various game theory related problems. The results showed that the serial dictatorship mechanism can be highly effective in achieving good quality approximations, especially in complex scenarios, and also demonstrated the effectiveness of its fairness implementation via payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of main belt asteroids 
were identified and flagged for potential binarity, and a statistical analysis 
of 1429 selected candidates resulted in the discovery of three previously known 
binary asteroids, and one newly found wide binary asteroid, with an estimated 
primary component mass of around 70 kilometers. This new finding, titled 390003 
Hermione, exhibits an estimated orbital path of 292 days and a notable distance 
of roughly 1760 kilometers from its secondary component. Additional research 
is needed to verify the existence of this binary asteroid and confirm its 
dimensions. This detection highlights the capability of these analysis 
techniques to discover notable binary asteroids within wide field surveys. 
Ultimately, our approach is offered to the scientific community as a resource 
for extracting binary asteroid data within wide field surveys, along with the 
specific results from the specific Pan-STARRS1 images mentioned. Citation:

The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing crustal deformation in Central and West Africa enabled researchers to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  Their model indicates that shifts in extension direction and speed significantly influenced the development of the Pre-salt sag basin and the S~ao Paulo High.  An initial, low-velocity E-W extension phase occurred between South America and Africa until about 126 million years ago.  Following this, rift activity increased and an NE-SW directed extension phase began between 126 and 126 million years ago and around 126 Ma.  In this 17 million-year period the conjugate Brazilian and West African margin Pre-salt basin widths were generated.  An intermediate phase of 126.57 Ma and Base Aptian featured strain localization, weakening of the lithosphere and increased velocities, with extension direction rotating towards NE-SW.  Breakup occurred around 113 Ma and finally an NE-SW directed extension phase between Africa and South America until about 113 Ma.  Upstream migration of a mantle plume caused increased velocities and lithospheric weakening, resulting in the formation of a central graben in both conjugate margins, with the resulting thickness variations influencing later allochthonous sediment thickness patterns.  This new understanding of the conjugate West African-Brazilian rift system, based on equal weighting of evidence from both margins, yields a coherent and plausible model of the pre-break-up history of these unique margins.  This in turn sheds new light on the development of the Pre-salt basin and the S~ao Paulo High.  This research is an example of the value of combining and reconstructing conjugate margin data, based on the principle of equal weighting of evidence from both margins.  This approach provides a coherent and plausible model of the pre-break-up history of these unique margins.  This study also highlights the importance of cross-pollination of ideas and data between the Brazilian and West African margins, based on the principle of equal weighting of evidence from both margins, for a deeper understanding of the Earth Sciences of these unique conjugate margins. Even with an abundance of annotated data, unsupervised pre-training for multiple scenarios remains unclear. This study challenges the common assumption that unsupervised learning can be beneficial, as we face a scenario with limited labeled images for the task of fine-grain object detection. To overcome this obstacle, we employed an unsupervised segmentation model that does not rely on object annotations from the pre-training dataset. By comparing various unsupervised methods with both weak and no supervision during training, we observed that using unsupervised learning under no supervision resulted in the poorest performance. In contrast, unsupervised and weakly supervised training models yielded comparable results, both outperforming the model trained on just a few labeled images. Notably, some unsupervised training methods even surpassed the baseline model without any unsupervised training. We also discovered that when the dataset is more robust, unsupervised training becomes less necessary. Our code and dataset are openly accessible for reference.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Additionally, we discovered that forming alliances can facilitate success in our D&D scenario by providing a clear collective goal that overrides individual desires and expectations. Moreover, we found a Duncan Master that understands the players' identities influences performance, which we attribute to distinction based on equal but distinct starting conditions. Lastly, we found a surprising capacity of our system to incorporate new players into its game dynamics, even with players maintaining their distinct identities, which we found capable of modeling through an external state variable outside its reasoning about the players' thoughts. The successful implementation of this complex, interactive system showcases the potential for guided learning through interactive games and also yields novel insights into the nature of dialogue-based interaction and the role of identity within it. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. This statistical approach can be applied to study other complex protein structures and may provide insights into various fundamental folding processes. Moreover, this research introduces knotted proteins as models for studying topological invariants and fractal properties. Additionally, several commonly used machine learning algorithms are used to identify whether sequence-based features are sufficient to classify these proteins efficiently. Although some classification success is achieved, the results also indicate that protein properties are difficult to predict due to their inherently disordered nature. A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A study of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential was analyzed to illustrate the anomalous NG theorem's application to relativistic field theories, especially those involving the spontaneous symmetry breaking of a Z2 symmetry. A comparison between the Heisenberg algebra derived from the anomalous NG theorem and that of a simple harmonic oscillator revealed a complex interplay between the Mermin-Wagner elasticity and the Heisenberg algebra's triangular inequality constraint. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. This study highlights the potential for developing highly lattice-mismatched Heusler compounds and reveals the complexity involved in achieving remote epitaxy on clean graphene substrates. The necessary conditions for a remote epitaxial process involve a combination of highly favorable surface energies of adatoms and atoms, highly restricted surface diffusion, and sufficient adatom-atom interactions, all reflected in the temperature-dependent rotation domain percentage in GdPtSb. This research indicates that while many factors contribute to the success of remote epitaxy on graphene, its achievement may rely on a delicate balance of surface energy parameters. This balance needs to be explored in more depth, with experiments and first-principles calculations, to better understand the underlying physics involved. This study lays the groundwork for a comprehensive investigation of remote epitaxy on graphene, with its implications extending to the broader field of van der Waals heteroepitaxy. This could potentially enable the efficient synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and the creative use of waste substrates, along with a deeper understanding of the unique physics and chemistry involved. This research may also provide answers to several persisting questions surrounding the epitaxial growth process itself. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.  The technique also proves particularly useful in scenarios with limited annotation.  The technique is also applicable to a wide range of applications including data augmentation, improving performance with only a single positive label per image without any additional information.  Code and models are available for download at https://github.com/zwang84/SMS.

This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods and computational tools to model portfolio returns, establishing essential formulas and efficient algorithms using techniques from computational geometry and splines. By leveraging these methods, our approach can efficiently handle large portfolios and accurately compute moments of the probability function within seconds. We primarily focus on the long-only strategy and develop an adaptable method for this type of investment. By representing the stock market as a geometric space, our cumulative distribution function enables a score for each portfolio based on the percentage of its returns exceeding a certain threshold. We derived closed-form equations for the first four moments and an innovative algorithm for computing all other moments, demonstrating a direct connection between the cross-sectional returns and the moments of the distribution. All of our methods are highly versatile, covering scenarios including when asset returns are equal. We used our score-based approach to design new performance metrics and found the portfolios it produced less concentrated and less prone to high risks than those from the mean-variance model. The code for our methods is now available online.

This study tackles a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly in time. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal cost function, as well as to demonstrate the existence of policies that minimize costs under this dynamic framework. Alongside, we examine the existence and distinctiveness of solutions to a system of stochastic differential equations featuring abrupt obstacles, whose characteristics depend on the unknown solution. Finally, the paper concludes by illustrating the applicability of our findings to two specific case studies. One involves an optimal switching problem with time-changing activation and termination costs, the other an optimal control issue with a moving target. Both scenarios yield novel implications on existing results from the literature. Barles, G, and Buckdahn have previously explored similar problems, though with continuous regime changes, in their published works. In contrast, our findings expand the scope of those studies to include regime changes that can occur instantly. Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001.
It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, where these two spheres
have centers that are at least d units apart.
In this research paper, we examine the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations
under a specific distance metric known as the Hamming distance.
To that end, we create a Cayley graph, identify the specific distance metric it uses,
and determine the exact value of the maximum possible overlap between two spheres in
this metric with r = 4 and a distance of d = 5, or with a distance of d = 2r. 
Additionally, we compare this result to current estimates and discuss how it may be
applied to various fields, including coding theory and channel capacity problems. 
Finally, we propose and solve a new subproblem, known as the subsequence reconstruction
problem, in which we seek to replicate only the initial portion of the transmitted
sequence. We also establish a new upper and lower limit for this problem.

Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. This modified approach, requiring no adjustments to the network architecture, facilitates easy addition or removal of categories. Compared to a non-hierarchical baseline, our proposed method yields a notable enhancement in accuracy and substantial reduction in errors on classes of instruments that weren't encountered during training. This project's results demonstrate that introducing hierarchy to the learning process addresses the issue of linguistic variability affecting the interpretation of musical sound and improves generalization across novel categories of instruments. Furthermore, our technique makes it feasible to incorporate newly identified instruments into the classification network without necessitating a rewrite of the network. This project's success centers primarily around the introduction of a hierarchical approach to metric learning in a few-shot learning setting, and its related code can be found at https://github.com/sonnacat/Musical-Instrument-FSL. This project's results are reported alongside that code's dependencies at https://github.com/sonnacat/Musical-Instrument-FSL/blob/main/code/report.tex. This work has been presented at the 39th IEEE International Conference on ICASSP (2022).

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction of up to 50 times in computational costs compared to other methods. This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control. Ultimately, our analysis underscores the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration to create models that are both analytically robust and capable of informing data-driven policy decisions. 

This work is Book Chapter 1 of the author's Ph.D. dissertation, defended on September 16, 2021, at Virginia Tech.

We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on the impact of a linear external potential on the particle's Shannon entropy. Next, we develop an ensemble of Majorana fermions to investigate their thermodynamic behavior. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating and implementing effective solutions to acronym resolution. Despite the existence of various methods and systems, several pressing issues persist: 1) the lack of a standardized approach to representing and solving acronym definitions, 2) limited operational compatibility across different research environments, and 3) the need for more sophisticated algorithms to achieve better performance. In response to these challenges, this project aims to introduce an open-source, multi-paradigm system called AcroSolver, capable of processing and resolving acronym definitions within written text. AcroSolver can handle both simple and complex acronym cases, where the acronym's origin is explicitly stated in the text. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. This innovative approach enables robust, efficient, and versatile DNA data storage. Each data object, no matter how large, can be efficiently recovered with minimal additional sequencing cost. This is made possible by our data update mechanism which ensures that recently updated data objects are stored in a separate sequence from older objects, enabling us to precisely locate and recover recently updated data with ease, even if the data storage sequence is many times larger than the actual data being recovered. This helps us to recover data with essentially no additional sequencing cost when the data itself is relatively recent. To further highlight this approach's efficiency, we've created a comprehensive analysis of our method's performance and scalability. This is accompanied by a fully functional, open-source DNA-storage system based on our proposed architecture and made available to the community under the permissive Apache License 2.0. This system consists of over 5,000 base pairs of DNA data, including both functional code and a range of data objects with varied addresses and meanings, along with additional tools to monitor storage performance, manage storage sessions, and retrieve stored data. This system serves as both a landmark demonstration and a flagship example of our novel DNA-storage architecture, and it is available for replication and further development by researchers worldwide. This is the first DNA-storage system to employ a method of data indexing that is compatible with PCR addressing, and it offers numerous other innovations that make it the most advanced DNA-storage system yet developed. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. Despite these challenges, the unique properties of nodal lines offer considerable potential for contributing to the development of topological quantum electronics and physics. The concluding section highlights the potential of artificial materials to bridge the gap between microscopic theoretical models and observable macroscopic phenomena. This review is structured to be accessible to readers with a condensed matter physics background, centered around three key sections: the basics of topological nodal lines, recent developments in artificial materials, and their implications and future directions. This review is designed to provide a comprehensive overview of topological nodal lines in artificial materials and their associated physics, encompassing both electronic and photonic realizations. It is essential to note that the field of topological nodal lines is continuously evolving, with many recent research achievements already making significant contributions to the field. Nonetheless, there remains a critical need to bridge the gap between theoretical models and experimental observations, particularly when studying the non-Abelian charges associated with nodal lines in momentum space. This review aims to illuminate the potential of artificial materials to contribute to a deeper understanding of these complex phenomena. It is hoped that this comprehensive overview will inspire further research and experimental investigations at the intersection of topological electronics and artifical materials. This review consists of three central sections focused on the fundamentals of topological nodal lines, recent developments in artificial materials, and their associated physics and potential future directions. A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention guided network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.  The model's effectiveness is validated on a separate dataset with real-world data, resulting in the highest accuracy and least side effects among comparison models.  The model's efficiency and performance make it suitable for use in clinical settings.  Code availability: https://github.com/soncodishen/MAG-Net. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Moreover, this method allows us to incorporate additional annotations, such as correspondences and normals, to further enhance our results. We support our method's efficiency and effectiveness with several experiments, showing state-of-the-art recovery results when compared to other non-differentiable and optimization-based techniques. A popular technique, widely used for enhancing video playback on television and recording, is interlacing. This technique doubles the perceived frame rate without boosting the bandwidth, yet generates undesirable effects like visual distortion and flicker during playback. Present methods aim to minimize these drawbacks, either by separating mixed scan lines or assuming separate capture devices for recording and playback. In contrast, our proposed model, interleave-to-parallel, is the first to successfully separate superimposed lines without prior knowledge of the mixing factor, enabling a practical and efficient solution for various interlacing applications. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on multiple scenarios, including real-world recordings, and compare its performance to other existing methods. The simplicity and flexibility of our approach make it suitable for multiple parallel-serial scenarios, including columns and mixed scenarios, with ease. Additionally, our method can be adapted for other cascade-to-parallel problems. We showcase the simplicity and flexibility of our approach through simple column-to-parallel and mixed-to-parallel demonstrations. The investigation revealed a disparity of approximately 0.1 fm in the root mean square radius of the neutron point distribution between non-relativistic mean field models and their relativistic counterparts. Further analysis revealed the discrepancy arises due to varying product values of the effective mass and one-body potential strength within the respective frameworks, with those values being governed by the Hugenholtz-Van Hove theorem. In contrast, the thickness of the neutron skin was found not to solely correlate with the symmetry potential but rather was heavily dependent on the nucleon effective mass. A generalised relativistic formula for the neutron skin thickness was derived and demonstrated its compatibility with non-relativistic approaches. Predictions made for several isotopes and specifically for the $^{78}$Ni, $^{79}$Cu and $^{82}$Zn skins proved notable for their thickness of around 0.5 fm. Additionally, both the relativistic and non-relativistic models displayed potential radius increases of the point proton distribution relative to the neutron at moderate proton excess conditions. Nevertheless, at high proton excess, both models predicted a thin neutron skin of approximately 0.1 fm with a marginally thicker proton skin of around 0.15 fm due to the onset of alpha cluster configurations. These findings provide new insights into the relationship between nucleon distributions and the behaviour of nuclear matter at extreme conditions of isospin excess. They also offer a framework for informing experimental initiatives on mass unknown isotopes with rare proton or neutron excess and could become relevant for studies of extended nuclei such as those formed in stellar collapse situations. Moreover, such knowledge may also contribute to a deeper comprehension of forces governing two body nuclear interaction at high isospin conditions also encountered in massive stellar objects. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. The proposed method is shown to be highly effective in incorporating new bathymetry data and is applicable to other fluid dynamics problems governed by the Euler equations. In addition, we derive an explicit closed-form solution for the steady-state shallow water equations on a straight riverbed, providing a precise reference for evaluating the accuracy of the fast solver models. Our findings highlight the potential of these fast solver models to tackle complex fluid dynamics problems involving unknown boundary conditions, with potential applications in other compelling use cases. Our code is publicly accessible on the UCI Machine Learning Repository. In this research, the parameters used are: $h_{ref}=1$, $g=9.81$, $L=10$, $T=1$, and $Fr=1$. We define the Rossby number as $Ro=\frac{T}{L}/\sqrt{L^{2}/(T^{2})}=1$. We normalize the Euler equations using these non-dimensional groups, resulting in the following equation: $\frac{1}{Fr^{2}}\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{Ro^{2}}}\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{Ro^{2}}}\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}+uv=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{Ro^{2}}}$, where $v$ and $u$ represent the flow velocities in the $y$ and $x$ directions, respectively. This study focuses on the rotationless case

Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. This will lead to more accurate and generalizable predictions and inferences, though significant hurdles remain due to the diverse nature of methods within this field. A new publication addresses this challenge by categorizing methods within causal deep learning, refining Pearl's causal hierarchy while considering parametric assumptions and input/representation structures. The resulting framework provides researchers with a map for benchmarking, comparing methods, and identifying knowledge gaps across machine learning disciplines, such as supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling. The authors open-source this framework for the research community to use, with potential applications in guiding related work sections and highlighting paper contributions. By sharing this framework with the scientific community, the associated guidelines can elevate the quality of presentations and facilitate more engaging communication in machine learning research. Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three-dimensional temperature maps produced as a result. The findings show significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, corroborated by optical temperature probe measurements, with an average error of 1.5°C. The presented MRI thermometry technique presents new avenues for the in-depth study of mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds, potentially being adapted for further applications in reactive gas-solid systems in the future. This method's capabilities are demonstrated through a comparative analysis of reactor temperature profiles at varying airflow rates, revealing the intricate effects of turbulent mass transfer on temperature distribution. The associated numerical simulation results from a state-of-the-art multi-scale reactor model validate the findings, highlighting the potential of this technique to investigate heat transfer mechanisms influenced by reactive mass transfer in gas-solid fixed beds. This novel imaging temperature distribution measurement method is anticipated to pave the way for a broader range of reactive gas-solid systems. This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work. Additionally, this report proves that another consequence of the b-principle, related to the derivation of colored mixed invariant varieties, is feasible only if the abelian category of Calabi-Yau manifolds from mirror symmetry has infinite growth. This report's conclusions lead to novel applications of the b-principle with maps to the derivation of colored mixed invariant varieties, the investigation of oriented colored broken submersions, and the exploration of infinite growth in the abelian category of Calabi-Yau manifolds from mirror symmetry. It also introduces the concept of geometric blow-up and its associated blow-up maps, which can be characterized as oriented colored broken submersions. Further, it discusses how geometric blow-up and its map can be viewed as an extension of the standard blow-up process encountered in algebraic geometry. This report also presents an advanced application of the abelian category technology from mirror symmetry at the stable map component, which can be viewed as a variation of the well-known Witten conjecture. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation. The results demonstrate the capability of these solvers to efficiently handle the intricate computations required for realistic simulations of heart function. The project's success underscores the potential of advanced numerical methods to benefit various other complex medical physics applications. The project's results are also expected to guide the development of more comprehensive modeling of heart disease. The researcher expects this project to contribute meaningfully to several fronts related to computational cardiology, including cardiac mechanics modeling, nonlinear finite elasticity formulations, high-performance, parallel, iterative solution methods, large-scale finite element applications, BDDC algorithms, algebraic multigrid methods, performance evaluation, and capability development for multi-block and coupled problems. The project's outcomes are anticipated to benefit various other complex medical physics applications, providing further guidance on heart disease development and informing future modeling improvements. The associated source code is now publicly accessible as part of the Solida project within the Claws project's GitHub repository. The standard scaled Wigner matrix and its corresponding semi-circular distribution, particularly its 2kth moment which relates to non-crossing pair-partitions of the set {1, 2,... 2k}, has been extensively studied. Building upon existing knowledge, this paper contributes a broader extension that also reveals novel insights. Given an $n \times n$ symmetric matrix with independently distributed entries under certain assumptions, our study confirms that a limiting spectral distribution indeed exists with probability or certainty. However, this limit can be understood through more extensive partitions, giving rise to intriguing combinatorial problems. As a result, several existing spectral distribution theories, such as those concerning standard Wigner, Erdos-Renyi graph, heavy-tailed Wigner, and variance-profile Wigner matrices, can be derived or further refined. Moreover, our findings cater to matrices with rapidly decreasing entry variances or shrinking entry magnitudes. To establish these results, new techniques are developed to accommodate (asymmetric) matrix arrays with dependent entries. Ultimately, our work empowers the application of spectral distribution tools to investigate the spectral properties of various quadratic forms and Toeplitz matrices. To demonstrate this potential, several specific problems are explored and several open questions are posed. By combining combinatorial and analytical approaches, our study weaves an intriguing narrative at the intersection of matrix theory, spectral distribution, and statistical physics. In doing so, it provides explicit formulas linked to non-crossing partition enumerators and related bi-variate Brownian motion excursion measures, further highlighting the relevance of our results to random graph and random process theory. While focused on symmetric matrices, the introduced methods also facilitate the extension of several results concerning quadratic forms and Toeplitz matrices. Lastly, our studies give rise to novel applications concerning the spectral distribution of random graph Laplacian and normalized random matrix arrays. By establishing these connections, our research offers a comprehensive exploration of the fundamental properties of random matrix spectra. Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at the MHz frequencies common in ultrasound imaging due to difficulties in fabricating complex microstructures. Advances in two-photon polymerization now enable precise manufacture of sub-wavelength structures in this range. However, shrinking structures in size introduces another challenge, where increased thermoviscous effects lead to considerable energy losses, which need to be factored into the design. This work introduces three novel microacoustic metagrating designs capable of refracting normally incident waves by approximately 35 degrees at 2 MHz, utilizing shape optimization techniques and the linearized Navier-Stokes equations. Using two-photon polymerization, we fabricated and experimentally validated microscopic acoustic metamaterials, successfully redirecting incident waves and verifying that a 0.29 wavelength-thick microacoustic metagrating can efficiently allocate 90% of transmitted energy into the -1st diffraction order. This breakthrough paves the way for creating complex acoustic phantoms and precise ultrasound imaging systems. Moreover, these microacoustic metagratings offer potential applications in manipulating a wide range of linear waves in fluids.

Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants. Notably, we discover that diffusion spread follows a specific distribution that describes standard diffusive spreading in populations over time. We further develop a simulation tool that allows users to personalize their own fractionally correlated diffusion scenarios. Through numerical analysis and visually stimulating animations, we illustrate the dynamic movement of the population and its resulting spatial distribution at any given time. This tool also highlights the interplay between individual characteristics, the population's spatial distribution, and the time-evolving nature of this interplay. It is available for download at the address listed in the authors' byline. The parameters that govern the fractionally correlated diffusion processes are not tunable in the provided software; however, the underlying processes are generally applicable and may be adapted to accommodate various parameters, including those associated with nonlinear diffusion processes. The understanding we have derived from this spread model can be applied across a broad spectrum, encompassing biological aggregations, nonlinear stochastic processes, and technical diffusion processes. A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to describe the dynamics of two identical counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and, under the condition of mode identity, it is proven that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation. This paper builds upon established connections between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in control systems that allow unbounded controls, encompassing polynomial control systems. Our analysis specifically addresses unbounded open-loop controls and discontinuous feedback stabilizers, which may lead to trajectories exhibiting chattering behavior near the target. A central aspect of our findings is the demonstration of the equivalence between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in these control systems or their impulsive system extensions. Moreover, we establish conditions under which controllers with chattering trajectories can be replaced by smooth, albeit infinitely long, control trajectories leading to global asymptotic controllability. These results are illustrated through application to a model involving competition between populations in an Lotka-Volterra systems and an impulsive system modeling the dispersal of insects. Additionally, we provide a theoretical framework and related proofs for key concepts, including the definition of global asymptotic controllability in control systems and impulsive systems, the existence of control Lyapunov functions, and the properties of discontinuous feedback stabilizers, along with conditions under which trajectories exhibiting chattering behavior can be replaced by smooth, infinitely long trajectories leading to global asymptotic controllability. This research is an extension of prior work by T. A. Henefski, addressing the smoothness of infinitely long trajectories in smooth control systems following target trajectories. A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed turbulent velocity patterns from limited-resolution data across a range of Reynolds numbers. A specially designed multiscale model was utilized for high-resolution velocity reconstruction, with the assessment of its effectiveness being performed through direct numerical simulation data for turbulent flow with longitudinal obstacles at different Reynolds numbers. The evaluation showed that this deep learning framework accurately replicates high-resolution velocity patterns and statistical measures from two low-resolution data sets. Furthermore, it was observed that this model successfully recreates turbulent velocity patterns at Reynolds numbers that it was not originally trained on. Additionally, statistical measures such as Reynolds stress were found to be closely replicated by this model across all tested Reynolds numbers. The findings also demonstrated that this deep learning framework can be trained in such a way that it can generate turbulent velocity patterns similar to those found in flows without obstacles, by training it on data related to flows with obstacles and removing the impact of obstacles statistically. Over time, this model's ability to accurately create turbulent velocity patterns across a broader range of large-scale wave numbers was confirmed through additional testing. It is hoped that this innovative approach will contribute to a deeper understanding of turbulent flows and the development of more effective numerical methods that can create high-resolution velocity patterns. The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration. Additionally, it is shown to excel in modeling uncertainty and can be particularly beneficial for applications involving sensory data, noisy data, and risk-sensitive scenarios.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is built around a central objective of locating a randomly placed target object on a map while subject to various rules and constraints. The system showcases its ability to evolve dynamically in response to changes, presenting a compelling showcase of a system that undergoes both gradual and abrupt changes, and requires learners to adapt their strategies accordingly. L2Explorer is designed to be highly customizable, with a modular architecture that makes it easy to modify the environment, transfer knowledge across related tasks, and compare the efficacy of various continual learning strategies. The platform has already given rise to several pioneering studies, and is now being made publicly accessible to fuel further innovation in this critical area of research. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors and incorrectly assess past performances. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, providing temporal process data and subsequently declarative process models. We validate this method through experiments and analyses, comparing it against changing real processes to ensure its effectiveness and accuracy. Our approach and associated test data are available online.

Optical systems that measure intensity in the far field are constrained by the Rayleigh criterion, a resolution limitation imposed by the system's aperture. Research has shown that using spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) allows for maximum collection of field information, thereby surpassing the Rayleigh criterion in certain cases. While previous SPADE approaches have relied on resolving the lateral splitting of a Gaussian wavefunction, our work investigates a novel scenario in which one of two photons from a bi-photon source, generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, undergoes a horizontal separation. Through coincidence measurements following the projection of both photons onto Hermite-Gauss modes, we demonstrate the ability to super-resolve this separation, a capability not attainable via standard SPADE techniques. Furthermore, our approach enhances the associated Fisher information by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$, where $K$ represents the Schmidt number that quantifies the entanglement between the two photons. We further illustrate the fundamental advantage of our SPADE approach over its counterpart by showing that it can reach values of $2K$ in situations where the alternative method fails short. Our proposed SPADE technique is applicable to any bi-photon source generated through spontaneous process, and associated with an unusual structure of the correlation function that is analytically exploitable only in cases where one of the photons exhibits complex Gaussian state. We hope that our work will inspire the creation of novel quantum imaging techniques utilizing SPADE. Moreover, our findings provide a framework for further research aimed at uncovering the potential limitations and advantages of other SPADE techniques.

We provide an in-depth explanation for this improvement, focusing on the unique structure of the correlation function associated with HG shaped photons and discuss how this outcome is attainable solely with complex Gaussian states.

This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties. Although the compactification problem has been a longstanding issue, this collection of observations aims to illustrate the value of Hodge-theoretic methods in this context. A key focus is on showing that certain compactifications, obtained through geometric construction, do in fact satisfy expected properties derived from the consideration of Hodge-theoretic invariants. This line of reasoning can be observed in the instances discussed here, involving the compactification of moduli spaces of varieties with certain properties and the construction of compact loci within parameter spaces of algebraic varieties. These discussions draw heavily from the research of Iwaniki, who used geometric construction to build a certain compactification and showed that its properties align with expectations based on the consideration of Riemann-Roch values. Similarly, the discussion here on the compact loci within parameter spaces of algebraic surfaces draws from the research of Ellveski and Koray, who constructed these loci through geometric construction and demonstrated that they do in fact contain the anticipated properties tied to the consideration of Hodge numbers. Lastly, the discussion here on the compactification of moduli spaces of algebraic surfaces draws from the research of Collet, Hayama, and Koray, who constructed this compactification through geometric construction and demonstrated that it does in fact satisfy the expected properties derived from the consideration of Hodge-theoretic invariants, specifically the volumes of singularities and the values of Delta-flatness. This collection of results highlights the effectiveness of both the geometric and Hodge-theoretic approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties. This work is further illustrated through the construction of compact loci within parameter spaces of algebraic surfaces and the compactification of moduli spaces of algebraic surfaces, drawing from the research mentioned above. In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the mixed-mode orbit, the model is reduced to a suitable normal form, located at the singular Hopf point. The resulting normal form reveals a separating surface that distinguishes two forms of oscillations, and the occurrence of a large amplitude oscillation depends on whether the trajectory crosses from the 'inner' to the 'outer' side of this boundary. Conditions derived from the normal form can predict whether the model will enter a regime of sustained oscillations and ultimately shift to its equilibrium state. These conditions, in turn, can be used to estimate the duration before the model reaches its equilibrium, and it is shown that this is comparable to the time it takes for the prey population to reach the model's equilibrium state. The concepts developed in this study can provide insights necessary to identify early warning signs for a prey population shift in real-world ecosystems. Furthermore, this study highlights the benefits of incorporating theoretical models in analyzing complex biological systems and predicting future developments. The methods employed in this analysis can also be applied to other models featuring a singular Hopf point and multiple coexisting populations in a food web. The data used in this study can be modified to accommodate additional variables, such as additional prey species or a different type of predator. The resulting models featuring multiple coexisting populations exhibiting mixed-mode oscillations, and the corresponding initiating factors for large amplitude oscillations, can provide valuable insights necessary to understand the dynamics of these complex biological systems. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. Recently, cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained more recognition due to their minimalistic design, potential for increased performance efficiency, and reduced energy consumption. However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to additional, unforeseen program behaviors and potential software vulnerabilities. In response to this risk, we propose a programming model and a corresponding type system to safely utilize coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade. By analyzing the relationships between memory accesses and taking into account the protocol's data dependencies, our type system can ensure that data consistency is maintained and prevent data access violations at compile-time. Moreover, it provides the greatest lower bounds on the accessibility of memory locations, thereby enabling optimizations for cache coherence protocols. To illustrate the effectiveness of our approach, we develop a number of examples, including a case study of a cache-coherent stream processor. The concept we present can also be applied beyond the specific cache coherence protocols mentioned. In particular, it finds application in any memory system where the interaction between writing and reading memory locations is defined by write semantics. The main concepts we introduce are available online at https://plume.17logic.com/cache-coherence/. The related code can be found at https://github.com/plume-ocaml/plume-cache-coherence/. The design was inspired by the Gengerelli et al.'s work on G-NOID and presented at ASPLOS 2020. In that research, designers implemented a specific cache coherence protocol based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade and a corresponding reordering engine for memory instructions. However, the researchers left unexplored the verification of safety properties related to data consistency in the presence of memory instruction reordering. In our work, we tackle this challenge head-on and establish that verifying safety properties concerning data consistency is possible even when memory instruction reordering is enabled. Furthermore, our approach can compile programs that run on machines utilizing coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade into verified programs. These verified programs can be executed by a model that incorporates the write semantics of the memory system, allowing for efficient optimization. Ultimately, our research paves the way for designing safe and efficient programs that can take full advantage of cutting-edge cache coherence technologies. In addition, our work opens up fresh perspectives on verifying safety properties concerning data consistency in the presence of memory instruction reordering. Conditions will be established under which the image $(B^{H}+f)(A)$ has a positive Lebesgue measure or a non-empty interior. This is achieved through investigating properties of the occupation measure's density for $(B^{H}+f)$, particularly proving that if the parabolic Hausdorff dimension of $f$ exceeds $Hd$, then its density function is square-integrable, or if $A$'s Hausdorff dimension surpasses $Hd$, then its density function admits a continuous version, thus providing a result already mentioned. Additional findings include: if the Hausdorff dimension of $f$'s range exceeds $Hd$, we can find a Lipschitz function on this range, and a similar conclusion holds for $f$ itself when its dimension surpasses $Hd$. These conditions are nearly optimal if $d>1$. Finally, an example showcasing a function with dimension equal to the Hurst index, whose range has the same dimension, is provided. This example also highlights the complexity that may arise when the function's dimension equals the Hurst index, particularly in regards to the density of its occupation measure. In the case where the function's range has the same dimension as the Hurst index, its density does not admit a continuous version, which contrasts with findings for fractional Brownian motion itself. This result implies that several results heretofore valid only for Brownian motion now extend to a broader class of self-similar processes. Moreover, this circumstance gives rise to several interesting phenomena, especially in relation to the density of the occupation measure's continuous version. Furthermore, this occupation measure's density function's continuity can be ensured through a much wider class of processes, including all those with stationary and invertible increments. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with severe symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies, this approach is shown to accurately identify key image characteristics associated with specific locations within the lungs. Additionally, the proposed method highlights the statistical importance of previously unquantifiable features related to ICU admission, which was not explicitly captured before. Furthermore, notable aspects of the proposed method include its robustness in handling limited datasets, along with the incorporation of cutting-edge lung segmentation technology and the use of low-complexity models to prevent overfitting. As a result, this approach has the potential to contribute to existing efforts dedicated to combating the COVID-19 pandemic. We re-examine and revise the predictions of the Universal Texture Zero (UTZ) flavour model as initially presented in the study arXiv:1710.01741. The revision is made with reference to more accurate experimental restrictions and refined numerical analysis methods. Specifically, our team developed an in-house Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to extensively evaluate the viable parameter range of the UTZ model, encompassing primary and secondary contributions in its effective operator expansion. Furthermore, we obtained for the first time precise UTZ predictions for previously underdetermined CP-violating phases of lepton interactions, and related neutrino mass characterizing ratio observables, that could be probed via oscillations, beta decay, and cosmological processes. Consequently, our revised analysis significantly surpasses the initial analysis and confirms that the UTZ theory remains a coherent and compelling flavour theory. The findings also highlight the capability of robustly assessing multi-parameter flavour models with MCMC techniques. Nonetheless, the study reveals that certain UTZ predictions exhibit sensitivity to certain lepton and quark interaction phenomena that have not been exhaustively explored within the framework. Consequently, the study anticipates that revisiting the UTZ model in the context of the most recent data related to quark mixing will be worthwhile.
