Current cutting-edge neural code models excel at generating individual code segments but often struggle with complex tasks, like entire function code production. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages static code analysis for weak supervision. Our neuro-symbolic method allows a deep generative model to leverage a static-analysis tool to identify code connections generated, and trains on this data to generate code based on this analysis during training. When tested on the task of creating full browser API utility functions, our results reveal our approach outperforms state-of-the-art transformer models and a method that tries to learn program meanings, exceling at error-free code accuracy (63.11% better than the best non-contextual baseline) and near-perfect error-free code rate (42.59% better than the best baseline). Moreover, code produced not only is highly functional, with 99% of our sample code collections working as intended, but also is more syntactically sound (43.18% better than the best baseline). We also observe that our approach produces more human-like code. We also successfully apply our method to a different domain, the generation of fully fleshed-out data access objects in Java. Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, can struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. We introduce a new technique for continuous real-time anomaly detection based on quantum measurements, which can process infinite data streams at constant $O(1)$ update complexity and effectively estimate changing densities through random Fourier features and an exponential moving average. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on 12 diverse data streams. The study involved a massive dataset comprising 1.2 million seconds of data from 50 classes and incorporated experiments using five frequent concept shifts, which showed our algorithm's ability to adapt quickly and achieve comparable or better results than other methods. The code and data are available at https://github.com/hengen Chen/quantro.

A pivotal question arises when a court possesses information that an individual knows the passcode to a device. To answer this inquiry, we develop a novel approach to an established legal doctrine, drawing on precedents set by the case of Fisher v. US. Our overarching objective is to create a framework that clarifies whether any action taken has already provided implicit evidence accessible to the authorities. Instead of addressing this overarching goal, this paper introduces a framework that identifies specific actions where any implicit evidence effectively becomes a foregone conclusion. At its core, this framework places the onus on the government to prove it is not leveraging the respondent's compliance. Building upon this, we introduce 'demonstrability' as a central concept to describe actions compelled by the authorities. Moreover, we develop a language that discerns whether an action is as efficacious as the government's intended goal. Subsequently, we apply our framework to evaluate the compelled actability of several cryptographic tools and phenomena. Notably, our assessment concludes that password entry, fingerprint scanning, and end-to-end encryption are not as efficacious as the government's intended goals, whereas encrypted communications and blockchain transactions could potentially be compelled acts. Lastly, we explore the interconnections between these various phenomena and the unique characteristics of each individual case. By doing so, we contend that even the most complex cryptographic tools hold value in being evaluated through the lens of our framework. Our work remains a starting point, and its contributions are intended to spark further inquiry into the interplay between cryptography and compelled actability in the context of law. Ultimately, we hope to contribute to the evolution of the Fisher standard in the era of modern cryptography. To this end, we propose a series of specific reforms that the courts and lawmakers could adopt. Lastly, we offer a broader theoretical framework that could be applied not just to cryptography but any technology or communication method yet to be invented. In this framework, we introduce the concept of 'functional compellability' to describe any action that can be accomplished through an individual's compliance, and we explore its connections to existing legal doctrine. Additionally, we contend that even the most sophisticated technology holds value in being evaluated through the lens of this framework, and we hope to contribute to the ongoing evolution of the law in this context. In doing so, we specifically address the case of end-to-end encryption and compelled decryption. Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an element that is at least as acceptable as all other elements.

A new PTAS is presented for general-valued CSPs with constraints that have distinct values, such as 0 and 1, but with specific limitations. The technique was previously applicable to classes where Baker's approach worked, except possibly fractionally-treewidth-fragile classes. The findings relax the monotonicity condition of the constraints, allowing a new property called diagonalisability. A diagonalisability test is also provided for classes that are already known to have a limited tree-width. The research also includes the identification of new classes with limited fractional treewidth and the implementation of a publicly accessible tool that can determine the applicability of PTAS to custom classes. The technology underpins the approximation solution of various CSPs, covering topics like combinatorial optimisation, graph theory and artificial intelligence. This study presents a novel, high-order numerical method for solving the linear Fokker-Planck equation under a constant diffusion term. The devised method integrates elements from the Lagrange-Galerkin and semi-Lagrangian techniques, yielding an explicit, conservative, consistent, and robust scheme capable of handling substantial time step sizes. A convergence analysis for the exactly integrated Lagrange-Galerkin approach is provided, along with an implementable alternative that employs approximate integration. The method is particularly useful in modeling time-dependent mean field games systems, enabling high-order solution approximations. A series of numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy. Notably, it is shown that the method can solve a heavy-traffic, systemically important financial institution problem with endogenous fundamental asset price dynamics. The problem involves a large number of state variables and the introduction of a robust solution technique for similar problems is seen as significant. Furthermore, possible directions for future research along with previously unpublished findings are presented, offering practitioners a comprehensive guide to efficiently develop, train, and understand the inner workings of DNNs. Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy, valley interference and the location of the dopants on Heisenberg's spin exchange interaction in silicon.
The findings indicate that exchange interaction becomes immune to valley interference by arranging in-plane dopants in particular directions aligned with the crystallographic orientation, ultimately retrieving vacuum-like characteristics where the exchange interaction maximizes the overlap between donor orbitals, and the variation in pairs is minimized to less than 10-fold.
This robust exchange interaction remains over a considerable distance range, from a high-fidelity quantum computation regime influenced by Coulomb interaction to coupled donor arrays used in quantum simulations in silicon.

We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory, utilizing the properties of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra. Moreover, we develop an approach to determine the generating functions for these counts, obtaining closed-form expressions that can be expressed in terms of an infinite system of equations over power series. We also explore connections to various combinatorial series, including the counts of Dyck paths, and present evidence suggesting these closed-form expressions are worthy of inclusion in established mathematical references. Furthermore, we introduce an alternative method to compute the stable homology modules of symmetric groups, obtaining results that align with existing knowledge for modules over the integers, while also establishing a direct relationship between the counts of certain binary integer partitions and the computation of stable homology modules. This relationship extends beyond the symmetric groups, applicable to a broader class of group actions. We also introduce an order-preserving map between finite sets in the context of finite sets equipped with binary partitions, establishing a connection to the combinatorial series represented by ordered sets. We then present new formulas and computational tools accessible via our online calculator link, providing an engaging introduction to the fascinating world of binary integer partitions. The speed at which massive spectroscopic surveys collect data directly corresponds to the time it takes to observe a given target, which is influenced by the method used to assign targets to astrobots. The current method assigns targets randomly, which results in astrobots spending equal time observing all targets and can lead to coordination issues. We propose a new deblensing strategy based on the publication of known extragalactic objects, which sorts targets by their detection probability and assigns them to astrobots in a probabilistic order. This approach reduces the time spent observing each target and results in astrobots spending up to 50% more time observing their assigned targets, which decreases the survey speed by 30%. However, with optimal telescope configurations and a moderate number of astrobots, our proposed strategy yields a 1.5 times faster survey speed while maintaining similar coordinate issues with a smaller but still significant tail of long observations. We also found that sorting targets by their relevance to ongoing surveys and assigning them probabilistically can further improve the speed gain to 2 times the original rate, which comes with an additional cost of data storage and target acquisition. We present our results through both simulation and data from the KI Doppler Instrument and suggest our method as a suitable way to optimize the performance of existing and future spectroscopic surveys. We also introduce a publicly available Python package to reproduce our findings and make our method available for broad adoption.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As evidence of the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits, a case study is presented showcasing the GP 2 compiler's application in optimising the runtime efficiency of a program aimed at detecting binary DAGs. This previously time-consuming operation is now executed at a linear rate following the compiler upgrade. In addition, the compiler's accelerated version contributes to the speed improvement of the original program by a factor of over two orders of magnitude. Moreover, the researchers prove that the time complexity of the modified compiler is significantly reduced due to the introduction of rooted rules, despite its overall complexity remaining unchanged. In particular, this optimized compiler exhibits two key features: (a) its overall complexity is still non-deterministic polynomial time (NP); (b) its improved efficiency is attributable to the accelerated graph matching capability of rooted rules. In particular, this acceleration enables the compiler to efficiently apply a crucial program transformation known as the elimination of variables from the program's abstract syntax graph. In this process, program nodes are efficiently reconnected to their successors and ancestors following the removal of each variable. Although the modified compiler excels at this task, its effectiveness is limited to graphs featuring directed acycles and binary components. In such domains, the compiler can locate any subgraph comprising a directed cycle in linear time. As an extension to Bak's compiler, the novel structure BigArray also accelerates the compilation of programs that utilise dynamic arrays. This is because the compiler can now quickly identify any subgraph of a dynamic array within the program's abstract syntax graph. In domains where program variables are dynamically defined and modified, this feature significantly enhances the compiler's efficiency. In order to further accelerate the compiler, a new subalgorithm known as the binary deep-first search has been developed. This efficient algorithm is capable of locating any subgraph of a binary DAG within the program's abstract syntax graph in linear time. Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised learning applications. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised learning applications. Moreover, two specific techniques, including a method for unsupervised learning application and a technique for supervised learning application, are proposed. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive simulations, including both unsupervised and supervised learning applications, by conducting multiple experiments. The results show that our proposed framework surpasses existing methods, with our technique for supervised learning application even achieving performance comparable to that of fully supervised learning methods. The code is available at: <https://github.com/zhengdw/Contrastive-Feature-Extraction>.

We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs. This category also includes the Johnson graphs $J_n$ for $n$ greater than 4 and certain distanced graphs, such as the Coxeter graphs $C_{2[3]}(4)$ and $C_{3[4]}(5)$. Moreover, our work extends a theorem of Zhi-qiang Wang on infinite groups containing a faithful, locally arc-transitive action. We demonstrate that any group featuring a locally arc-transitive action on an infinite graph must contain a finite, arc-transitive subgroup with an infinite, star-or-twisted-star partitioning. This achievement culminates in the extension of a conjecture of Giudici, Li, and Praeger to its full generality. It is also shown that any group with a locally arc-transitive, infinite graph action must have a finite, abelian, addable subgroup or be non-amenable. This research is accompanied by numerous open questions waiting to be explored. Some of these questions have already been answered through additional research. Still, many others remain unanswered, promising further discoveries within this captivating field of mathematical study. This paper is part of the longer PhD thesis of the first-named author, completed under the supervision of the second-named author. It is also accompanied by an appendix detailing the construction of a new locally arc-transitive graph, the Generalized Coxeter graph $C_{3[4]}(5)$, whose order is $2^{25}$· $3^{15}$· $5^{10}$. This new graph is a key part of the infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs described by the main theorem. It is essential to note that in the original thesis, the determination of the degree of the vertex in the twisted star orbit had been incorrectly identified as $d$ instead of $d-1$. Similarly, the original version incorrectly stated that the graph $C_{3[4]}(5)$ would have a vertex degree of 20, when in fact it has a vertex degree of 19. Model selection and sparse modeling are crucial in dimension reduction for high-dimensional categorical data. However, creating algorithms for such tasks is complicated by the lack of a standard distance metric for categorical variables. This paper introduces a novel technique that leverages a distributed model, allowing for the dimension reduction of high-dimensional categorical data in a sparse and compact form. This method first identifies a primary category that represents the largest proportion of data and ranks the remaining categories in descending order of their relevance. A category's relevance is determined by its ability to distinguish between different observations and its ability to predict the corresponding value of the primary category. Through extensive simulations and real-world applications, this paper demonstrates the superiority of its proposed technique over established methods such as PCA, MDP, and the Hamming distance-based method in reducing dimensions while maintaining high recovery rates and minimal error. This technique is also highly efficient, with an average runtime that is at least 5 times faster than other methods for medium to large datasets. It has been implemented as an R function available on the author's personal website.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly improves performance when utilizing smaller knowledge graphs. One key advantage of this method is the absence of a requirement to synchronize knowledge graphs with text data, making it highly suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs. Available data and implementation can be found at https://github.com/ghruus/wikidata-pair-precise. Overall, our experiments represent a crucial breakthrough, as this work lays the groundwork for utilizing large knowledge graphs with rich structure to enhance LLM's conceptual understanding and multi-step reasoning capabilities. In doing so, it paves the way for more effective use of structured knowledge within these models, ultimately enabling them to better navigate complex domains and scenarios. This work's effectiveness is further highlighted by its ability to accurately complete knowledge graph triples by selecting relevant entities within a larger set of options. In this context, our approach achieves a 50% increase in Wikidata's quality when selecting top 5 entities for each statement. Moreover, we successfully employ this method to enhance the performance of LLMs in three additional evaluation benchmarks, involving both natural language inference and the integration of knowledge graph descriptions. These results validate the potential of this approach to enhance the structural knowledge capabilities of these models, enabling them to effectively utilize complex knowledge graphs that incorporate vast amounts of information. When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly, thus reducing the necessary alignment parameters to one dimension. Taking advantage of this assumption, novel simplified approaches to stitching panoramic images from rotating cameras have been developed, focusing on cameras with the same optical centers. Four realistic scenarios, accounting for unknown and varying focal lengths as well as radial distortion, are explored in this context. Comprehensive testing of the proposed methods was conducted using artificially created scenes and over 500k pairs of real images obtained from the Sun360 dataset and from scenes taken with the aid of smartphones equipped with sensors that track the direction of gravity. These methods demonstrate superiority over current techniques in terms of precision and processing speed. Moreover, detailed analysis of factors influencing performance is included, demonstrating that spherical reconstruction accurately reflects the alignment performance when compared to actual reconstructed spheres. All methods have shown performance on par with professional software like Microsoft PCF. The code is available for review at https://github.com/alexmikee/Simplified_Panorama_Stitching. The findings related to the effectiveness of aligning cameras to the vertical axis on the accuracy of stitching images are also presented. Data processed and methods analyzed demonstrate that the accuracy of stitching can be improved significantly, with an average error of 0.695 degrees when images are aligned vertically and 13.52 degrees when they are not aligned this way. Further research is needed to determine if these findings are representative of all capture scenarios. The work presented concepts and methods that could contribute to the development of automated panoramic capture systems using portable devices equipped with sensors that track the direction of gravity. This study develops a novel biophysical brain model for areas associated with Parkinson's disease, utilizing local field potential data obtained from marmoset monkey brains. Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupts normal basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex function. Despite multiple contributing mechanisms, a comprehensive explanation and effective cure for the disease remain elusive. In response to this gap, computational models incorporating aspects of animal models have been suggested. Our model leverages a data-driven strategy to optimize parameters with a differential evolution method. Successful outcomes from the evolved models closely matched observed firing rates and spectral characteristics of local field potentials from healthy and diseased marmoset brain data. Notably, this research presents the first Parkinson's disease computational model built from concurrent electrophysiological recordings across seven marmoset brain regions. The findings suggest our proposed model can facilitate the exploration of disease mechanisms and contribute to the development of novel therapeutic approaches. Additionally, it may be applied to various computational neuroscience challenges where biological data can inform multi-scale brain circuit models. In particular, this work proposes several potential research directions to explore the interplay between dopamine and the basal ganglia in relation to action and movement, and suggests that such models could be used in conjunction with training methods such as reinforcement learning to examine the pathophysiological mechanisms associated with Parkinson's disease. The model and associated code are available online. 

This work is part of the brain research project led by Professor Kenji Doya at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology. The project aims to create a computational brain model by integrating electrophysiological recordings from a marmoset monkey brain and solving a puzzle represented by the animal's behavior. The project's goal is to resolve the mystery of how the marmoset obtained food that was partially hidden in a complex box-based puzzle setup. The project consists of several sub-projects, one of which is the Parkinson's disease-related research project presented in this paper. The project's leader is Dr. Taro Sasagawa, and the research was conducted at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology. The project resulted in a paper published in the journal Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience. The project was supported by the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology and the Japan Agency for Medical Research and Development. The associated code is available online at https://github.com/sasagawa-lab/PD-model and the model is registered on the Open Source Brain repository

However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance algorithm utilizing two triangles to replicate fan-shaped line joins via alpha operation. Our findings indicate this technique yields a genuine anti-aliasing effect while reducing memory consumption, raising frame rates, and preventing overlap rendering in map visualization. Our novel anti-aliasing method has been applied in notable applications such as Tencent Mobile Maps and Tencent Automotive Maps. Moreover, our technique boasts ease of use as it can be incorporated into existing rendering engines with minimal modification. Our research also includes a detailed analysis of optimization techniques employed to meet high automation standards in the gaming industry. The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy. In particular, we observe that using this new interpolation function leads to lower errors compared to the traditional multivariate interpolation method.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations. 
Our experiment reveals that initial over-reliance on complex architecture is counterproductive and ultimately achieves a precise classification rate of 65%. 
This research serves as a starting point for further development of transportation systems that can adapt to diverse weather conditions.

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model. The code is available online at this link: https://github.com/hjdw/hh20210126_DPCRN.

A new statistics methodology is introduced, focused on the turn-around radii of cluster halos to break the degeneracy between $\Lambda$CDM, alternative $f(R)$ gravity models, and massive neutrinos cosmologies characterized by fifth force strength and total neutrino mass. By analyzing the rockstar halo catalogs at the present epoch from the DUSTGRAIN-pathfinder $N$-body simulations of four distinct cosmologies, including $\Lambda$CDM, fR6, fR6+$0.06$eV, and fR5+$0.15$eV, the method evaluates the probability distribution of ratios between turn-around radii and virial counterparts, effectively distinguishing between these cosmologies. It is found that fR6 and fR5+$0.15$eV can be differentiated by $10\sigma$ difference and $\Lambda$CDM and fR6+$0.06$eV can be differentiated by $3.2\sigma$ difference. Furthermore, the models exhibit decreasing differences in the probability distribution at higher redshifts. The method provides a possible solution to the cluster mass function tension and implies that future cluster counts with significant statistical power will be sensitive to fifth force and neutrino properties. Additionally, it is anticipated that future constraints from this method, in combination with weak lensing and cluster physics, will be capable of tightly constrain the total neutrino mass to be less than $0.045$eV or have negative values for certain $f(R)$ gravity models. The method is robust and model-independent, focused on the ratio of turn-around to virial radii, exhibiting minimal dependencies on simulation parameters, such as resolution, smoothing, and gravitational softening. The method is applicable to turn-around radii within $10^{-2}<s/ R_{\rm virial} < 10^2$, covering the majority of cluster halo profiles. The method is envisioned to be an invaluable tool for interpreting future observations of cluster sizes and masses. The code used for the method is publicly available and can be adapted to turn-around radii-based statistics in various cosmological contexts. Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. This study explores a single-column, turbulent convection model based on the Eulerian multi-fluid framework and investigates various solution strategies for the equations. Ultimately, a simple forward-stepping method was discovered to successfully replicate the development of gravity waves and accurately predict the enhancement of vertical wind speed and temperature fluctuations within models. While this model still underrepresents the magnitude of wind and temperature variance when compared to observations, it marks an important step towards creating a more realistic multi-fluid model of convection through the simulation of highly non-linear atmospheric turbulence. This research is also accompanied by an open-source code that can be used within the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts model frameworks. Lastly, the simplicity of this model allows for faster computation, taking around 10 minutes to replicate one month of convection per core on a modern computer. This model's speed and openness provides for further research possibilities, including the exploration of its suitability for assessing the impacts of changing climate and geography on convection. This could one day serve as a precursor to more complex multi-fluid models of convection, which will rely on its results to inform their development. This preliminary model is now available online at GitHub, along with the code necessary to replicate its outcomes within the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts model structure. This includes the option to run the model with localised changes that reflect specific geographic regions, such as high-latitude or tropical territories. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to the creation of more realistic multi-fluid models of convection within weather and climate simulations, which will be capable of replicating the scale of wind and temperature variance observed at these levels of resolution. While this model represents a significant step in this direction, much work remains to be done before it becomes a viable alternative to the mass-flux scheme. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior. Our study provides a theoretical basis for using shadow radius as a thermal entropy probe in future multicomponent non-linear gravity frameworks. Moreover, it highlights the potential for shadow radius to reveal hidden phase transition details in black holes and suggests that it can serve as an effective tool for investigating the thermodynamics of black holes that interact with scalar hair components. Lastly, it paves the way for further research into the interrelation between shadow radius, thermal profile behavior, and non-linear gravity multicomponent frameworks. This could lead to a deeper understanding of how black holes interact with their surrounding environment and shed light on the characteristics of gravitational waves emitted from these complex gravitational systems. This could ultimately enable the direct detection of gravitational waves produced by black hole mergers involving scalar hair components. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Additionally, we propose practical experiments to demonstrate this concept at different levels of complexity, involving a single cavity field, two coupled cavities, and an extended network of cavities. Our findings showcase the value of optical tomogram analysis beyond state reconstruction, offering a simpler yet still revealing approach to study complex phenomena involving the entanglement of continuous-variable systems. This new perspective is expected to lead to a deeper understanding of these intricate quantum systems. 

This work is part of the special collection of selected papers from the 19th Congress of the Latin-American Physical Society held in Buenos Aires, Argentina from November 16 to 20, 2020. 

Keywords: optical tomogram analysis, Wigner function, entanglement in continuous-variable systems, quantum synchronization, cavity QED system.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, thereby enabling the creation of role-compliant dialogue
datasets from scratch. Furthermore, we examine various open-domain dialogue
system architectures in terms of their ability to meet role specifications and
maintain natural conversation. Results from both automatic and human evaluations
reveal that our models perform satisfactorily in terms of role conformance, while
still delivering competitive performance on overall conversational metrics. The code
and models developed as part of this project are openly accessible at https://github.com/ghrua/open-domain-dialogue-role-constraints.

Farmers utilize pesticides to minimize crop losses, but their effectiveness often depends on analyzing average treatment benefits and risks. Evaluating pesticide efficacy using certainty equivalents and ranking treatment efficiency through stochastic efficiency is a common practice. However, the major drawback of this approach is collecting sufficient and relevant field data. Since farmers typically perform multiple pesticide applications and cannot feasibly test each pesticide individually, a new method using optimal design strategies is proposed to rank pesticides based on in-field data collection. This method considers the variability of each pesticide's effectiveness and optimal field data collection points are identified through optimization techniques. A comparison of this method with random data collection strategies reveals significant improvements, resulting in more accurate rankings. To apply this method, a publicly accessible Pesticide Data Collection Optimization software tool was developed and demonstrated using real-world data scenarios. This tool provides users with previously unknown optimal design strategies, leading to more effective pesticide usage and reduced data collection costs. As a result, farmers can make data-driven decisions to optimize pesticide efficacy. This approach can be adapted to other applications involving multiple treatments and variable efficacy in different locations. To facilitate further research, all developed methods, including a comparison of numerical solutions to optimal design strategies, have been incorporated into an openly accessible MATLAB code repository linked to this paper. To ensure effectiveness in various scenarios, the proposed method was tested with multiple real-world datasets, presenting opportunities for numerical analysis and further improvement of data collection efficiency. As such, this innovative method has the potential to benefit various fields involving multiple treatments and variable efficacy in different locations. 360-degree streaming videos offer engaging and immersive experiences but
require significant bandwidth. A common strategy to minimize this demand is
streaming just the part of the video that is within a viewer's field of view.
To accomplish this, a precise forecast of a viewer's viewpoint is crucial. In
the current approach to viewport prediction, primary emphasis is placed on
tracking user head movements and identifying areas of high visual importance
within the video. Nevertheless, neither of these methods takes into account
the crucial navigation data embedded in video subtitles. Such data, particularly
found in 360-degree virtual tourism videos, can significantly steer user
attention toward certain parts of the video. Consequently, it indicates that
video subtitles have substantial value to contribute in this context. Hence, a
new subtitle-driven viewport prediction model for 360-degree virtual tourism
videos has been proposed. By integrating data from video subtitles in addition
to head movements and visual importance, the proposed model's precision in
predicting user views is significantly enhanced. Experimental results confirm
that the proposed model performs superiorly when compared to the existing
baseline approaches relying solely on head movements and visual importance for
viewport prediction. Moreover, an observation made is that the navigation
guidance contained in video subtitles will grow in importance as more video
content with embedded subtitles becomes available in the future. The proposed
model's capabilities can be harnessed through a newly introduced subtitle-driven
attention prediction framework, in which attention at each video frame is
forecasted in accordance with the navigational data embedded within the video
subtitles. This framework's efficacy in predicting user attention across 360-degree
virtual tourism videos was successfully demonstrated. The proposed model's
code is openly accessible for replication and extension at this link: https://github.com/ananag5/svd-apm. As the number of frogs per site grows, the frog model's behavior shifts from transient to recurrent on a d-ary rooted tree. We demonstrate that this critical transition occurs roughly around the tree's degree. Specifically, we show that if the tree is a d-ary rooted tree and the frog model uses parameters (c, p), where c is the average number of frogs per site and p is the probability of a frog moving, the model exhibits a persistent behavior if the tree is a k-ary rooted tree and the parameters satisfy the condition k < c/p. The condition k < c/p is also sufficient for the model to be transient. Furthermore, we outline various methods to calculate the model's transient expectations and prove that the frog model's speed on a d-ary rooted tree is approximately (c/p) * (1 - 1/d). We also explore the implications of our results on a binary tree and provide more precise analyses of the model's behavior under different parameter settings. Lastly, we discuss the challenges and possibilities associated with extending our findings to other types of graph structures. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite some existing methods for constructing sublattice components, few approaches exist for building the total lattice of submodules. In this study, we introduce an algorithm to construct the join irreducible submodules of a given module, and demonstrate its applicability by leveraging these submodules to build the total lattice of submodules of a given prevariety type. This method's efficacy is illustrated through specific examples of modules and their constructed lattices of submodules. The proposed algorithm is then compared to existing construction methods, with an analysis conducted on its computational efficiency for multiple sample modules. The source code related to this research is freely accessible online. The research is grounded in the context of order theory and module theory. A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. SGR is found to be NP-complete. Research into SGR is conducted, and comparisons of computational complexities are made across various graph types, including the derivation of efficient algorithms, NP-completeness proofs, and preliminary results on parameterized complexity, which provide insight into the complexity of SG, particularly in chordal graphs. A chordal graph containing a strong geodetic subset can be identified in linear time. The determination of the strong geodetic number in chordal graphs is NP-hard. The development of a exact algorithm for SGR on chordal graphs is achieved, utilizing a vertex elimination order, and an iterative search method, with an algorithmic complexity of $O(|V| \cdot |E| \cdot 2^{|V|})$. An iterative deepening depth-first search is employed to enhance computation efficiency, particularly in finding a minimum strong geodetic subset within graphs, which has been shown to be NP-hard. The development of a exact algorithm for SGR on minimal chordal graphs is achieved, with an algorithmic complexity of $O(|V|^5)$, and is derived from a general approach applicable to all graphs. Research is also conducted on a generalized version of the Strong Geodetic problem (SGG), which involves the selection of a vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$, which establishes unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$, and covers the remaining vertices in~$G$. The determination of SGG is NP-complete, with an algorithmic complexity of $O(|V|^5)$ for minimal chordal graphs, and an algorithmic complexity of $O(|V| \cdot |E| \cdot 2^{|V|})$ for all graphs. The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal expert examples. Nonetheless, getting numerous high-quality examples from human experts is very costly. On the other hand, getting vast amounts of low-quality or irrelevant paths in a task can be quite easy, but these paths aren't helpful for imitation. Nonetheless, these suboptimal paths still provide insight into the system dynamics and what actions are feasible within that environment. This study investigates whether these suboptimal paths can be utilized to enhance imitation learning performance using new objectives that learn a factored transition model. The learned model allows us to derive a latent action space, making downstream imitation learning much more efficient by reducing the necessity for extensive expert datasets. This is achieved by leveraging additional non-expert data. Specifically, this is shown through experiments on both gridworld and robotic manipulation simulations, where performance is enhanced when using the derived action space in both offline and online settings. This study's results demonstrate its performance superiority to multiple baselines, leading to a significant performance improvement over imitation learning methods that don't account for system dynamics. This leads to a considerable performance improvement over baseline methods that don't consider the underlying dynamics of a system when provided a large amount of non-expert data. This is demonstrated through experiments conducted on gridworld and robotic manipulation simulations. The code for this study is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/factored-transition-models. This work is licensed to the Creative Commons Attribution License CC-BY @2023 The authors.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often expensive, limiting the adoption of imitation learning in resource-constrained scenarios. In response to this challenge, we propose a resource-aware imitation learning framework that allocates available resources between learning policies and collecting expert data, with the goal of maximizing future learning performance while adhering to budget constraints. Our framework is versatile and compatible with both maximum likelihood and minimum prediction error methods. We evaluate our approach on a multi-vehicle management problem, a complex and dynamic scheduling scenario that requires concurrent action taken by multiple agents, subject to individual capacity constraints. Our results show that our approach outperforms conventional global optimization methods and offline multi-agent reinforcement learning methods. This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which significantly improve average decoder computations. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate that search-limited PAC codes can achieve error-correction performance near that of polar codes under successive cancellation list decoding, with a list size of 64 and a threshold of 0.492. Further investigation into our results suggests that the performance advantage of PAC codes can be attributed to the rarity of costly decoding computations rather than the benefit of biased metric functions. Consequently, our proposed method may be beneficial for various applications, such as battery-efficient communication devices that can handle complex encoders and decoders in low-energy modes. In such scenarios, our results imply that PAC codes, despite their computational efficiency in typical scenarios, may exhibit considerable decoding flexibility, which can be exploited through adaptive computation protocols that adjust decoding computations based on the specific application requirements and environmental conditions. Moreover, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in other contexts, such as the decoding of binary linear codes, turbo codes, and low-density parity-check codes, as well as the encoding of polar codes, convolutional codes, and binary linear codes. Lastly, our work paves the way for further research into the fundamental properties of PAC codes and its potential generalizations to other coding schemes. Moreover, our results are a starting point for investigating the potential connections between PAC codes and other cutting-edge research areas, such as the study of tail-spitting codes and the applications of computational statistics in coding theory. In addition, our work provides several new research directions, such as the extension of our results to multi-bit codes, the development of innovative search-limited decoding techniques, and the exploration of new metrics and computation models that can enhance the error-correction performance of PAC codes and other coding schemes. Lastly, our results feature several coding-theoretic phenomena that remain unexplained

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose based on rotation and keypoint data. Enhanced system robustness is achieved through a combination of advanced algorithms, including the iterative closest point method, multi-frame processing, filtering, and outlier detection. Results show our method's calibration and pose estimation capabilities can be as precise as sub-centimeters and sub-degrees with minimal and unseen test poses; we have also found that incorporating data from just one optimal pose yields comparable accuracy. Notably, our approach boasts significant advantages over traditional approaches that utilize fiducial markers by eliminating the need for hardware modification and marker-related calibration issues. Additionally, it offers a simpler, more efficient alternative to calibration systems that rely on simulation. With no assumptions or constraints needed, our method can be used with any object and end-effector design. Our system's code is openly available online.

This study introduces two key concepts, quasi-finitely separating maps and quasiapproximate identities, which form the basis for the definitions of QFS-spaces and quasicontinuous maps. Building upon these definitions, various properties and characteristics of QFS-spaces are investigated. Key findings include: Firstly, any QFS-space is inherently a quasicontinuous space; secondly, closed subspaces, as well as quasicontinuous projection spaces, derived from QFS-spaces are themselves QFS-spaces; thirdly, continuous retracts of QFS-spaces possess the same characteristic and specific types of QFS-space retracts can be constructed; lastly, upper power spaces of continuous QFS-spaces correspond to FS-spaces. Moreover, the paper demonstrates that QFS-spaces can be generalized to create more extensive types of functional spaces and explores potential applications in the study of functional spaces within the framework of point-free topology. Additionally, an appendix provides a detailed analysis of the relationship between QFS-spaces and the FS-space constructor. Lastly, the paper suggests a novel approach to constructing lower separation types within functional spaces. Consequently, this research provides a foundational groundwork for a broader study of quasiapproximate identities and their associated spaces within the context of point-free topology. Moreover, potential usefulness of lower separation types in general topology has also been revealed. A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem in integer base systems. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that both natural order relation and modulo-q operator are not recognisable within base p/q systems. Finally, our research provides an example of a recognisable but not decidable set in base p/q systems. This set, named Sn, comprises words that evaluate to natural numbers n in base p/q. Although we can determine if a given word belongs to Sn, there is no automated method to determine if a word's evaluation will consistently be greater than or equal to a specific number. This is in contrast to base systems that rely on prime numbers, such as base p systems, where natural order relation is recognisable. Our research expands the parameters of finite automata-equipped number systems by showing that simple systems like base p/q can exhibit complex behavioural traits. This is demonstrated through the existence of a set that is recognisable but has an undecidable property when considering all possible extensions of base p/q systems. Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis to examine the nature of dark matter within this framework. The presence of an inflection point within Higgs inflation is found not to significantly impact dark matter composition, and thus the model instead presents a multicomponent DM system involving axions and sterile neutrinos. As a result, we are able to relate the axion parameters, including the axion decay constant, to the neutrino parameters within this DM system. The model incorporates a variety of DM creation mechanisms such as the axion production resulting from both the alignment mismatch and the decay of topological defects. In addition, it also includes sterile-neutrino creation via both the resonant and non-resonant mechanisms as well as a more recently proposed model involving CPT symmetry. The resulting analysis allows us to explore the connections between the parameters of these DM components and how they influence the neutrino spectrum and other areas of the model. The model is found to be consistent with all experimental limitations and constraints. The next generation of experiments, consisting of axion and sterile-neutrino searches as well as a more refined understanding of the neutrino spectrum, will be capable of providing further insight into this model's parameters and thus itself. The implications of this model are also considered within the context of the Grand Unified Theory. The quantum gravity effects are also analyzed and the model is found to satisfy the conditions of the String Theory moduli space when unified with the $SO(10)$ GUT. The existence of a stable, light axion-like particle is also confirmed within this model's GUT framework. The existence of a high-scale GUT is found to influence the neutrino spectrum more greatly than the axion spectrum. The model is also found to contain a variety of other interesting features, including the possibility of both matter-antimatter parity and lepton number violation within this framework. The theoretical analysis of this model is further validated through the success of its numerical implementation within the 5d Effective Field Theory. The deconvolution of the 5d theory into its 4d components is also demonstrated and the parameters of the 4d theory are shown

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 in about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours, resulting in about 478,000 spectra with a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 in about 80% of its spectra. This study covered a total of around 11 million sources and a broad range of fields in the Milky Way, including areas with low and high extinction levels, areas surrounding open and globular clusters, and areas with ongoing and moderate star formation near bright blue giants. These new spectroscopic data will significantly enhance our understanding of various phenomena such as stellar streams, globular and open clusters, and the interstellar medium. Additionally, these data will also improve our knowledge of mass-clump systems and the distribution of massive clusters around Sgr A*. Furthermore, these observations marked the beginning of a new program called HOPE-PAL5 that aims to conduct various follow-up observations of pulsational patterns in stars located along the Pal 5 stream. These observations, which include medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, are expected to lay the ground work for a broader range of follow-up observations of the stream such as radial velocity surveys of streams and findings of stellar clusters within the solar radius. The effectiveness of this strategy was validated through a pilot study of around 2,600 low-resolution spectra from the LAMOST survey that showed a large number of its samples, around 84%, had a signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10. However, this study ran into schedule conflicts due to higher priority tasks such as the K2-18 exoplanet system discovery and the follow-up observations of the TESS discovery candidates. Consequently, the additional observations that were approved during this period were moved to a later observing period. Notwithstanding these conflicts, this study delivered a significant amount of valuable data that includes around 478,000 medium-resolution spectra with a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 in about 80% of its spectra, all of which were collected during 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours of observations. In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, capable of processing edge and texture information simultaneously. By prioritizing edge extraction and incorporating an auxiliary supervision, the EG-CNN module refines its output and merges it with original network predictions. We validate the performance benefits of the EG-CNN module when integrated with mainstream CNNs across two public benchmark datasets, highlighting consistent improvements in semantic segmentation precision and overall robustness. Moreover, explicit extraction of edge information enables future annotation guidance capabilities, paving the way for more engaging human-machine interactions. To facilitate replication, the code and model weights are freely available at https://github.com/yunhsun/Edge-Gated-CNNs.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. To facilitate future analysis of MongoDB's transaction protocols, we published our definitions and consistency guarantee checks on our website. Our work can serve as a reference point for understanding MongoDB's transaction protocols and their consistency guarantees, and it offers a practical approach for analyzing the transaction protocols of other distributed storage systems. Using the elementary symmetric function basis, we re-express the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths with a bounce number of three via a combinatorial interpretation related to the inverse of the Kostka matrix from Egecioglu-Remmel (1990). This analysis shows the positivity of specific coefficients and confirms $e$-positivity for an expanded class of these functions, beyond a particular instance explored in Cho-Huh (2019). Furthermore, we propose a broader conjecture relating to the Schur basis. Our approach is rooted in the recent study by Cho-Huh (2019), where the authors examined Dyck paths with a bounce number of three and extended the results to a broader class of posets structured as Cartesian products. We particularly investigate the underlying structure of these posets and suggest they comprise interval posets. By analyzing this interval structure, we are able to apply a combinatorial approach to re-express chromatic symmetric functions and provide support for a more comprehensive conjecture. This method may be useful for investigating other posets with similar structural characteristics. We also introduce a new polynomial expression called the inverse Kostka polynomial and list its properties. Moreover, we propose that this polynomial has a connection to the $h$-vector of posets. We begin by defining a task for few-shot continual learning and propose a theory to explain how executive function works through a self-updating decision-making system that reprocesses perception data through a review of past experiences in order to minimize prediction errors. This idea becomes practical due to the incorporation of a regression model that reflects the dynamics of an external environment and can be used to interpret neural network representations as forms of internal awareness and their relationships as forms of external reality knowledge. Our approach demonstrates excellent performance in learning new tasks with only a few examples, especially compared to standard cognitive architectures. Additionally, our approach makes significant contributions to the understanding of executive function, lesson learning, and the structure of the brain. It also sets a new standard for evaluation in research on artificial general intelligence. Furthermore, our approach has applications in the development of more realistic and effective artificial intelligence systems that learn through experience in a simulated or real world environment. We compare our approach to other methods for few-shot learning and found that it performs better than all of them. We also show that our approach is able to learn new languages easily and that it is able to combine existing knowledge in innovative ways. We present our approach as a new model for how the brain works and could be applied to other areas of machine learning, such as the study of learning in deep neural networks. We plan to expand our research to study how executive function learns new skills and abilities and how it is affected by external factors such as aging, injury, or different environments. We also plan to use our approach to create more realistic and effective artificial intelligence systems that learn through experience in a simulated or real world environment. The success of medical image analysis using machine learning largely relies on high-quality datasets.  However, when these datasets contain biases, the models can learn them, compromising their ability to generalize and produce reliable results.  While research exists on developing unbiased models, the problem lies in identifying and mitigating the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  In an effort to address this issue, we first establish a metric to quantify data intrinsic bias and propose a new framework for detecting biases in medical image datasets.  Our proposed framework, comprising of two primary components, namely KlotskiNet and Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis, aims to identify and quantify the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  Our experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in accurately identifying biases.  Furthermore, our findings highlight the critical difference between intrinsic and extrinsic biases in medical image datasets.  Our study represents a significant step towards creating unbiased medical image datasets capable of producing reliable results.  The code and models developed as part of this research are available for public access.  To further advance the field, we invite researchers to contribute their findings and share their own benchmarks within this framework. Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a higher-level structure that can be characterized through aggregates of interconnected triangles. To uncover these concealed geometric patterns, researchers are using topological methods and advanced graph theory to analyze and study dynamic processes occurring within these complex networks. This study leverages a recently developed model for triangle-based network assembly, where nanoscale triangular structures undergo spin reversal due to magnetic forces between connected nodes, fostering geometric frustration that drives novel phenomena in condensed matter physics. By manipulating the model's parameters, researchers observe how the shift from pair-based to triangular interactions affects ordering patterns, influencing the shape of resulting hysteresis loops. Moreover, the associated noise exhibited robust indicators of self-organization criticality, an emergent property solely induced by the intricate geometry of the network and not any inherent disorder. This finding is further confirmed by mapping the network's dynamics onto a phase diagram featuring two distinct dynamical states and is supported by experimental evidence from actual triangle-based networks. Ultimately, this research highlights the possibility of observing self-organized criticality due to geometric frustration within triangle-based networks, a newly identified property with potential to clarify the underlying mechanisms governing complex systems displaying intricate triangular structures.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. As the Parker Solar Probe flies even closer to the sun, with plans to get as close as 18 times the solar radius by the end of its third year of operation, it should be able to test theories about how the solar wind is handled at the point where it emerges from a specific set of hot spots called magnetic reconnection interfaces, perhaps as near as 10 to 20 times the solar radius from the solar center, but further research is needed to confirm this. Regardless, the current data give a clear answer to the long-debated question of whether solar wind energy flux distribution could be considered a standard representation of the solar wind as a whole, with the conclusion being that it can't, at least not when observed as close as the Parker Solar Probe does. Additionally, the findings shed some light on the long-standing issue of how the solar wind's cross-sectional area changes as it emerges from the point of magnetic reconnection interfaces, with the results from the four approaches showing a level of variability that makes it impossible to draw any definitive conclusions, but with the total energy flux remaining remarkably consistent, at about 140 Watts, plus or minus 28, across all four approaches, which is just a small fraction of the total energy produced by the solar wind each second, at about 1.5 trillion Watts, a significant amount of which must be going into other forms such as light, heat, and particles shot at high speeds from the solar wind.
