In this paper, we offer a groundbreaking reimagining of set theory through a
paracomplete and paraconsistent four-valued logic system. Unlike classical logic,
this approach accommodates propositions that may be neither entirely true nor
entirely false, as well as propositions that can simultaneously embody both
truths. We have devised a user-friendly axiomatic system, dubbed BZFC, by adapting
the ZFC-axioms to the parameters of a four-valued logic in a systematic manner.
Our key innovation involves the anti-classicality axiom, asserting the existence
of non-classical sets, with the unexpected outcome that the existence of a single
non-classical set allows for the generation of a wide array of non-classical sets.
Furthermore, our analysis encompasses the relationship between our proposed system
BZFC and classical ZFC, demonstrating that the two logics exhibit bidirectional
interpretability. We also demonstrate an interesting application concerning Tarski
semantics by showing how the traditional definition of the satisfaction relation
faithfully represents the non-classical properties inherent in our proposed meta-theory. Moreover, our analysis is accompanied by a concrete model consisting of
non-transitive eggs, demonstrating the validity of the anti-classicality axiom.
Finally, our findings are complemented by a formulation of the Church-Turing thesis
within our four-valued logic framework, resulting in a formulation of the Church-Turing thesis that simultaneously endorses and repudiates itself. This final outcome provides a paradigmatic embodiment of the logic's paraconsistent and paracomplete characteristics. Our research provides a comprehensive framework, showcasing the feasibility and utility of a four-valued logic system modeled off set theory. Additionally, it offers an innovative framework for exploring mathematical intuition through a logical system that can be employed towards the analysis of other foundational theories within mathematics and computer science. Our work is available in an openly accessible arXiv publication.

The associated model of non-transitive eggs is the subject of [3]. The paper's results have been presented in lectures delivered at the 20th Panhellenic Conference of the Greek Operational and Computer Science Chapters and the 9th Annual Conference of the Federation of Greek Computer Societies.

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Ultimately, this work demonstrates the feasibility of developing a BCI that can reliably decode and utilize gait patterns from high-resolution cortical recordings, holding promise for the development of more sophisticated mobility prosthetics. Additionally, this research provides evidence that the same population of neurons responsible for voluntary walking can be voluntarily controlled, as demonstrated by the absence of significant differences between walking in a virtual reality environment and actual walking. This finding has important implications for our understanding of voluntary motor control and its potential applications in the development of more effective rehabilitation strategies for motor function recovery. If a right-angled Artin group acting minimally on a tree that is not a line has a non-trivial action, we prove that its graph $\Gamma$ contains a connected component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree. Additionally, we demonstrate that this component's vertex set comprises more than one element. Furthermore, we establish the congruence of adapting this component's action to the entire group action on the tree. Consequently, we show that this component's underlying graph is connected and contains more than one vertex. Moreover, the graph $\Gamma$ itself has a connected component whose underlying graph is connected and contains more than one vertex. This outcome achieves a long-standing objective in the field of right-angled Artin groups. Lastly, we explore applications of this discovery to some specific groups, including the group associated with the graph that consists of two connected components, one being a triangle and the other being a pentagon, and the group associated with the star graph of 5 vertices. These groups are now known to have non-trivial actions on trees that are not linear. Such trees can assume various forms, including a line, a double ray, a binary tree, a tree that is a spider with more than one long leg, or an arbitrary tree. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. We showcase DECENNT's expertise in multiple tasks, including semantic sentiment classification from speech, predictive movement analysis from EEG, and the detection of seizure onset from EEG. We provide DECENNT as an open-source framework, along with comprehensive benchmarks and training protocols, to empower researchers to create precise, dynamic graphs for their own domains. This pioneering work lays the foundation for future research on dynamic graph neural networks. The code is available at: https://github.com/ghulam-eissa/DECENNT.git

Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To facilitate accurate phylogeny reconstruction, various stochastic processes have been developed to generate random phylogenetic trees or networks, which can be used to validate results or inform Bayesian analysis. Notwithstanding the creation of numerous network generation tools, a shortage of discourse and comparison among these tools persists. To address this disparity, we undertake a comparative analysis of a range of phylogenetic network generators by evaluating and contrasting the topological characteristics of the generated networks as a function of the number of reticulations present. The comparative assessment is conducted across a diverse range of phylogenetic networks comprising 24 distinct topological configurations, as well as binary and multi-labeled trees. The comparative study reveals significant variations in the ability of different network generators to replicate the topological features of real-world networks. The findings of this analysis are expected to guide researchers in selecting the most appropriate network generator based on the specific characteristics of their data. To facilitate replication and extension of our findings, we have developed a comprehensive software suite that comprises Greader, a cutting-edge comparative analysis tool enabling researchers to compare and contrast the performance of different phylogenetic network generators. Greader is readily available for download at https://sourceforge.net/projects/greader/. Our comparative assessment is the subject of a companion technical report that is accessible online at https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.10824. Our research is underscored by the inherent hypothesis that the topological configuration of phylogenetic networks exerts a critical influence on their ability to distinguish between different reticulate evolutionary mechanisms. To validate this hypothesis, we propose the use of methodological assessments involving various statistical measures, comparative network analysis, and graphical visualization techniques. The proposed assessment framework is expected to equip researchers with a robust toolkit to compare and contrast the performance of different phylogenetic network generators, track variations in the topological characteristics of generated networks, and guide future methodological developments in phylogenetic network analysis. The proposed framework is anticipated to catalyze further research in phylogenetic networks, facilitate accurate phylogeny reconstruction, and contribute to a deeper comprehension of the underlying evolutionary processes. Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. This detection capability has potential applications in enhancing animal camouflage, improving wildlife observation, and developing interactive animal-related software. It may also contribute to biomedical research related to human locomotion and could be useful in creating educational videos highlighting the movement of different species. In addition, this detection method can be employed to determine the location of animals within video footage, their overall shape, and their internal structure. The proposed method is versatile, with potential uses extending beyond the current focus on animal detection and could be adapted to address other unresolved problems in computer vision. In particular, it may be useful in addressing the challenge of detecting non-rigid objects within complex scenes, with further research required to fully explore its potential in this area. The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. In conjunction with an integrated Python module, we provide detailed parameters for ten datasets, yielding a 2-10 times faster inversion rate on real-world datasets with a Tesla V100 GPU compared to classic direct inversion. The Nested Neumann method has been found to be comparable to state-of-the-art iterative methods like PCGM and BGSM. The code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/zheng0625/Nested-Neumann. We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological characteristics can be identified by mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic systems, providing an extension of previous work to include correlated disorders. This research provides a theoretical framework that can be applied to atomic, photonic, superconducting quantum interconnects, and other quantum systems connected in sequence.

This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The analysis highlights the importance of incorporating correct on-shell properties for the external Higgs bosons through finite wave function normalisation factors, obtained from the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code. The results have been incorporated into an extension of the $\texttt{SusHi}$ code, referred to as $\texttt{SusHiMi}$. The outcomes will be displayed through specific benchmark scenarios, showcasing the influence of complex parameters on Higgs self-coupling correction factors and total production cross-sections at the LHC and future colliders, including CERN's HL-LHC, FCC-ee, FCC-hh and ILC, with a particular focus on the impact of $\texttt{R}_{\text{BB}}$ corrections. The effective vertex and decay width of the Higgs boson, considered as a function of energy and complex parameters, are also presented. The code $\texttt{SusHiMi}$ is available online at [here].

A new quasi-score linearity test has been developed for assessing linearity in continuous and count-based network autoregressive models. The test's asymptotic distribution is analyzed under various scenarios, including fixed and increasing network dimensions, null hypotheses, and specific alternative hypotheses. Key findings indicate that when model parameters are identifiable, the test's distribution converges to the chi-square and noncentral chi-square forms. Notably, the results are robust to parameters at their space boundaries. For non-identifiable parameters, an alternative test has been proposed, along with an established asymptotic distribution for a fixed network dimension. Given the challenges of tabulating test critical values, an empirical approach is implemented for p-value calculation. This includes the use of feasible bounds and bootstrap approximations. The theoretical framework is supported by consistency and asymptotic normality findings for the quasi maximum likelihood estimator, under specific conditions. A simulation study and empirical analysis provide further insight into the test's performance. The methodology is applied to real-world data sets, with one examination focusing on healthcare costs and another on electricity consumption. The implementation of the proposed test is made available through an R package. As the network dimensions increase, the test's efficiency is compared to alternative methods. The comparison reveals the proposed test's superior efficiency, with results indicating its potential for extending the quasi-score linearity test to other dynamic network models. This has the potential to embed mathematical optimization problems within trainable end-to-end models. By providing an alternative expression for computing derivatives, this differentiability enables significant reductions in memory requirements, obviating the need for unrolling optimization procedures during backward passes. The concepts developed here can serve as a guiding framework for enhancing the computational performance of innovative declarative network components. A cell's behavior during spreading and movement is influenced by various interrelated events that are activated by external stimuli at different scales. Due to the cell's living nature and complex response mechanisms, it is not sufficient to apply traditional material mechanics principles to it. Rather, cells comprise constituents with repeatable reactions such as contractility in single fibers and actin networks but also exhibit non-deterministic reorganization upon external stimuli. With consideration of this complexity, our goal is to develop a multi-faceted framework, incorporating differential equations and stochastic processes, to model cellular spreading and locomotion driven by external stimuli at different scales. This proposed method aligns with established physiological theory and can be applied to understand how gradient sensing in cells leads to spreading and navigating responses. We demonstrate our approach's relevance through numerical simulations and a computational study of a simplified reaction diffusion system, inspired by the expression of a key cellular gradient-sensing molecule. This theoretical framework and associated simulations may contribute to clarifying the underlying biology of cellular spreading and gradient sensing. Due to its general applicability, this method could be employed to investigate other cellular phenomena involving interrelated reactions and spatial rearrangements within the cell's network constituents. The unique combination of decentralization, redundancy, and pseudo-anonymity in public blockchain platforms has made them appealing for cryptocurrency adoption. However, these same features have enabled cybercriminals to exploit vulnerabilities in blockchain technology and deceive users through social engineering to execute malicious plans. Existing methods for identifying malicious actors typically rely on transaction history from specific wallet addresses, but often neglect the underlying money trails. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach centered on money trail analysis, incorporating new features to detect suspicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains. Specifically, we investigate the applicability of modern machine learning techniques, including classification and clustering, to recognize malicious transactions and identify patterns of criminal behavior among cryptocurrency users. Our study utilizes the Ethereum blockchain and addresses various challenges posed by cryptocurrency data, including transaction isolation, anonymous transactions, and data labeling requirements for machine learning. We evaluate various classification and clustering methods, experimenting with different features and algorithms to establish their efficacy in detecting criminal patterns of behavior. Our findings provide valuable insights into effectively employing machine learning within cryptocurrency blockchains, emphasizing the importance of adequate data quantity for reliable outcomes. We make available a comprehensive, open-source framework consisting of a data preparation module along with a money trail analysis library, aptly named CryptoTrail, to facilitate widespread adoption of this research. As the cryptocurrency sector continues to evolve, there will be growing value in conducting related data analytics, and we believe CryptoTrail will serve as a valuable tool for scientists and practitioners working in this field. In addition, we have published our research findings, featuring an exploratory analysis of the Ethereum blockchain, with accompanying papers also included in the package. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Furthermore, we showed that code performance improves drastically when using these deepQ learning decoders, especially in scenarios with intense errors and biased loss values. Additionally, we developed a hybrid approach combining deepQ learning with the minimum weight perfect matching algorithm, resulting in codes with exceptionally low error rates even in scenarios previously considered insurable. All code data and training processes are openly accessible online. This innovative decoding framework also facilitates our exploration into code tolerance to faulty measurements, a fundamental ability necessary for large-scale quantum computing. This research serves as an early exploration into applying computational intelligence within the context of quantum computing and provides a previously undiscovered decoding code openly accessible at https://github.com/QuanergyHQ/surface-code-decoding. Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring an open quantum system and inducing correlations with the assistance of quantum feedback control. This method is utilised to study the measurement of relative phases in optical systems consisting of two interconnected cavities, and controlled by quantum feedback from laser pulses. The approach is shown to exceed the standard quantum precision limit, without needing highly complex quantum states and with greater scalability and practicality. The principles underlying this system also have implications for improving the performance of optical memory based on two-level systems. The approach also offers potential solutions to other problems related to the loss of information in open quantum systems. The potential of this method to contribute to major scientific discoveries is highlighted by illustrating its application in the measurement of gravitational waves, the determination of atomic scattering lengths, the measurement of optical free-space propagation, and the study of phase transitions in optical reservoir computing systems. The durability of quantum states is significantly improved when measuring interaction times of less than 100 microseconds, a significant improvement over previous studies. The precision of this method is measured to have achieved Heisenberg's uncertainty limit, as demonstrated by performing interferometry with optical free-space propagation distances of up to 13.6 metres. The effectiveness of this approach is attributed to the combination of continuous quantum monitoring, the generation of correlations, and the removal of measurement results, all accomplished through quantum feedback control. The study also offers the possibility of exploring other systems that could benefit from this approach, such as optical superfluids, optical lattices, and biological systems. The study is further backed by the feasibility of implementing the required quantum feedback control manually, as well as the potential of the system to deliver the highest possible precision when measuring interaction times of less than 100 microseconds. The study also highlights the possibility of studying phase transitions in optical reservoir computing systems, an area expected to contribute significantly to the field of quantum physics. The study provides the basis for the development of quantum-inspired metrological techniques that can be more practical and scalable in complex systems, and is the result of theoretical work informed by discussions with experimentalists in the field of quantum physics. The study is also the outcome of a broader investigation into quantum-inspired metrology, described in a companion paper

However, there are significant differences between the network architectures of cloud and on-premise HPC systems.
These discrepancies stem from variations in network protocols used, leading to potential network noise and scalability limitations.
This study assesses the performance, scalability, and cost implications of running HPC applications on cloud infrastructure.

Our study investigates outcomes of the Event Shape Engineering method implemented in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.  Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.  Various models simulate our findings, showing that data on charged hadron distributions and elliptic flow coefficients can be replicated with the iEBE-VISHNU transport model that incorporates isospin degrees of freedom.  However, reconstructed multiplicity distributions cannot be simulated accurately by any of the models under consideration.  Additionally, we draw out implications for studying initial state conditions and the study of radial and elliptic flow phenomena in nuclear collisions.  A notable discovery in our analysis is that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by collision energy, observed in our results for 2.76 and 5.02 TeV collision energies.  Furthermore, we observed that the event-shape selection's influence on charged hadron distributions is unaffected by transverse momentum but is steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, a characteristic also visible at a 5.02 TeV collision energy.  Also included in our analysis are results for strange hadrons, showing a greater elliptic flow coefficient and a greater event-shape selection's influence on charged hadron distributions compared to non-strange hadrons.  Lastly, we compared our results to 5.02 TeV collision energies with 2.76 TeV collision energies, showing that increased particle production at a higher collision energy leads to a larger event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient.  Also observed at a 5.02 TeV collision energy are higher initial state elliptic deformations, greater radial flow, and a greater event-shape selection's influence on charged hadron distributions.  All findings from our study further delayer the intricate physics underlying nuclear collisions.  Additionally, our results from 5.02 TeV collision energies provide new insights into the physics underlying nuclear collisions.  These new insights include increased particle production leading to a larger event-shape selection's influence on charged hadron distributions and how increased particle production and initial state conditions influence the elliptic flow coefficient.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. This new method has been applied to the simulation of a river with sand waves and was found to be highly efficient while producing accurate results. Our algorithm offers significant potential for improving simulations of highly complex particle flows that involve numerous particles across multiple scales.

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot's size exceeded the width of the hopper itself. Ultimately, the robot reached 75% of the desired height in a single hop with the larger foot size. This project's findings have implications for the control of multi-legged robots navigating soft ground terrain. In such environments, precise force control is crucial to successfully propagating the base force that drives locomotion, and can be achieved through a combination of feedforward and feedback control systems. In this paper, the contact interaction model is applied to the study of meson elastic form factors. Quark and meson dressed masses are derived from gap and Bethe-Salpeter equations, with a specific focus on mesons comprised of distinct flavor quarks. An analysis of the generic $M\gamma \to M$ scattering process is performed. Furthermore, calculations for the charge radii of various meson types, including scalars, pseudoscalars, vectors, and axial-vectors, yield explicit elastic form factor values. These values demonstrate the interrelation between the spin-parity characteristics and the internal structural configuration of these mesons. Notably, the scalar mesons exhibit larger form factors compared to their corresponding vector mesons, while the axial-vectors display a significant form factor extension beyond the pseudoscalars. Additionally, the introduction of strange quarks into the system leads to a expansion or contraction of the internal space of the quark component within the meson, with the degree of expansion/contraction dictated by the flavor composition of the meson. The concept of a 'flavor radius' is also introduced and explored across the various meson categories. The calculations are carried out utilizing the infrared finite gap equations, with the results indicating an intricate interplay between the internal structure of the quarks and the flavor composition of the mesons and their respective scalar, vector or axial-vector nature. The predicted flavor radius trends are estimable by the current theoretical framework and await verification through future experimental data. The introduced approach is applicable to any system of quark system quarks, whether it involves the study of quark properties or the internal structure of baryons, a perspective on this concept is provided from a baryon perspective in the accompanying paper. The results highlight the significance of distinct flavor quarks on the internal structure of mesons, with the degree of a quark's contribution to the meson's overall size influenced by its flavor composition. While the current framework effectively determines the quark and meson form factors and internal space measurements, the results also indicate the necessity for a more comprehensive understanding of the interplay between flavor and the internal structure of the fundamental particles. The proposed flavor radius concept may offer a potential solution to this complex problem, with further investigation needed to explore its broader implications across the field of quantum chromodynamics. The results presented in this paper also demonstrate the usefulness of the contact interaction model as a tool for studying the internal structure of the fundamental particles and its potential applications in the study of quark systems

Although previous research has thoroughly analyzed the complex interactions of a liquid droplet under an electrical influence in air, the droplet's effects on the surrounding gas phase have been underrepresented. A notable phenomenon arises when the droplet undergoes significant oscillations, induced by the presence of a resonating electric field. The air circulation patterns that emerge as a result create localized aerodynamic forces that impede the droplet's ability to attract particulate matter in its vicinity, especially when the droplet is immersed in an aerosol cloud. The interplay between the droplet and its surroundings sparks curiosity in scientists, who see the potential for further discoveries in this two-phase system, encompassing both gas and liquid components, especially with regards to the transport of heat and mass. The current study delves into an aspect of this phenomenon, specifically to explore how the droplet's electrical properties influence its interaction with airborne particles, by incorporating the droplet into a broader numerical framework that models the behavior of the surrounding gas phase, before using this combined model to simulate various scenarios, including the deployment of a droplet in a flowing gas stream, the interaction between two droplets, and the influence of oscillating droplets on local particle distributions. The findings of the study have the potential to contribute to a deeper understanding of the multi-scale interactions governing the behavior of liquid-gas systems, with applications in various contexts, such as the design of advanced heat transfer systems, the modeling of volatile liquid components in flowing gases, and the study of precipitation-driven chemical reactions in aerosol clouds. The developed numerical framework is also expected to facilitate the improvement of models that describe the behavior of volatile components in flows, such as those employed in atmospheric models, by incorporating the effects of droplet dynamics and mass transfer. Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. Despite the random nature of these Hamiltonians, the dynamics of the annealing gap exhibit an unexpected level of universality, showcasing robust, model-independent behavior across various Hamiltonian architectures. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that neural network training, even when operated in a noise-prone environment, can recover intricate, gap-point functions consisting of multiple minima and sharp peaks, thereby attesting to the robustness of this paradigm-shifting outcome. This research is made possible by the recent development of an exceptionally powerful, high-performance simulator of quantum annealing dynamics and associated quench scenarios. This simulator, capable of modeling incredibly intricate situations, can also manipulate extremely large-scale Hamiltonian matrices and offers a previously unachievable level of simulation efficiency. When combined with a novel data analysis technique, this simulator can train neural networks to model intricate, annealing gap functions consisting of multiple local minima and sharp peaks, even when subjected to excessive noise. When applied to random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex instances of the exact cover problem, the resulting models can optimize quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency, a previously unachievable outcome. This study paves the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics of the annealing gap by identifying key quench parameters that can be explored through simulated and actual experiments on quantum annealing machines. Conformance checking focuses on comparing modeled process behavior to observed process behavior from actual event data. A recent technique, called alignments, identifies and measures deviations between process executions and predefined reference models, pinpointing the discrepancies in process traces. Notably, alignments require entire or initial segments of process runs from start to finish; this paper explores new methods to analyze partial process runs and assesses these methods with real-world event data. Additionally, the paper introduces new measures to evaluate the reliability of partial process runs based on conformance checking results. These techniques are applied to a case study involving the evaluation of business process quality at a hospital. Specifically, the analysis reveals that process variations occur frequently even among fully completed process instances, thus requiring attention from both practitioners and researchers. Conversely, our results show that most hospital staff do not struggle with basic process tasks, as indicated by low error rates in partial process runs. These outcomes underscore the significance of conducting conformance checking throughout the business process lifecycle, from process design to process performance evaluation, to mitigate process variability affecting efficiency and employee performance. Furthermore, our approach highlights the value of evaluating process runs of any duration, whether partial or complete, to capture the full range of business process insights. Consequently, this research paves the way for the development of advanced quality evaluation methods to analyze business process quality across various performance indicators. Ultimately, these methods can inform discussions about process improvement initiatives at both the individual case and business process design levels. To facilitate this research, all developed techniques, case study data, and technology have been made publicly available to support further scientific development. This inclusive technology package includes source code, data sets, and results, along with detailed documentation and guidelines to ensure ease of use for researchers and practitioners. $d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-corrrelated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $d$-electrons to dominate and the resulting one-band
model exhibits a more complex phase diagram featuring competing ground states. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to equal mixing of $d$ and $s$-electrons
and the one-band limit behaves very closely to the full model. 
Thus, the two-dimensional physics is very well represented by a one-band model
with strong screening, where the effective on-site interaction $U$ is equivalent
to the actual $U$'s value of around 5.5 eV, obtained from Hirsch's calculation. 
This result is valid for a wide range of band fillings and lattice sizes. 
Furthermore, we found that this one-band limit's phase diagram is very
sensitive to the actual value of the screening, with an integral part
being the Coulomb's internal structure itself. 
This finding is an initial step towards our primary objective of
understanding the fundamental relationship between the layered nickelates' ground
state and the Doping vs. Screening phase diagram.

This paper examines the long-term behavior of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation under weak collisions in an infinite space near a global equilibrium, specifically focusing on soft potentials. By analyzing initial conditions with sufficiently small magnitudes regardless of the collision rate, the study reveals various dynamic processes arising from the combination of the phase-mixing/dispersive effects of the transport operator and the singular collision operator. In regions where high-frequency fluctuations are prevalent, an accelerated decay phenomenon is observed, characterized by an exponential decrease in a time scale that inversely correlates with the collision rate and the frequency magnitude. In contrast, for regions where fluctuations are minimal, Taylor dispersion leads to an accelerated decay governed by the inverse of the frequency squared, multiplied by the collision rate. Moreover, this research proves the existence of almost uniform phase mixing estimates. Consequently, for observable quantities such as density, almost uniform bounds in terms of the collision rate are derived for decay rates, influenced by Landau damping and dispersive decay processes. Lastly, this research establishes a rigorous connection with a stochastic Schr\"{o}dinger operator by establishing an almost uniform bound for the gain part of the fluctuation operator. This bound, expressed in terms of the collision rate and magnetic field strength, serves as a critical component in establishing uniform bounds for observable quantities in the kilnef case. Notably, this research's methods can be applied to extend results to the cutoff Boltzmann equation under certain conditions. This work is a collaborative outcome, and some of the developed techniques may have additional applications. Nonetheless, the paper presents a comprehensive framework for describing the dynamic processes of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation and its collisions system. Moreover, this study provides a theoretical foundation for further numerical and analytical investigations of the long-term behavior of the Boltzmann equation and its variants. In particular, this research paves the way for exploring scenarios characterized by time-scale separation, phase mixing in non-equilibrium initial conditions, and the interplay between different dynamic processes arising from the interplay between the transport operator, the collision operator, and the specific form of the equation. Long-term observations from satellite and in situ measurements at various open ocean locations have demonstrated the consistency of wave slope statistics, notably skewness and kurtosis, when recorded over distances of 10-60 meters. Despite wave conditions varying significantly, these statistics remain relatively stable, suggesting that a universal probability distribution describes wave characteristics under all conditions and phases of wind interactions with the ocean surface. Research indicates that the Rayleigh distribution, often used to model wave slopes, requires a more complex formulation that accounts for multifractality. A recent study proposes a alternative approach, using a generalized beta distribution which can be defined through a lesser number of parameters. In this work, we draw inspiration from this model, using the beta distribution to model the second moment of wave slope, and thereby derive a one-dimensional multifractal wave spectrum. We test this approach using data from the open ocean and find that it accurately replicates observed wave characteristics up to 10 times the wavelength. However, larger-scale wave patterns, influenced by boundaries such as islands and sea floors, may follow a different statistical distribution. These findings also imply that the Rossby wave patterns observed in oceans may be linked to wave slopes under different conditions. Moreover, this model suggests that the energy containment of ocean surface waves is governed by the third moment of the wave spectrum, and that this moment plays a crucial role in determining the Rossby wave period. We believe that this approach holds promise for enhancing our understanding of ocean surface wave patterns and their interactions with internal waves and boundary conditions. We also propose that this model be applied across different types of rotating fluids, such as the Earth's atmosphere.

When design changes impact multiple components, the software development process can be challenging and error-prone, especially when considering the difficulty of tracking down and validating the effects of these changes. To mitigate risks, it's essential to implement regression testing, which involves executing and verifying the software components that have been modified or affected by these changes. However, given the complexity and time-consuming nature of manual testing, many software systems lack adequate regression testing, often resulting in undetected defects. Our study explores methods to automate regression testing by leveraging the software's formal specifications and verification properties. By analyzing the software components that have been modified or affected by design changes, we can execute and verify the relevant components through testing. This approach is demonstrated using interactive proof assistants and a reachability analysis tool called FDR2, which can verify and validate the software components against its formal specifications. Our research also considers different design change scenarios and associated testing costs. Finally, we present methods to analyze the software's component dependencies and change propagation to improve the effectiveness of regression testing. Examples showcasing our approach are provided in the appendix. Despite the promising outcomes, our study faces several limitations, including the reliance on existing verification techniques and tools and the need for further research in scaling the approach to larger software systems. Overall, this study offers a novel framework for automating regression testing to address software complexity and testing challenges. By exploring methods to identify and validate the software components affected by design changes, we can efficiently execute and verify these components through testing, thus enhancing the effectiveness of regression testing. Although this study employs an automated approach using formal specifications and verification properties, the concept can serve as a foundation for further research in testing methodologies, such as combining testing and verification or leveraging machine learning to improve testing efficiency. Ultimately, this research can contribute to the development of more reliable and less prone-to-errors software systems, which can better adapt to changing requirements and ensure the highest possible quality in their operations.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties.  Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, thus providing the groundwork for a new type of quark star equation of states that may be tested through high-precision pulsar radius measurements.  Interestingly, such quark stars might have interface tension that's compatible with QCD's estimates obtained from the bulk QCD phase diagram.  Furthermore, we discovered that the adiabatic index remains over 2 within approximately one density unit below the dense star's density range, making it an unsuitable indicator for the hadron-quark phase transition.  Instead, the interface tension could be inferred from the sound velocity's relationship with density, thus allowing for the reconstruction of the quark phase's density-dependent profile.  Our research highlights the significance of studying sound velocity's fundamental properties in dense matter and suggests that its unique behavior could unveil the presence of a hadron-quark phase transition.  As such, it deserves close examination in future studies of dense star microphysics.

In protoplanetary disks, dust growth can occur rapidly due to collisions and the presence of gas dissipation, eventually stabilizing a vertical shear instability caused by the interaction between corotation and differential rotation. The process begins with small grains that experience rapid growth, eventually becoming larger and more stable, thus resisting the forces driving instability. Larger particles then continue to grow, influenced by gas drag, until they reach a point where they become stuck in the disk's vertical shear layers due to their inability to keep up with the surrounding gas. As a result, these larger particles play a key role in stabilizing the disk layers and reinforcing instability in the outer regions. This specific vertical shear instability can lead to the development of horseshoe vortices, and it is possible that these features could contribute to the planetoid migration slowdown observed in transition disks. Furthermore, dust growth may also lead to the formation of dust rings, and it could represent an essential process in the evolution of protoplanetary disks. It is also possible that dust growth, particularly in the inner regions of disks, could be linked to the presence of exoplanets, and it may provide a possible solution to the planetary population synthesis problem head-wind. This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and a semi-reliable server. The goal is for the client to obtain the inference output while the server learns nothing. Although initial studies by Lehmkuhl et al. have demonstrated significant advancements in this domain, their work still has limitations. Our proposal addresses these constraints by designing an innovative two-phase encryption framework. In the first phase, a reliable client establishes a secret shared key with an uncooperative server. This key is used by the client to perform a linear encryption on the ML model. In the second phase, the server, without knowledge of the encrypted model, transmits it to the client. The client then performs a non-linear decryption on the received model using the previously established key. Our framework has several key benefits. Firstly, only one communication exchange is required between the client and server. Secondly, the server, even with infinite computational power, cannot access the inference output. Thirdly, the encryption process protects the output from the server's physical attacks. Furthermore, our framework reduces the storage requirements of the server and makes the encryption process efficient even for complex ML models. Additionally, the linear and non-linear transformations are reverse-comparable, which facilitates secure ML model updates. We validate our proposal by conducting a range of experiments, including transfer learning and secure ML model updates, with up to 85% accuracy improvements over existing studies. The accurate protection of sensitive data, such as facial information, is also achieved with minimal distortion. Our framework is compatible with various ML frameworks and can handle large-scale ML models, also showcasing secure ML inference performance comparable to that of trusted clients. Our research includes a sensitive radio telescope observation of nearby spiral galaxy M101 and its surrounding region, conducted using the FAST. This allowed us to identify an enlarged and irregularly shaped HI disk around M101. Inside the optical disk of M101, the HI velocity field appears ordered, whereas there is a significant disturbance in the extended disk. In addition, three previously undetected HI clouds have been discovered near the southern edge of the M101 disk. These HI clouds have estimated masses of 1.3$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$, 2.4$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$, and 2.0$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$ respectively. The HI clouds in M101 rotate in sync with its main HI disk. In contrast to a similar nearby galaxy, NGC 5477, which also shares a disk, these HI clouds in M101 have no visual counterparts. Also, a newly found HI tail in M101 supports evidence that the galaxy is interacting with its dwarf companion, NGC 5474. This interaction may be the origin of the extra-planar gas and HI tail observed in M101. Its disk disturbance is likely the result of a past interaction with this same companion. A potential HI tail connecting M101 to its another companion, NGC 5463, needs further verification. In any case, the complex CP map of HI in M101 underscores its dynamic evolutionary history. This includes a range of past interactions with nearby galaxies which have left their mark on its residual gas. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. The knowledge-aware nature of the framework is further validated through rigorous experimentation, showcasing a notable increase in robustness when confronted with additional noise in knowledge sources. Although molecular cations generally exhibit stronger and longer wavelength electronic emission than their neutral counterparts, comprehensive spectral models are hindered by existing limitations in data availability. For the most straightforward species, including oxygen-based molecules such as water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and hydroxyl, there are significant gaps in spectral reference data in some frequency ranges. It also highlights possible observations to acquire reference spectra for water, water$+$oxygen, carbon monoxide$+$oxygen, and carbon dioxide in a cometary context. Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects.

We outline two innovative design approaches based on Bragg reflectors and Bragg reflectors integrated with micro-resonators, both utilizing host materials with deliberately introduced point-defects to modulate the transmission spectrum. Furthermore, we delve into the fundamental operating principles of these devices, discussing their potential applications beyond spectroscopy, such as sensing and communication systems.

In addition, we review our design developments, featuring Bragg reflector-based devices coupled with pyramidal etchings and anti-reflection coatings, as well as Bragg reflector micro-resonators with varying cavity lengths. We examined two prototype devices, performing on-device spectral cross-correlation and demonstrating their ability to identify specific molecules by comparing the recorded spectrum with that of a reference template. This innovative approach has the potential to advance the field of spectroscopy, making it feasible to build elaborate, high-performance spectrometers with this technology. This could also pave the way for the development of sophisticated sensors and communication systems, enabling the accurate detection of substances or objects from anywhere in the universe. This could further enable the creation of increasingly complex, ground-breaking astrophysics missions in the near future. In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. This algorithm exhibits robust performance across different communication budgets and graph topologies. Moreover, our results show that it outperforms other random walk algorithms in terms of convergence rate both numerically and experimentally under realistic scenario settings. This involves learning a linear model on a ring graph, a non-linear model on a small scale expander graph, and a deep learning model on a more comprehensive data set at a larger scale. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/gholamkassian/FedRW. Firstly, our results demonstrate the negative impact of a communication budget on the convergence rate of an idealized federated learning system. Secondly, the distribution of nodes' data sets significantly affects the convergence rate of the ideal federated learning system. Lastly, the ideal federated learning system performs better than various distributed learning algorithms, including Federated Averaging and Synchronous Federated Learning. In a rotating system, there are two distinct types of turbulent phenomena: geostrophic turbulence and wave turbulence. Geostrophic turbulence involves the breakdown of a stable wave barrier, resulting from an ongoing battle between enstropy-enhancing and dissipative mechanisms. This type of turbulence has been observed in mid-latitude jets and is also found in laboratory experiments using rotating containers filled with layered fluids. In contrast, wave turbulence arises when a weak external force fragments a dominant global wave into a scattering of smaller waves. This study focuses on the interplay between these two phenomena: a rotating system filled with two fluids of significantly different densities. Surprisingly, even in the absence of any external driving, a prominent global wave can emerge and eventually lead to the development of geostrophic turbulence when it is disrupted by the dense fluid's downward motion. Notably, this two-fluid system provides a realistic laboratory analogy for studying mid-latitude jet turbulence. Experiments conducted using a rotating container filled with air and water demonstrated the occurrence of both fluid types' turbulent phenomena and investigated the influence of various parameters on their development. The results were validated through numerical simulations, and the findings have significant implications for understanding the fundamental differences and similarities between geostrophic and wave turbulence in rotating systems. In particular, the research highlights the crucial role that relative density plays in determining the type of turbulence that develops. Additionally, it identifies several essential parameters that govern the transition between these two distinct types of turbulence, including the ratio of the two fluids' densities, the density of the more dense fluid, and the rate at which it falls, as well as the intensity of the wave it generates and the ratio of its energy to the total energy of the system. In essence, this research offers a theoretical and practical framework for studying the intricate relationships between global waves and turbulence in rotating systems, with broad applications spanning laboratory experiments, planetary atmospheres and oceans, and potentially even astrophysical contexts. It also paves the way for a more comprehensive unified theory that addresses the underlying connections between geostrophic and wave turbulence. In doing so, it is likely to yield valuable insights into the fundamental mechanisms that govern the occurrence and progression of these two-enigmatic phenomena that underpin turbulent rotating flows. In this study, a major breakthrough is reported in the ongoing research into the interplay between global waves and turbulence in rotating systems, specifically in mid-latitude jets and rotating containers filled with layered fluids. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  However, the research also reveals that racial disparities exist within the justice system's distribution of mental health treatment, with African Americans given treatment at a rate 10 percentage points lower than that of Caucasians.  An additional finding shows that providing mental health treatment as part of probation does not raise the odds of an offender finding employment within three years following their release.  Ultimately, the data implies that, despite existing inequalities and room for improvement in delivering treatment equally, providing mental health treatment as part of probation is beneficial and its advantages outweigh its expenses which could cover and exceed future costs associated with offenders.  The most effective method to deliver treatment equally and make it more accessible is left for future research to determine. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub.

To handle increased luminosity at the Large Hadron Collider in 2021, the ATLAS collaboration will undertake a major upgrade to the LHC's detector system. This enhancement includes upgrading the Level 1 trigger based on calorimeter data to utilize finer details of the data, courtesy of the Feature EXtractors (FEX) system. Specifically, the jet FEX (jFEX) system aims to enhance jet identification and calculate global variables within an extremely tight latency constraint of under 400 nanoseconds. This will involve six distinct modules, where each module on an ATCA board contains four high-end Xilinx FPGAs to process the data at an astonishing 3.6 terabytes per second rate. This ATCA board utilizes an array of components such as electrical-optical devices and multi-gigabit transceivers for data transfer, as well as a custom 24-layer PCB to minimize interference while maintaining high signal integrity. This project has successfully overcome design hurdles and has demonstrated its performance capabilities with the fully assembled final prototype having achieved up to 12.8 gigabits per second during in-house and CERN integrated testing. With production scheduled for completion by the end of 2018, the full jFEX system will be ready for deployment before the LHC's anticipated 2021 restart. This paper provides an in-depth look at the design, fabrication, and functionality of this complex system, as well as its components, with a focus on its design innovations and performance capabilities. This work also highlights the collaborative design, manufacturing, and testing processes involved, highlighting the technological and engineering advancements achieved despite significant design constraints. This project has a clear implications for the development of future LHC upgrades and other cutting-edge particle physics projects. Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis. The method is applied to estimate the average treatment effect in the Scandinavian job training experiment from Angrist and Pischke (2009). The estimates obtained are comparable to modern Bayesian methods and match the results from the classical literature. The implementation is readily available in R. The paper's contributions are a natural extension of the previous work from Ghosh and Ghosh (2006) and it is hoped that the results will enhance the understanding of GMLE's applications in mixing distribution settings. The paper is fully self-contained with the necessary estimation framework clearly outlined for readers without a background in the subject. The most significant part of this work is the investigation of the specific GMLE estimators that can be derived for various parametric families of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$. These estimators are applicable to commonly used distributions such as normal, exponential, gamma, beta and Bernoulli which are extensively used in many scientific disciplines. The associated discussion is supported by theoretical results as well as graphical illustrations from simulated data. The estimators obtained are compared to the modern Bayesian methods, the classical literature and the results from Angrist and Pischke (2009). The implementation is readily available in R. Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing.

Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition. Furthermore, we explore obstructions to operators like $P$ being injective or having a defined range within $C^k(M)$. These findings are then applied to address several geometric concerns, including the validity of Helmholtz decomposition on certain types of open manifolds. In particular, we prove that for any manifold $M$, there exists an orthogonal decomposition $L^2(M) = H^1_0(M) \oplus H^1_M(M)$. This decomposition relies on determining a function $a \in C^\infty(M)$, where $H^1_M(M) = \{v \in H^1(M) : \int_M v \, \mathrm{d}x = a\}$. We also establish that on solenoidal fields, the gradient operator has a defined range within $H^1_M(M)$. Moreover, we demonstrate that for any non-compact manifold $M$, there exists a constant $C$ such that for any $f \in L^2(M)$, there exists $v \in H^1(M)$ such that $\Delta v = f$ and $v = 0$ on the boundary.
