As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals. Our results show that, under certain conditions, the algorithm achieves a convergence rate of $O(1/T)$ for regressing and classifying tasks when the data distribution satisfies certain conditions. Furthermore, numerical experiments validate the algorithm's performance on synthetic and real-world datasets. The variation of the FedBuff algorithm that relaxes the gradient bound constraint demonstrates comparable or superior convergence rates in various scenarios. In particular, the FedBuff algorithm converges at a rate of $O(1/T^{1/3})$ for matrix regression and outperforms existing methods for image classification. Additionally, the results show that the FedBuff algorithm can handle substantially larger numbers of participating devices. In experiments involving dataset splits, the FedBuff algorithm achieves comparable or better performance than conventional deep learning methods and federated learning baselines. The implementation of the modified FedBuff algorithm, including the code for the numerical experiments, is available online. The paper's findings demonstrate the potential of secure, cross-device federated learning to converge efficiently while protecting user privacy. The proposed algorithm's performance in concurrent learning applications, such as natural language processing, further highlights its feasibility. The paper's results also indicate that the algorithm's performance can be improved by optimizing parameters, such as batch size, but this may depend on the specific dataset being used. The paper's results provide a foundation for exploring the FedBuff framework in parameter-agent federated learning scenarios, where devices can adjust their own learning parameters. The paper's results open up new research paths, such as investigating new convergence conditions, comparing the algorithm's performance against other methods, and examining the algorithm's applicability to additional concurrent learning applications. The paper's results also suggest that the algorithm's performance can be improved by optimizing the delay interval, but this may depend on the specific dataset being used. The paper's results provide a foundation for exploring the FedBuff framework in scenarios involving diverse data distributions. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). Our best outcome, achieved by combining the alphabet transfer with coarse-fine training, resulted in a 16.4% WER decrease on a mobile speech dataset and a 12.3% decrease on a grid dataset, resulting in state-of-the-art results for Czech ASR. Our method's versatility was demonstrated through low WERs on two out-of-domain datasets. We also found that the benefits of our techniques increased with the quality of the training data. We believe our findings to be valuable not just for further exploring this unusual ASR scenario, but also for understanding the dynamics of multi-lingual ASR systems. Our code and models are available online at https://github.com/fraunhofericd/frico-asr.

This could potentially lead to faster and more precise force control in SEAs, enabling them to meet the demanding requirements of human-robot interaction tasks.

A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately decides the length of clusters within the raft. Any change in this balance, whether it is expanded to include other forces like magnetic force or changed by altering the viscosity of the surrounding fluid, will result in a specific pattern of cracks that is a direct result of the expanded state of the surrounding fluid. This concept is relevant to many situations, such as how rocks break apart after a lake has been expanded, or how a layer of ice breaks apart as a lake warms up, or even how a layer of snow breaks apart as a lake warms up further still. This paper explores the concept of sorting networks consisting of comparators with more than two input values. We focus on the interplay between three parameters: the comparator arity (k), the number of inputs (n), and the depth (d). Our model has significant relevance, as studying it helps us comprehend the inner workings of sorting networks and its connections to the construction of recursive and efficient circuits for sorting. In particular, we aim to identify the lowest required comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with limited depth. Through our research, we found lower bounds on the comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with constant depth. Specifically, we found the smallest k that allows a sorting network with depth d = 1, 2, 3, or 4. We found that k is equal to n for d = 1 and 2. We also discovered that k is equal to n/2 (rounded up) for d = 3. Interestingly, we found that k is equal to n^2/3 when d = 4, indicating that it grows sublinearly in n. Notably, we found this sublinear behavior occurs earlier in sorting networks than in majority circuits, which require d = 3 to achieve k = n^2/3. Additionally, we found that k scales linearly with log(d) for large n, indicating that deeper sorting networks may be analogous to "ladders" composed of multiple layers of comparators. We believe our research will contribute meaningfully to our understanding of sorting networks and its connections to circuit design. We hope our findings inspire further exploration of our results and the potential application of our methods to other problems. We thoroughly examined our bounds using extensive simulations, confirming that they align with our theoretical findings. We also experimented with over 10,000 unique sorting networks to verify our results. We found that our bounds are tight up to a small additive term for sufficiently large n. We also found that our results may be generalized to specific types of functions beyond sorting. We propose several open questions and possible research directions, including the optimization of comparator placement and the potential connections to graph theory. We also think that our approach can be applied to other problems, such as finding minimum-width sorting networks or analyzing other comparative functions. We think that our work can benefit from hybrid recursive architectures composed of both comparators and inverters, such as finding whether narrow-width sorting networks exist or what comparator widths are optimal for specific recursive depths. By direct resolution and reconstruction, new exact solutions for this two-fluid case are found. Additionally, three theorems applicable to the single-fluid scenario can be adapted to yield two-fluid solutions from their single-fluid counterparts. A specific example is constructed using the single-fluid solution found by Mychel'kina and Delidand, and new solutions are presented for a particular two-fluid configuration involving a non-rotating isotropic star. The framework proposed can be extended to scenarios involving more complex multi-fluid configurations.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method involves comparing three different function estimators and evaluating the approach through rigorous few-shot domain adaptation experiments on the CoNLL-2002 corpus, with notable improvements over strong baselines that serve as source domains. The adapted model's performance is also compared to a complete domain adaptation model trained from scratch on the target domain. The code is openly accessible on GitHub at the address provided in the paper.

Rounding is an essential concept used extensively in research, yet its implications on discrete random variables have not been extensively explored. To understand changes in rare events such as suicides, officials may release rounded statistics of deaths, which can distort the actual findings if rates are already low. In this research, we focus on estimating non-negative discrete variables using rounded averages, specifically when U equals the average of Y divided by n. Theoretical measures including the probability generating function, expected value, and variance are utilized to analyze how rounding impacts data and assess the impact on distribution parameter estimators. Our analysis reveals that in certain cases, rounding has a minimal effect but can severely distort results in other situations as demonstrated through practical applications. The simple techniques proposed are capable of mitigating some of the errors caused by rounding to some extent. However, the efficacy of these methods depends on the specific characteristics of the data.  Throughout this research, the impact of rounding is examined under different scenarios, including when the sum of rare events is estimated from rounded averages of much more frequent events. The consequences of rounding on event rate distribution and its effect on suicide rate distribution within the context of suicide incidence are also discussed. This research is an extension of previous related work. The methods proposed are applicable to any non-negative distributed variable and a discussion on further improvement techniques is also included. Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical analysis. A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was formed by two inequivalent Gd3+ ions. The results from direct current susceptibility and specific heat measurements indicate two transitions into antiferromagnetic states at 2.3 K and 1.02 K. Additionally, the analysis of isothermal magnetization revealed a unique 1/3 magnetization plateau, corresponding to an 'up-up-down' arrangement of the Gd3+ ions. A notable increase in magnetic entropy was also observed in the GdInO3 system, originating from the inherent magnetic frustration within this compound. A model incorporating a classical spin Hamiltonian was employed to develop the theoretical phase diagram, showing a ground state dominated by weak easy-axis anisotropy and closely resembling that of an equilateral triangular-lattice system. This theoretical framework may be a valuable reference point for the interpretation of future experiments utilizing NMR, ESR, or muon-spin relaxation spectroscopy. Lastly, the total magnetic entropy of the ground state was found to be 1.60 k_B, indicating that a significant fraction of the magnetic entropy is retained within the ground state despite the presence of a weak anisotropy. This finding is anticipated to be common to all honeycomb-lattice compounds exhibiting magnetic frustration and two-dimensional spin architectures. Notably, the spin-lattice relaxation rate is expected to display an abrupt increase upon approaching these compounds' ground states, making them promising subjects for experimental investigation utilizing inelastic neutron scattering. This integrated study provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the multifaceted nature of the GdInO3 system and offers several research opportunities at the intersection of theoretical and experimental research.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, we established that for any mechanism with any number of agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EF1 allocations, this fairness condition holds in an even weaker form, along with a discussion on potential extensions of our findings. Through our exploration, we established lower bounds on the price of anarchy in both scenarios, as well as providing an upper bound on the price of fairness for EF1 allocation among three or more agents. Lastly, we introduced a new method for allocating one good fairly among any number of agents, based on the concept of a specific ordering, along with an investigation of its price of fairness compared to Round-Robin. Through our investigation, we discovered that this new method always produces allocations that are fair up to one good, both in a selfish and non-selfish setting, and has a high price of fairness compared to Round-Robin, based on both binary and extended hierarchies, except for one specific case, where the price of fairness is one. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. The exceptional nature of UGC 8839 makes it an ideal subject for studying the interplay between dark matter, disk stability, and gravitational interactions, all of which can influence a galaxy's shape and star formation patterns. The discovery of several compact radio sources within UGC 8839, including one supercompact narrow-line region, suggests the presence of an active galactic nucleus or a population of massive compact objects. The AGN nature of these sources could provide a suitable explanation for the galaxy's unusual features. The low surface brightness and extensive disk of UGC 8839 make it susceptible to gravitational influence from nearby galaxies, with the potential to cause tidal features and channel extra gas to the outer rim. The exceptional HII region in UGC 8839, along with its unique disk dynamics and possible AGN activity, make it an interesting subject for further observational and theoretical studies of galaxy interactions and the impact of dark matter on disk evolution. Researchers propose using paleo-detectors, an experimental technique, to detect dark matter. Unlike conventional detectors, which require massive and expensive set-ups, paleo-detectors utilize naturally occurring rocks with deep geological history that contain tiny damage tracks from dark matter interactions. Thanks to advancements in microscopy and the ability to study samples over billions of years, paleo-detectors can potentially offer more sensitive detection at significantly lower costs. This could significantly expand the range of sensitivity in dark matter research. Using updated analytical methods, scientists have simulated the capabilities of paleo-detectors under various conditions and found them robust against inaccuracies in age measurements and the composition of samples. Even with relatively high concentrations of radioactive contaminants, the sensitivity of paleo-detectors can surpass current limits, offering the possibility to detect dark matter interactions below existing detection thresholds, even when masses are less than ten GeV. Furthermore, paleo-detectors can tackle unique dark matter scenarios, such as the existence of dark matter components with masses greater than hundred MeV that could interact with electrons but have gone undetected by conventional experiments. Due to their scalability, researchers anticipate a new era for dark matter research, with multiple sites operating simultaneously and offering results that could rule out or confirm theories related to supersymmetry and other fundamental physics concepts. Although the first-generation paleo-detectors are likely to have limitations, such as being only capable of detecting dark matter interactions above a certain energy threshold, researchers believe that future advancements in microscopy and measurement techniques will continue to enhance the sensitivity of paleo-detectors, making them a promising approach to understanding dark matter. The extensive use of Machine Learning (ML) in high-security sectors necessitates a transparent understanding of its methodology. Nonetheless, research into decoding ML models like Random Forest is in its nascent stages. To bridge this knowledge gap, we employ rigorous mathematical techniques and logical reasoning to create a pioneering method for explaining the predictions made by Random Forest. Our approach revolves around Minimal Unsatisfiable Cores and furnishes an exhaustive analysis for feature importance, encompassing both localized and broad aspects, along with adversarial sample examination. Empirical results across multiple datasets showcase the precision of our feature importance assessments. Furthermore, our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art adversarial analysis technique and offers the ability to generate user-centric reports that can inform recommendations in real-world scenarios. The comprehensive implementation of our method is freely accessible online. By providing a thorough explanation of RFPex, our tool can benefit both practitioners seeking to employ Random Forest and ML researchers working to understand the underlying methodologies behind deep learning models. Current public datasets for re-identifying individuals are limited due to the difficulties associated with labeling them. Despite the abundance of unlabeled surveillance footage that can be easily obtained, it's unclear how to effectively utilize this content to develop useful re-identification representations. Typically, existing methods focused on unsupervised and domain adaptation use publicly available datasets and then apply them to the target domain after removal of the labels. Given that the target domain typically has an abundance of unlabeled data with useful learning signals, it's surprising that these methods haven't incorporated them into their training processes before adapting to the target domain. This study proposes an innovative technique called Self-adaptive Contrastive Learning (SCL) that aims to create useful re-identification representations from scratch with no labels, utilizing only the visual information from the source domain. A dataset with plenty of images containing partial information about the identities of the people present, is used to evaluate our technique. To assess our method's effectiveness, a comparison is made with multiple baseline methods that utilize various unsupervised and domain adaptation techniques. The results show that our technique outperforms these methods, with sample code available here: https://github.com/zwang84/SCL. Notably, our technique improves the state-of-the-art in the large-scale person re-identification dataset, i.e. MSMT1M, without relying on labels. An analysis of the different components of our technique, including the impact of the source domain dataset and the effectiveness of our contrastive learning approach, is also conducted. Ultimately, our technique yields public releases of over 200,000 unlabeled surveillance images with associated re-identification information, along with code and pre-trained models that can be used for further research. These resources are available here: https://github.com/zwang84/SCL code and here: https://github.com/zwang84/SCL_models for the models. An evaluation of the method's effectiveness when using a more challenging protocol is also presented. In this protocol, only a portion of the dataset with more detailed information about the identities present, is used during training. An analysis of the method's robustness is also conducted by conducting experiments under different conditions that simulate real-world scenarios. An additional evaluation is also conducted on two other public re-identification datasets, i.e. Market-1501 and CUHK03, with instances of code and models available here: https://github.com/zwang84/SCL_code and here: https://github.com/zwang84/SCL_models respectively. Recent findings from global pulsar timing arrays suggest a nano-Hertz gravitational wave background signal remains elusive in current data. Nevertheless, enhanced datasets are expected to yield statistically significant evidence in the future. This study endeavors to eliminate sampling bias in data analysis. By examining various configurations of nested samplers and traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, we aim to identify the time efficiency and consistency of these sampling techniques on pulsar timing array data. Despite producing consistent parameter results across methods, our research suggests the implementation of two robust sampling methods for cross-validation and realistic run times in future analyses. Nonetheless, we derive marginally significant constraints on the gravitational wave background signal and a potential pulsar pair, reinforcing previous studies' findings. Moreover, we introduce the code's open-access platform, comprising three distinct codes for cross-validation, available at https://github.com/yanmlu/PTA-sampling-comparison. This study's outcomes will inform future data analysis strategies, particularly with increased datasets on the horizon.

Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of correlation functions of two quark currents within a pion is conducted, yielding clear signals for nearly all significant combinations of quark field contractions except one. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory. Our study confirms that, to an acceptable level of precision, the difference in energy between the ground and first excited states of the pion can be explained by a correlation between a quark and its corresponding antiquark that takes into consideration the mass of the quarks and their movement within the pion. Additionally, our research provides a more detailed examination of a phenomenon known as the quark condensate within the pion, where the movement of a quark is directly linked to the movement of the antiquark from the same flavor category. Our study further explores the distribution of momentum across the quark and the antiquark and investigates the impact of the mass of the quarks on this distribution. Our findings are also compared with experimental data derived from semileptonic decays of the pion, and our results show a level of consistency acceptable to the level of precision achieved. Our research provides a series of predictions that can be tested through additional lattice simulations, particularly those that involve evaluating the rate of change of the correlation function between the quark and the antiquark within the pion as the momentum of the pion increases. These findings, coupled with the knowledge of how the movement of a quark affects the movement of the corresponding antiquark, could prove valuable in gaining a deeper understanding of the internal structure of the pion and potentially inform the development of effective theories that describe the interactions of hadrons within high-energy particle physics. Our study's findings can also contribute to a greater understanding of the relationships between the quark and the antiquark within other mesons, such as the kaon, and could have implications for research into nucleus physics through lattice QCD, particularly when involving the movement of quarks within a confined space. Ultimately, our research provides a foundation for a series of additional studies that can further investigate the internal structure of hadrons and clarify the relationships between quarks and their corresponding antiquarks within various types of hadrons, leading to a deeper understanding of the fundamental components of matter within the universe. This study explores how uncertainty about chance influencing job success and earnings impacts redistribution policies in a diverse group of people. We gather responses from a group of participants, who consider various scenarios in which good luck can affect worker outcomes. The results show that participants generally want to reduce the gap in earnings, but are less motivated to do so and react differently to circumstances where luck has an impact on job success rather than overall income. These findings have implications for research aiming to model people's opinions on income inequality and the apparent disparity between laboratory research and real-world inequality trends in the US. Specifically, existing laboratory research may underestimate the impact of luck on people's opinions on inequality due to methodological limitations. In contrast, field research finds that people overestimate the role of luck in determining individual income. These findings also suggest that people's opinions on inequality are more flexible than previously thought, with luck's influence shaping people's opinions on redistribution in a complex manner that depends on people's perception of the role of luck in determining worker outcomes. In particular, people are more willing to close the income gap when luck has an impact on job success rather than overall income, indicating that the flexibility of their opinions on inequality depends on their understanding of luck's influence on worker outcomes. The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a positive relational algebra query and a K-nearest neighbor classifier. DataScope's novel approach enables the computation of the Shapley value for a wide range of canonical pipeline subfamilies with near-linear time complexity, outperforming state-of-the-art Monte Carlo-based methods by several orders of magnitude. The system's practical effectiveness is demonstrated through various experiments, including the debugging of machine learning models in real-world settings. The underlying technological components of DataScope also give rise to new research opportunities, bringing the focus on computational cost reduction for machine learning debugging efforts into sharper relief. We discovered that radio source counts within the clusters' cores are influenced by collision rates among stars and the clusters' masses, whereas collision rates among stars had greater impact on radio source counts outside the clusters' cores. We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and its extensions, with impressive results that outperform baseline methods by a significant margin in accuracy, particularly on difficult datasets. Our implementation and data are freely available for download.

The proposed techniques are applied to a theory-driven design of dielectric lasers with high symmetry factors. Notably, an efficiently directived emission is achieved in a structure lacking a mirror layer, surpassing previous records for emission intensity at a specific angle for lasers above 800nm. Successfully manufactured and tested at 850nm, our prototype showcases the strongest directed emission reported to date. This research paves the way for optimizing highly efficient, low threshold microcavity lasers utilizing a design feedback loop incorporating simulation and experimental analysis. This approach could also be adapted for other laser types by considering unique factors associated with each device.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. The empirical studies confirm that our method not only outperforms current offline and semi-supervised methods but also provides a stronger benchmark for future research. A type of genuine two-dimensional crosscurrent that flows counter to the heat flux direction has been lacking in scientific knowledge since its one-dimensional counterpart was discovered. A setup for realizing these currents on a three-dimensional cubic lattice has been devised by coupling a Hofstadter model to two separate heat baths of varying temperatures. Research demonstrates that the robustness of these currents can withstand various imperfections and tilting within certain nonequilibrium conditions. Additionally, boundary currents with robust stability were found, and the condition of being three-dimensionally robust indicates they require tunneling capabilities across all three spatial dimensions. The model exhibits robust surface currents applicable to both bosons and fermions, and the mechanisms of discrete symmetries were found to significantly contribute to the surface currents' stability. Furthermore, the models exhibit robust surface currents at both low and high temperatures, and the temperature at which the surface currents transition from one regime to the other can be precisely tuned. Also, research demonstrates that the models can be experimentally implemented using superconducting qubits, and the proposed method can be adapted to create robust surface currents in other systems, such as photonic systems. Lastly, the crosscurrents can be directly observed through dynamical parity oscillations, and the findings provide opportunities for studying nonequilibrium phase transitions and robust surface currents in quantum systems.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can produce detections similar to GW190521, specifically in a mass range typically found for pulsational pair-instability supernovae with a merger rate of 0.01-0.09 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our framework further enables the assessment of characteristics such as the distribution of nuclear star clusters and the likelihood of mergers involving Population III binary remnants within specific regions of the universe. This understanding is crucial for preparing for and analysing data from upcoming gravitational wave detectors. Our model introduces a comprehensive nuclear star cluster merger rate prediction that accounts for the formation of Population III binary remnants and their subsequent evolution. This model opens up possibilities for further enhancements, such as incorporating N-body simulations and developing more detailed binary evolution models. This study provides a foundation for a deeper investigation into the characteristics of Population III binary remnants residing within nuclear star clusters, a crucial step in preparing for potential data related to these remnants and their mergers. This research is part of a broader project that aims to explore the potential for detecting nuclear star clusters featuring Population III binary remnants, including GW190521, which may originate from such a system. This project involves analysing and modelling the characteristics of nuclear star clusters, evaluating the likelihood that these clusters host Population III binary remnants, and assessing the potential for detecting Population III signals in gravitational wave data. This work is also relevant to ongoing and upcoming ground-based gravitational wave detectors, such as LIGO, Virgo, and the Einstein Decimal Plan's goal to detect gravitational waves from nuclear star clusters. To ensure the performance of GECAM's Gamma-Ray Detectors (GRDs) and test its onboard triggering and localization software before launch, a portable device that simulates Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) was developed using a grid controlled X-ray tube and direct digital synthesis technologies. This portable GRB simulator, which modulates an X-ray flux powered by up to 20 kV, demonstrates its capability of generating high-energy bursts. Before its launch in December 2020, both GECAM satellites were tested using this simulator, which produced short and long GRBs that were detected and analyzed by the onboard GECAM/GRDs. The results showed a strong consistency between the observed data and the programmed simulation functions, indicating excellent performance of the GRDs and the GRB simulator. The successful development of this simulator has not only benefited the GECAM mission but also provided a valuable reference for other GRB simulators. These conditions are achieved through a new representation of the dual operator of T_g on BMOA. Lastly, our study includes a discussion on the relationship between Volterra-type operators and the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA_p. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
Notably, no performance compromise was made in developing the accelerated versions – they perfectly match the original challenging standards set by they experts in the field. 
As a result, researchers and developers can now conduct in-depth, prolonged experiments to evaluate virtual agents more effectively.  To ensure the integrity of existing research, we also developed a compatible version of our accelerator that can be used by those who conducted their studies before it was created.  It may be applied to any similar game environments as well. The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is often expressed through its effect on the mass-to-charge ratio of a particle. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy. Interestingly, this formulation shares common ground with the recently proposed Charge Convexity Conjecture, which suggests that the spectrum of charges in a conformal field theory should exhibit a specific property known as convexity. The relationship between these two possible formulations of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is explored, and it is shown that they imply the convexity of the mass-to-charge ratio spectrum. A specific example in an $SU(N)^3$ theory demonstrates that the Mass Convexity Conjecture, which states that the mass spectrum exhibits convexity, follows from the Charge Convexity Conjecture. Moreover, this line of reasoning suggests that both the Mass Convexity Conjecture and the Weak Gravity Conjecture could be formulated in terms of the convexity of a particle's mass-to-charge ratio spectrum. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the Binding Energy Convexity Conjecture, another recently proposed fundamental principle, also stems from the Charge Convexity Conjecture. The proposed framework also offers a possible approach to formulating the Weak Gravity Conjecture in terms of its effects on the mass-to-charge ratio of a specific particle and suggests that both the Mass Convexity Conjecture and the Binding Energy Convexity Conjecture could be fundamental principles derived from the Charge Convexity Conjecture. The relationship between the Mass Convexity Conjecture and the recently proposed Entropy Convexity Conjecture is also explored and finds that the latter follows from the former. The proposed framework is further extended to theories with multiple fundamental charges and theories with non-linear symmetries. The implications of the proposed framework on the fundamental principles of the 'hierarchy problem' are also considered. This model-space QITE method iteratively expands the model space while maintaining its orthogonality, enabling simultaneous description of multiple states. We enhance model-space QITE by integrating the quantum Lanczos algorithm, which boosts its convergence rate. In simulations, our approach outperforms both standard quantum Lanczos and the folded-spectrum QITE in calculating excited states. We show that spin contamination can be mitigated through an imaginary time propagator shift, efficiently obtaining excited states with specific spin properties without descending into lower-energy states with mixed spins. Additionally, we examine how the degree of unitary approximation within MSQITE influences its results. Lastly, we apply MSQITE to calculate excited states in a Hamiltonian used in studies of quark confinement and demonstrate its capability to detect shape transitions in quark potentials. Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings. If the ring has a specific dimension, we demonstrate the connection between the tight Hilbert function and its lower bound, achieving this condition implies that the ring is $F$-rational. However, this condition does not hold without further constraints, as evident from constructed examples. Based on the ring's properties and test elements, we find formulas to compute various coefficients, which are in turn used to establish the relationship between $F$-rationality and these coefficients, ultimately leading to the condition for $F$-rationality as depth $R \geq 2$ and a specific equality of these coefficients. Consequently, we conclude that depth $R \geq 2$ is a necessary and sufficient condition for $F$-rationality, which was already known, and that this condition is equivalent to the equality of these coefficients, providing a new characterization of $F$-rationality in rings with a prime characteristic and its $\mathfrak{m}$-primary ideal, especially without the restriction of having associated primes. Furthermore, we propose a new approach to studying weak formalities, which is based on the tight Hilbert function and its relationship to its lower bound, and we demonstrate the connection between this study and $F$-rationality. Moreover, we examine the relationship between this study and a one-dimensional local excellent domain with a specific parameter, providing its $\mathfrak{m}$-primary ideal and tight Hilbert function, which is in turn used to analyze the associated projective variety and the Jacobian matrix of the ring, ultimately aiming to contribute to the study of weak formalities. Lastly, we offer additional conclusions on the ring's properties and its associated objects. The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, the following effects are produced: the risk is minimized for market participants due to complete order fulfillment, but this may lead to increased trading of imbalances during intra-day and dispatch ramp risks in the following days, resulting in higher activation costs during redispatch. Activating these design issues in the model may provide valuable insights for designers and decision-makers of ancillary services acquisition systems. The model and results can also serve as a starting point for more comprehensive research on agent-based modeling of electricity markets and ancillary services acquisition systems. R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the polynomial equivalent of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the Chowla's conjecture regarding autocorrelation, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields. Additionally, we present an effective version of the Chebotarev density theorem for polynomial extensions over function fields, extending on the work of Drayton. Furthermore, we establish the prevalence of non-abelian Galois groups among polynomials composed with a given irreducible polynomial, confirming Drayton's conjecture on the density of solvable Galois groups within a specific context. Our research also investigates the distribution of random number fields with a fixed degree and a randomly selected Galois group, demonstrating that the frequency of a specific Galois group architecture converges to one over the number of possible architectures as the degree increases infinitely. This finding is expanded to a scenario where a polynomial is composed with multiple irreducible polynomials, resulting in a field whose Galois group resembles the product of the Galois groups of the individual components. The generalization of this scenario to an infinite number of components extends the current understanding of the Galois group of iterated polynomials beyond Odoni's initial discovery. Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through seasonal chemical compound analysis. The formation of the vortex, detected by examining the distribution of methane and water ice, was found to follow a gradual polar cooling pattern in the winter months. This cooling effect, powered by the reduction of solar insulation as the planet tilts away from the sun, causes a temperature drop that becomes sufficiently low to support the formation of a polar vortex. The temperatures remain sufficiently low throughout the winter, allowing the vortex to maintain its shape and warm temperatures to remain trapped within it. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario. This approach allows us to establish the optimal blow-up criterion under these conditions. Furthermore, we are able to demonstrate the long-time existence of mass-subcritical solutions, both with positive and zero energy, provided that the nonlinearity does not depend on energy too heavily. This informal note begins by illustrating some technical concepts, including the re-normalization of measures on orbital integrals from the works of Langlands, Frenkel-Langlands-Ng\^o, and Altug's research on Beyond Endoscopy. We discuss specific measures related to algebraic tori and explain how they relate to Tamagawa numbers. We then examine the GL2 case in depth. Additionally, the appendix by Matthew Koster clarifies the connection between the geometric measure of orbits and Kirillov's measure of co-adjoint orbits within the dual space of certain Lie algebras, including sl2 and so3. 

This discussion originated from a broader investigation into Beyond Endoscope's Gl3 case and its potential applications to automorphic representations and Galois representations, particularly with regards to Serre's conjecture.

This paper's final section explores a novel perspective on the endoscopy computational framework and its relationship to the geometry of reductive groups and their representation theory, inspired by the works of Lusztig and Deligne on mixed Tate motives.

The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation. Furthermore, this method may be adapted for other experiments that involve interacting with x-ray sources and are interested in extracting more information from two-dimensional spectra, a type of data that is becoming increasingly common with the advancement of present-day x-ray light sources.

In quantum computing, errors during operations can cause valuable information to become lost. Some codes, such as the surface code, can limit the spread of these errors, allowing for retrieval of the original information. A problem persists, though - even with these codes, errors will eventually reach a point where they cannot be fully reversed without some loss of data. A notable group of codes addresses this issue by holding information in a form that can be transformed back to its original state without loss, much like how data can be recovered from a damaged disk if it's rewritten onto a new drive. These codes maintain their effectiveness despite reaching this error threshold and can correct themselves up to certain point without outside intervention. Developing these codes in larger sizes is often the biggest challenge in creating reliable quantum computers. A new proposal aims to compensate for this difficulty by introducing a separate code that can generate these large, reliable sizes from smaller, initially pure areas - essentially spreading purity across a larger area. This code works even when errors reach a point where they cannot be fully reversed without some loss of data and can correct itself. When combined with the other codes, this new code enables the efficient creation of large, reliable sizes and can handle high-error scenarios. Additionally, it can effectively manage multiple codes at once and even facilitate communication between different parts of a quantum computer by transforming the state of one area into that of another. These capabilities make this new code invaluable tools for developing practical quantum error correcting codes. Furthermore, this code showcases a broader potential for other applications, such as enhancing the performance of quantum simulations. Given its advantages, this code seems poised to play a crucial role in bringing quantum computers closer to reliability.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Our numerical data indicates that our approach offers highly comparable performance to existing literature methods. The major benefits of our approach include its versatility with respect to mesh type and fracture configuration, as well as its ability to maintain pressure symmetry. This has substantial implications for any up-scaled methods that may derive from our approach, particularly in relation to greater complexity problems, such as multiphase flow and flow with reactive chemicals. This paper's innovations provide a crucial foundation for several potential future research projects. This includes investigating how this approach could be expanded to account for fracture surfaces with various shapes, integrating screening concepts, and developing new numerical algorithms. Furthermore, incorporating scalar conservation equations is also deemed worthwhile. This is especially given the already established framework for modeling reactive chemical flows. This paper introduces our novel method in such a way that it is accessible to a wide range of researchers within this field, with the associated numerical data and implementation details available at no cost on the FEniCS Project website. This includes custom-built Python scripts and pre-built executable examples for both the GUI assisted Dolfin-CEASAR and the command line driven Dolfin. This is particularly useful for researchers to test and adapt this methodology for their own specific use cases. This methodology is specifically designed to be used within the FEniCS Project framework, an open-source and widely-used finite element method (FEM) platform. This new approach has the potential to become a standard method for modeling blocking fractures and could serve as a foundation for the development of new methods within this field. A comprehensive examination of a spin-triplet superconducting device, which involves a spiral magnetic arrangement, is conducted. The underlying metal exhibits unique magnetic characteristics that may arise due to competing isotropic exchanges or an asymmetrical magnetic arrangement. Depending on its anisotropy, the metal can transition between spiral and uniform magnetization orders. A specific type of magnetic arrangement known as the B20 structure further contributes to the device's operation, influencing the long-range pairing of superconducting electrons under intense exchange fields. However, numerical simulations demonstrate the feasibility of controlling the device's behavior using a spiral magnetic arrangement, thereby facilitating the operation of a spin-triplet superconducting quantum interferometer on a nonmagnetic surface. This concept may enable the development of more complex spin-triplet superconducting quantum devices that combine multiple components, each functioning through unique magnetic arrangements that interact globally. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factor results across multiple replications and sampling methods. We also investigate the tendency for Bayes factors to become stuck in local minima and propose a alternative method for model comparison using parallel sampling. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can follow to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their specific analyses, including model specification, model fitting, and model comparison. We apply this approach to two ongoing projects in the laboratory for cognitive neuroscience and psychology, examining the stability of Bayes factor results across multiple replications and sampling methods, as well as the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates in comparison to traditional measures of model fit. To facilitate the adoption of these methods, we provide an open-source R package called Rtbfr that enables researchers to easily replicate our analysis, execute our code, and adapt our methods for their own cognitive science research. We anticipate that this package will contribute to the advancement of computational methods in cognitive science research by making reliable Bayes factor analysis more accessible and achievable to a broader range of researchers. We also hope to encourage open dialogue and collaboration among researchers, paving the way for a greater understanding of the challenges associated with Bayes factor analysis and the development of innovative solutions. To facilitate this dialogue, we invite researchers to share their own experiences, contribute to the development of the Rtbfr package, and participate in a publicly accessible repository containing the code related to our study. Ultimately, we aim to promote a culture of openness and cooperation among cognitive science researchers, emphasizing the importance of making data and computational methods publicly accessible to ensure the integrity, reproducibility, and reliability of research findings. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous studies have explored the interconnections between discourse indicators and other linguistic aspects such as sentence structure and sentiment but are constrained by their focus on specific cases and categories. This work utilizes a highly saturated BERT model to predict indicators between semantically connected sentences and aggregates the results to reveal a broader pattern of discourse indicator usage across various relationships. In addition, it incorporates a theoretical framework consisting of three dimensions (sentiment, role, and sequence) to organize the observed discourse indicator patterns and examine instances that do not conform to these patterns. Furthermore, enhancements to an existing lexical knowledge system with over 1,600 words and 100 indicators have been made. WordNetLexicalized is an enhanced version of the original WordNet Lexicalized, which is derived from WordNet 3.6 and combines the predicted indicators with other types of lexicalized information, such as the parts of speech and the distribution among the various WordNet synsets. This updated resource is accessible through the MGED website at https://mged.cse.ohio-state.edu. In the context of existing research on discourse indicators, this work is positioned as the initial comprehensive study of predicted indicators in relation to semantic relations and is intended as a starting point for the development of more sophisticated theories and the integration of discourse indicators into broader grammatical structures. Alongside this, an initially structured but formally ungrammatical corpus has been created to support this investigation and existing parsing models can be leveraged to further explore these findings. As the field of computational linguistics continues to evolve with advancements in deep learning models and large, annotated corpora, research on discourse indicators is likely to be shaped by three key developments: the increasing effectiveness of predictive models, the growing availability of annotated data and the expanding scope of possible research, enabled by both these developments. We investigate the properties of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under high-temperature and vacuum conditions.  By combining optical detection of magnetic resonance (ODMR) and optical spectroscopy, we studied the spin resonances and radiative transitions at high temperatures.  Our findings indicate that increasing temperature leads to a reduction in the intensity of visible and infrared light emitted from the diamond, as well as a decrease in the frequencies of ODMR resonance and a shift in the emission line towards longer wavelengths.  By comparing our measured data to theoretical predictions, specifically from the Mott-Seitz model, we estimated that a significant nonradiative energy barrier has a height of approximately 0.24 electron volts.  Furthermore, by analyzing the temperature-dependent shift of the emission line, we determined that there is a very slight electrical polarization of the diamond, equivalent to around two hundred volts per centimeter.  We also demonstrated the capability to accurately create and manipulate the spin resonances in the diamond at high temperatures.  This research reveals the intricate interplay between optical, electrical, and mechanical properties of the diamond and highlights its potential as a reliable and robust platform for various quantum technology applications.  In order to replicate our results, we recommend utilizing a diamond that has been treated with vacuum stability, as this helps minimize the impact of residual gases on the results.  Additionally, we found that varying the temperature within the range of 20 to 700 Kelvin had a very minor impact on the stability of the diamond's optical and electrical properties, likely due to the presence of a large energy gap.  This research paves the way for exploring the fundamental properties of the nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond and developing stable, robust, and accurate quantum technology tools, capable of functioning effectively across an extensive temperature spectrum.  Possible applications for this technology could involve developing accurate magnetic field sensors, robust quantum memories, and reliable optical communication systems capable of operating over long distances, aided by the ability to entangle the diamond's spin resonance with those of other particles.  In order to take full advantage of the capabilities offered by the diamond, it is necessary to develop methods for creating, controlling, and reading the spin resonance that can handle data at a gigabit speed. Using field-theoretic methods, researchers studied a spin model on the triangular lattice, where the SU(3) representation was placed on each site, mimicking an antiferromagnetic Heisenberg spin model with p-box symmetry. We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under this specific Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and cite connections to previous local analyses. Additionally, we establish a correspondence between stationary points of the original and factorized problems. Given sufficient geometric conditions, we demonstrate that any stationary point of the factorized problem corresponds to a stationary point of the original problem, and vice versa. Further, we identify and analyze the null space of the factorized problem's Jacobian matrix. To facilitate optimization algorithm design, we conduct numerical experiments to visualize and describe the factorized problem's landscape in different scenarios. 

This research is relevant to matrix optimization problems, particularly for matrix factorization applications, and provides a framework that can be applied to other self-concordant functions on Euclidean and Riemannian spaces. The paper's findings can inform optimization algorithm design within the Burer-Monteiro factorization framework.

High-energy particles with masses beyond the TeV range are difficult to access experimentally. Current constraints from Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis already set a strict limit on their lifespan, at under 0.1 seconds. Next-generation gravitational wave detectors have the potential to drastically improve these limits to the point where their lifespan could be constrained to as short as 10^-16 seconds. This could be possible if these particles once controlled the universe's energy density and led to a transition to a matter-dominated period before decaying in time for Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis to occur. As a result of such an early history of the universe, we could detect unique signatures in gravitational wave backgrounds that originated from primordial sources. Furthermore, we propose that detecting the gravitational wave spectrum from long-lived objects like cosmic strings can serve as a probe of fundamental particle physics parameters, ultimately providing more stringent constraints on the universe's early conditions through various UV extensions of the Standard Model, for example the case of supersymmetry, where the scale of scalar moduli and gravitino masses could be constrained up to 10^10 GeV, or models of only-gravitationally-interacting particles and their reheating temperature, or dark photons with an incredibly low kinetic mixing of 10^-18. The ability to make these new, very-highest-energy physics markings visible to future gravitational wave detectors would allow for a fundamental re-assessment of the feasibility of various UV extensions of the Standard Model within the context of the entire known cosmological history. Our experiments examine how the geometric structure of force-free rigid swimmers interacts with different fluid properties: Newtonian and viscoelastic (specifically Boger fluids).  By changing the swimmer body and its helical tail dimensions, our findings reveal that viscoelastic properties' influence is largely dependent on the swimmer design, potentially amplifying its speed by as much as five times, or instead, diminish its velocity by a similar amount, or leave its locomotion mostly unaffected. Analysis and corresponding theoretical modeling suggest that viscoelastic forces on these swimmers are dictated by a similar'snowman effect' found with linear swimmers, in which asymmetry in the swimmer causes an elasticity-related force that may aid or impede propulsion. Moreover, our results demonstrate that in viscoelastic fluids, swimming velocities are largely governed by a dimensionless parameter based on the swimmer's overall dimensions and the length of its tail, in addition to the same'snowman' asymmetry parameter. This research provides critical insights into the interplay between swimmer design, fluid properties, and the efficacy of bi- and nano-inspired swimming machines. Moreover, our study offers a framework that can be applied to a broader range of swimming mechanisms and apparatus. Lastly, our findings introduce the possibility of developing specialized swimmer designs optimized for viscoelastic fluids, offering potential applications in complex industrial and biological environments. The COVID19 virus is spread through contaminated droplets expelled by infected individuals when they cough, sneeze, speak or breathe. Understanding how these virus-carrying droplets behave under changing environmental conditions is essential to tracking the infection's spread. To investigate this, we examine the movement of evaporating droplets influenced by gravity and varying weather, observing how they change in size until either settling on the ground or breaking down into small particles that can linger in the air. Our analysis reveals significant impacts of humidity and temperature on evaporation, with large droplets falling due to gravity's dominance despite evaporative losses and smaller droplets suspended in the air due to diffusive forces. The size of intermediate droplets is highly dependent on weather conditions and is critical to infection spread, underscoring the need for physical distancing and making face masks essential. Finally, our research demonstrates that surface contamination is less significant in spreading the infection compared to airborne transmission methods. Graphic visualizations of our findings are included to facilitate public understanding of this complex issue. Our analysis also predicts that warmer temperatures and lower humidity can accelerate the spread of infection through airborne transmission methods. Ultimately, our research highlights the importance of simultaneous implementation of physical distancing measures, wearing masks, and environmental temperature and humidity control to mitigate the spread of infection through airborne transmission methods. This research is applicable to understanding the spread of other respiratory viruses like SARS and influenza. It is also relevant to industrial applications involving the dispersion of biological agents in various environmental conditions. It is hoped that this analysis will contribute to the ongoing global fight against the COVID19 pandemic. It is also hoped that this research will inspire further educational and research projects to explore other aspects of the interplay between gravity-driven droplets and their surroundings. It is further hoped that this work will motivate the development of more engaging visualizations to effectively communicate these complex issues to a broader audience. We also explore non-uniform data restriction techniques that efficiently minimize silent errors and hardware-induced data corruptions. The efficacy of our approach is shown through a vehicle classification test, using the ResNet-50 architecture and the MIOVision traffic dataset. The results provided can serve as a starting point for further research and more comprehensive evaluations in the area of reliable computer vision. The European Central Bank's definition of clearing or netting has far-reaching effects on a nation's economy, affecting transactions and business-to-business interactions. Essentially, netting represents a different method for companies to make payments to each other, involving an agreement in which each party deducts debts owed from debts owed to it. By combining the debts between parties, the usual payment process can be substituted with a direct settlement. In this research, we present a suite of graph algorithms capable of generating optimal netting solutions suitable for a national economy's scale, yielding efficient results in a timely manner. Our analysis utilizing Romanian Ministry of Economy invoice data demonstrates that conventional graph algorithms can still tackle highly significant contemporary challenges effectively. Additionally, our findings highlight notable scalability and performance achievements. Specifically, our study shows that even the most advanced contemporary graph algorithms, including the best-known ones, can produce high-quality solutions suitable for a national economy's scale and yield fast, efficient results. Consequently, companies and central banks can rely on these algorithms for optimal netting solutions, leading to increased adoption of this efficient payment method. In this research, we also present novel applications of our netting solutions, including debt tracking, debt rescheduling, and debt reduction. Moreover, we present innovative visualizations of our solutions, including debt trees and settlement paths. Our experimental analysis using large-scale graph instances demonstrates the exceptional scalability and performance of our algorithms, producing high-quality solutions in a timely manner. This research is significant because it makes complex graph algorithms applicable to major contemporary challenges and paves the way for more widespread adoption of optimal netting solutions. This, in turn, can contribute to companies adopting efficient payment methods, leading to better interactions and a more robust and prosperous economy.
