Current retrievals of cloud optical thickness and particle size using passive satellite imaging techniques fail for complex convective clouds. These failures stem from the limitation of using one-dimensional radiative transfer theory to analyze three-dimensional cloud morphologies. Cloud tomography offers a promising alternative to treating clouds as fully three-dimensional objects. Developing efficient forward solvers for three-dimensional radiative transfer will be crucial for applying this method from space. By acknowledging the existence of optically thick cloud cores, where scattered photons do not contribute useful information, we can refine future 3D retrievals. Investigating this phenomenon using data from the MISR and MODIS satellite imagers, we identified key insights to streamline cloud tomographic reconstruction. Notably, we determined the veiled core of optically thick clouds to typically be at an optical distance of around 5 from the cloud's boundary, allowing for more efficient use of computational resources and potential improvements to reconstruction algorithms. To test this finding's implications, we developed a prototype algorithm incorporating these insights and applied it to MODIS image data, achieving more accurate results compared to standard methods. However, further research is needed to fully leverage the potential of this approach. Additionally, we contributed a high-performance computing framework tailored to cloud tomographic reconstruction, which can be adapted to other computer vision problems involving large datasets. This framework is particularly well-suited for exploring fundamental questions about cloud geometry and how it affects radiation transfer and subsequent reconstruction algorithms. As such, it could be especially beneficial for developing new numerical methods and evaluating their performance before moving on to actual data analysis. This research lays the groundwork for developing more effective cloud reconstruction algorithms and could have broader implications for other computer vision challenges involving complex scenes and limited information. We examined how a laser pulse with a changing frequency impacts its passage through a sub-wavelength target and the acceleration of ions. Our investigation focused on a laser pulse with frequency variations, which results in a critical density threshold dependent on time. The model we applied goes beyond the initial assumption of linear variation. Our analysis shows that in cases of negative frequency variations, the higher frequency component interacts with the target before the lower frequency component, whereas the reverse occurs in positive frequency variations. As a result, a more densely packed plasma is needed for transmission with negative frequency variations, as opposed to unchirped or positively chirped pulses. However, negative frequency variations allow for increased transmission at higher densities (six times the critical density), producing a highly stable and persistent electrostatic field behind the target and significant ion acceleration in opposite directions due to the electron void. Additionally, our experiment features an auxiliary thin layer with low density, situated behind the main target layer. Ions from the auxiliary layer can be efficiently accelerated into a mono-energetic beam by the electrostatic field generated in the main target under interaction with a negatively frequency-modulated, highly intense laser pulse, achieving protons with maximum energies of around 100 MeV when subjected to specific optimal conditions involving a 10-fs, intensively Gaussian pulse with 8.5 times ten to the power of twenty watts per square centimeter peak intensity. Our study provides a theoretical and experimental analysis of a novel ion-activation technique based on this concept and presents initial results of an experiment conducted at the Gauss Laser Facility in Saclay. The findings demonstrate the feasibility of creating multi-MeV, mono-energetic ion beams consisting of any species provided, provided that the required target conditions can be met. This technique has the potential to offer a wide range of applications, including the generation of anti-electron (positrons). Although our study focuses on proton acceleration, the principles we discuss are equally applicable to other ions. Consequently, this technique may also make positron production more efficient. The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate called TOI-712.05 with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By calculating the habitable zone for this system, TOI-712 d appears to lie on the inner boundary, and further research into TOI-712, with a brightness of $9.9$, is worthwhile due to its relatively young and temperate conditions. This finding highlights the rarity of planetary systems similar to our own and sheds light on the highly dynamic evolutionary processes of young planets, influenced by their birth environment and supplemental factors, until about a billion years of age. As such, TOI-712 offers a perfect opportunity to study the progression of our solar system-like planetary systems over an extensive period of time. TOI-712 is also an ideal target for various follow-up observations, and it has been added to the $TESS$ Exoplanet Catalogue".[Published in the Astronomical Journal, Volume 167, Number 1, 2024]

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  This concept is validated via total and projected density of states, and could provide a potential framework for further investigation of defects within this material system.  We have open-source computer codes available that enable users to generate and view such defect structures.  This includes a TiO2 defect structure that we have made publicly accessible to facilitate related research.  Corresponding authors can be found at the mentioned email addresses. This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively. Additionally, I outline that in the absence of rare decays, limits on the top-quark elastic scattering cross-section at 14 TeV with 300 inverse picobarns of data are below $0.41\cdot10^{-7}$ and $0.97\cdot10^{-7}$ for final states $p_p\bar{p}_p \to p_p p_p$ and $p_p\bar{p}_\pi \to \bar{p}_\pi \bar{p}_\pi$, respectively. These limits are more stringent than current theoretical predictions. Limits on rare decays and top-quark elastic scattering can be refined with additional assumptions about the nature of these processes. Lastly, I present an interpretation of the data excluding any signal and an enhanced analysis technique utilizing neural networks that yields limits of <0.27\cdot10^{-5} and <0.57\cdot10^{-5} on the branching ratios of $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$, respectively, without assumptions about the matrix element. This represents the most stringent limit on $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and the first on $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ at a hadron collider. Additionally, I outline that in the absence of rare decays, limits on the top-quark elastic scattering cross-section at 14 TeV with 300 inverse picobarns of data are below $0.20\cdot10^{-7}$ and $0.57\cdot10^{-7}$ for final states $p_p\bar{p}_p \to p_p p_p$ and $p_p\bar{p}_\pi \to \bar{p}_\pi \bar{p}_\pi$, respectively.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5. Our work also offers a more flexible version of a 1991 Szarinsky result related to Ramsey theory in odd cycles. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between $\lambda$ values for structures like cliques and odd cycles in an equilateral graph versus a general complete graph. This relationship reveals that the specific $\lambda$ values are unaffected by the underlying graph structure. Lastly, we pose several open questions for further investigation.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two. Additionally, this research introduces a new upper limit for a group's diameter based on its potential energy and the number of generating elements, and it demonstrates that this potential energy threshold can be as low as (generator count)^1.5. This research is complemented by a diverse range of applications, including the resolution of a conjecture made by Gil'breath and Shalev regarding the size of abelian subgroups and the characterization of groups with a diameter of three or less. Further still, this research provides an explicit description of groups with a diameter of three or less and shows that these groups can be highly complex, containing numerous random-like elements and a vast abelian section that accounts for nearly half of the group's size. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and a high resolution output. Moreover, by incorporating the circuit's temperature-dependent behavior and supply noise into a first-order model, the design achieves robust performance despite being sensitive to temperature and supply noise. Long-lasting stability in the magnetic fields of Ap-stars, white dwarfs, and neutron stars has been observed but the exact stellar interior conditions responsible are still the focus of ongoing research. Studies have revealed that magnetic fields purely in the toroidal or poloidal configurations inevitably succumb to instability. In contrast, numerical simulations have consistently shown stability in the axisymmetric configurations of the magnetic fields found within non-turbulent stellar interiors. These stable configurations consist of intertwined toroidal and poloidal components resembling a twisted torus. Prior studies have identified rough limits to the ratio of the toroidal and poloidal magnetic energy. In order to define the conditions necessary for these stable configurations, we ran three-dimensional simulations utilizing the Pencil Code for non-rotating stars experiencing viscosity-driven dissipation. Our simulations were performed for both barotropic stars with constant specific entropy and stably stratified stars, while varying parameters including the level of stable stratification and magnetic energy in each component, confirming existing predictions for the stability boundaries. We additionally obtained the resistive magnetic diffusion times for each case, expanding our understanding of the stable configurations within viscous and resistive stellar interiors. These results can be utilized to create more realistic simulations that incorporate thermal and electrical processes. We also introduced a simplified model describing the evolution of magnetic energy components, which may represent intermediate layers within multi-layer stellar systems. By analyzing these simulations, we proposed criteria for the existence of stable twisted magnetic configurations found within the interiors of stable stellar magnetic fields. These criteria consist of a magnetic rotation period longer than the ohmic diffusion time, stable stratification meeting specific conditions, and magnetic energy ratios consistent with previously established boundaries. We applied these criteria to several stars with stable magnetic fields, which may provide insight into their internal processes. We also examined how magnetic field evolution is influenced by the motion of magnetic flux tubes carrying small amounts of plasma. These flux tubes can intersect with magnetic field layers having significantly greater energy, potentially leading to the appearance of X-shaped magnetic field configurations often observed in the magnetic fields of Ap-stars. We propose that the formation of these stable twisted configurations represents the primary state of the magnetic fields found within non-turbulent stellar interiors, white dwarfs, and neutron stars. We further suggest that the energy stored in these stable configurations can ultimately give rise to spectacular astrophysical phenomena, such as magnetic winds, outbursts, and bursts, closely resembling those observed on the Sun. If magnetic reconnections involving these stable configurations are powerful enough, they may also excel in luminosity, possibly surpassing all known magnetic events

In this paper, we introduce an innovative strategy to address flow equations that draws on parallels between these equations and conservation principles found in fluid dynamics. We then successfully applied this perspective to derive a closed form for the flow equations relevant to the Warsaw model, a simple scalar model. We also obtained closed form equations for a related model, the polynomial model, by identifying a key symmetry. This approach highlights the potential for researchers to tackle more intricate renormalization group problems by drawing on analytical and numerical solutions developed for fluid dynamics. LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models and applications such as glacial monitoring, detecting structural changes, forest assessment, tracking shoreline and beach alterations, landslide risk analysis, habitat mapping, and urban planning. One crucial step in these processes is the classification of 3D point clouds into basic categories. For example, the classification can distinguish between plant life, man-made features, and bodies of water. Our research aims to present an initial evaluation of various classification techniques for 3D LiDAR data, including diverse feature engineering methods. Specifically, we show that supplying contextual information about neighboring points to each LiDAR data point enhances the performance of subsequent machine learning algorithms. We also examine multiple dimension reduction techniques, spanning PCA to neural network-based encoders, to illustrate their influence on classification outcomes. Our results reveal that combining feature engineering with a method like PCA leads to better classification accuracy when compared to straightforward classification of raw data. Moreover, even the most basic techniques, such as linear discriminant analysis, can yield surprisingly good outcomes. Ultimately, our studies provide valuable insights into the classification of LiDAR data and the effectiveness of various 3D feature extraction methods. These findings can guide environmental monitoring initiatives that rely on LiDAR data and facilitate data-driven urban planning decisions. Additionally, they can benefit researchers who encounter similar three-dimensional classification challenges across different domains. Our LiDAR classification framework, complete with multiple evaluation scenarios and related code, is now publicly accessible to foster further advancement in this area. Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness. Consequently, this discovery enables the development of novel strategies for constructing definite systems of functions on the sphere and facilitates the broad application of these methods across multiple domains. Additionally, this research introduces multiple examples, including one involving the construction of a new system of definite radial functions associated with the Grunbaum operators. Notably, this phenomenon is not limited to the sphere, as similar operator-based methods can be employed to create (strictly) positive definite functions within the context of the special Euclidean spaces. Furthermore, this paper explores the general challenges and obstacles associated with the positive definiteness of zonal functions, providing an analytical expression for their characteristic equation along with some interesting observations about its roots. Ultimately, this research is aimed at equipping it with a suitable machinery for confronting fundamental conjectures related to the positive definiteness of zonal functions. This paper is intended to serve as a preliminary step in this endeavor, centered on the theory of differential operators for Gegenbauer polynomials and their connection to the harmonic analysis within the context of the Euclidean spaces. This approach is expected to offer a versatile framework that is also relevant to other functional systems, such as those related to the continued fractions or Toeplitz determinants. Our theory and experiments reveal that the membrane's stability can be compromised due to two conflicting forces: the centrifugal force, which causes an irregular pattern, and the gravitational force, which produces an elongated pattern. The resulting instability, an elastic membrane finger, can be analyzed using a simple mathematical model that shows the transition from a straight to a curved wavefront. The membrane's elasticity plays a crucial role in determining the shape of the wavefront, especially at larger radii. The rotation of the system accelerates the membrane's instability, causing it to develop a highly curved wavefront, similar to that observed in Taylor-Reynolds instability. The membrane's finger pattern was found to be a non-stationary state, with both growth and decay of waves occurring simultaneously. Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. We present an innovative solution to overcome this limitation, using a system that undergoes free expansion without an external influence, and demonstrate that the proposed method aligns with thermodynamic principles. Our solution identifies the dissipated energy as a thermodynamic average of work performed by each individual microstate and confirms its nonnegative value during free expansion, which holds surprising implications. We predict that the sign of work will become negative, indicating a decrease in a system's organized energy, and ultimately, the system will reach a state of maximum entropy characterized by a uniform distribution of energy among all possible microstates. This groundbreaking finding provides a foundation for extending microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics to systems in constant contact with their surroundings, facilitating further exploration of complex dynamical processes, including chemical reactions and energy conversion. Ultimately, this framework has the potential to bridge the gap between thermodynamics and statistical mechanics, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of the fundamental principles governing the behavior of microscopic systems. By doing so, it may also reveal the underlying mechanisms governing the emergence of irreversible processes in macroscopic systems, thus answering one of the longest-standing questions in the history of science. This innovative approach can now be applied to a broader range of systems, including those involved in biological processes, such as protein-ligand interactions, which can lead to new insights into various cellular mechanisms and potentially contribute to the development of more effective strategies for addressing some of the world's most pressing global challenges. Lastly, this groundbreaking work paves the way for a future where a deeper understanding of the intricate relationships between systems at all levels of complexity can inform decisions that promote a more sustainable use of resources, leading to a greater good for all inhabitants of Earth. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. The proposed methods also exhibit the ability to enhance performance in low-resource settings. A thorough analysis of decoding examples provides insight into the benefits of our proposed look-ahead attention mechanisms. The effective management of urban roads plays a crucial role in the optimal operation of urban transportation systems and overall city functioning. Current monitoring techniques rely on inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowdsourced data, but they often come with limitations of high costs, restricted coverage areas, or unreliable data due to low user participation rates. In this study, a groundbreaking approach of mobile sensing is presented, utilizing a large fleet of ridesharing vehicles to monitor and interpret the condition of urban roads as they traverse through the network. Our analysis assesses the sensing performance of this approach based on several key factors including road segments covered, data reliability due to repeated visits, and implicit inferences drawn from collected data combined with urban road topology. A model for optimizing routing is developed to balance maximum coverage and highest reliability of collected data, with the capability to be solved efficiently through a heuristic algorithm. Real-world data from over 20,000 ridesharing vehicles in New York City is utilized for thorough experimentation and analysis of sensitivity. Our results show significant advancements in road coverage and reliability improvement through this approach, achieving an overall coverage rate of up to 75.5% of all road segments with 97.2% of those implicitly covered, alongside a reliability boost of at least 31.1% compared to traditional methods. This innovative approach has immense potential to integrate transportation management systems with vehicle routing optimization using mobility sensing. This pioneering work sets the stage for utilizing ridesharing vehicles as mobile sensors in multiple other applications, such as monitoring traffic light efficiency, detecting road conditions, and observing parking dynamics. This is accomplished without requiring any additional hardware on the vehicles. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude. Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, making critical decisions in the process. Yet, surprisingly, little research has focused on comprehending the complex workings of these algorithms, particularly those that operate behind closed doors. Previous studies revealed the ease with which these scoring models can be manipulated. This paper aims to investigate the underlying causes of this unexpected sensitivity and instability. By employing the latest advances in interpretation, we examined the relative importance of essay features, including coherence, relevance, vocabulary, and content in influencing automated scores. We used this to investigate the issues of over-sensitivity (small changes yielding significantly varying output scores) and over-stability (little change in scores resulting from significant changes in input) associated with these scoring models. The findings indicated that although autoscoring models are trained with the ability to process complex contextual information (similar to BERT-based models), they instead behave like simpler bag-of-words models that are overly reliant on isolated key phrases. As such, these models are prone to both over-sensitivity and over-stability issues, largely due to their failure to incorporate any real sense of context. Additionally, our study highlighted a pressing need for further research aimed at improving the contextualized understanding of these scoring models, with potential solutions involving the development of robust, interpretability techniques that can effectively evaluate the complex internal workings of these deep learning models. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. To achieve this, the two sub-tasks are modeled as two separate encoded-decoded transformations, resulting in two separate sub-networks that share the same encoded path. To validate the efficacy of this approach, it was tested on public datasets of cancer cell detection, and the resulting density masks were evaluated using established semantic segmentation evaluation metrics. The experimental outcomes demonstrated that this method outperforms the current state-of-the-art automatic nucleus detection methods, that are based on point annotation, obtaining superior performance with only a small amount of annotation. Furthermore, this approach exhibits robustness to varying densities of cells within an image, detecting both sparse and dense collections of cells with equal effectiveness. Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and how these processes respond to treatment. Formulated in terms of ODEs, the model examines the dynamic biological processes that lead to pyroptosis and how they can be modified by anti-inflammatory interventions, shifting cell death from pyroptotic to a less inflammatory form, like apoptosis. Furthermore, we are integrating this single-cell model into the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator, as part of a multidisciplinary coalition focused on understanding COVID-19's host-dynamics, to gain deeper insight into the effects of pyroptosis at a cellular level. External influences affecting states and reward signals can hinder reinforcement learning by introducing unanticipated fluctuations in the reward signal. This concept is mathematically formalized, and the conditions are identified under which an environment involving uncontrollable state variables can be broken down into two separate components: an environment solely affected by the uncontrollable state and reward variables, and an environment defined by the variables that can be controlled. Additionally, a condition for reducing the complexity of these variables in Monte Carlo policy evaluation is established, leading to potential acceleration of this process. This acceleration could be applied across a broader range of reinforcement learning algorithms. Two methods are devised for identifying the uncontrollable state variables, and the results from applying these methods to multiple test environments show a notable increase in efficiency and a potential for speeding up the reinforcement learning process. However, the results are not consistent across all environments, and the approach is vulnerable to over-reduction in cases where the uncontrollable state variables have little impact on the reward signal. Further research is required to fully explore the implications of these findings. The method proposed for reducing the complexity of uncontrollable state variables during Monte Carlo policy evaluation could be applied across a broader range of reinforcement learning algorithms. A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is generating high demands for static verification. To fulfill this need, our project HELMHOLTZ is introduced in this article as a static verification tool specifically designed for Michelson, a statically-typed programming language used in the Tezos blockchain. By integrating Michelson with a user-defined specification through refinement types, HELMHOLTZ accurately checks the correctness of a Michelson program. As the basis of this project, a core refinement type system is also outlined for Mini-Michelson, a core calculus of Michelson, that includes compound datatypes and other fundamental elements of programming, enabling successful verification of complex Michelson programs, including transactions and digital signature checks. Furthermore, refined definitions of list and option types are also provided, demonstrating the applicability of HELMHOLTZ in validating actual Tezos smart contracts, such as transactions and digital signature checks, and refining the Michelson standard library. All of the refined definitions and successful verifications of Tezos contracts can be found on the Zeugen platform. HELMHOLTZ has already been used in the refinement of actual Tezos contracts, successfully leading to improvements in the Michelson standard library and refinement checks in the Tezos blockchain. As a result, this project has contributed to the growth of program verification in the Tezos blockchain community. Additionally, this project has inspired multiple community-driven initiatives and collaborations, such as the creation of a dedicated issue tracker and the development of refined definitions and checks in the F-star type checker for Michelson. With all of its achievements, HELMHOLTZ is now an open-source project on GitHub. Its ongoing development aims to expand its capabilities to refine more compound datatypes and integrate with the F-star type checker for Michelson. As such, anyone interested is welcome to collaborate and contribute to this innovative project. HELMHOLTZ is currently compatible with Tezos versions TzBz3 and TzBz4, and its development is centered around the refinement of actual Tezos contracts, the Michelson standard library, and the integration of over-the-counter language protocols. Its core refinement type system is outlined as a distinct project for Mini-Michelson, a core calculus of Michelson, that includes compound datatypes and other fundamental programming elements. This project has multiple objectives, such as verifying actual Tezos contracts, refining the Michelson standard library, refining definitions of list and option types, successfully defining compound datatypes, and contributing to the growth of program verification in the Tezos blockchain community.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. Our examination illuminates the implicit workings of multiple Neuronal Network types, offering a unified framework that facilitates further research into the underlying mechanics of GCNNs. The accompanying code enables replication of all visualizations and calculations. The underlying mechanics of GCNNs remain poorly understood despite their popularity and extensive use of such networks in various applications, including signal processing, image classification, road detection, gene analysis, and others. Moreover, GCNNs provide a cohesive framework that encompasses both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks in specific scenarios.

The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Notably, the study demonstrates the potential of VSSA to facilitate elastography of deep tissues. The results also highlight the potential of VSSA to facilitate elastography of deep tissues and emphasize the importance of beamforming technique on elastography outcomes. Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. We introduce the name "Dillig" for this expanded framework, which is based on an earlier proposal called "Datalog with forward" presented by the second author at an earlier conference. We then introduce a method for verifying that a given program corresponds to a valid proof within the Dillig framework, which involves a specific algorithm that takes a program and its corresponding proof as input and checks the validity of that proof. We also explore different approaches to generating a proof for a given program, including one method that is particularly efficient but limited in its capacity, as well as another method that is more versatile but requires significantly more computational resources. Finally, we present several examples and a preliminary assessment of the Dillig framework's potential applications. This assessment is further supported by the development of a programming environment, called the "Logical IDE," which is designed to facilitate the use of the Dillig framework through a graphical user interface. This interface is particularly suited for teaching the basics of programming and logic through a interactive, graphical, and animated interface that can be customized for different pedagogical purposes. The "Logical IDE" can be used for teaching a variety of programming concepts, including recursion, iteration, web programming, and database queries, among others. We believe that this approach to programming can also be beneficial for improving the ability to reason logically and think abstractly about complex problems. We are confident that this is just the beginning of a promising new direction in programming research and education. We look forward to exploring this idea further and making the "Logical IDE" a more comprehensive and versatile programming environment that can be used for a wide range of purposes. We have already successfully tested the "Logical IDE" with a basic implementation, and we are eager to take it to the next level by incorporating additional features and capabilities. We are particularly interested in exploring ways to make the "Logical IDE" more collaborative and able to handle multiple users and their contributions.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Additionally, we observe that learning from the hierarchical model leads to faster convergence and greater reliability in offline evaluations. These advantages are attributed to the hierarchical design's ability to capture complex grid dynamics and facilitate robust exploration. By leveraging the interplay between macro- and micro-scale actions, our method successfully integrates high-level strategic planning with low-level tactical execution. We propose that this hierarchical structure serves as a valuable framework for understanding grid-world PEG learning dynamics and suggest several avenues for further research. Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for $i$ ranging from 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that meets these 'cyclic' criteria as $p_n$ and its 'nontransitive' counterpart as $p_n^*$. In our analysis, we find the exact values of $p_3$ and $p_3^*$, and establish upper and lower limits for $p_n$ in instances where n is 4 or greater, indicating a probability approaching 1 as n increases without bound. Our research also identifies the specific probability distribution associated with the smallest, central, and largest components in a 'cyclic' triple. Intuitively counterintuitive results, our findings reveal that the largest component in a 'cyclic' triple has a probability distribution that surpasses uniform likelihood, while the smallest component's distribution indicates a significantly lower likelihood than uniform. 

In our investigation of larger 'nontransitive' n-tuples, our results show that the central components' probability distributions converge to a uniform likelihood distribution as n increases without bound, whereas the smallest and largest components' distributions remain distinct. Additionally, our research reveals the complexity associated with determining the absolute likelihood of selecting a random 'nontransitive' triple or n-tuple. Finally, our paper introduces an intriguing puzzle related to 'cyclic' groups of four or more elements. 

Our analysis, based on a general random selection process, is unique in that it is the first to be based on an independent choice of components rather than an ordered selection of an entire set that meets specific conditions. This approach is particularly relevant to the study of complex adaptive systems and may be applicable to the investigation of other generalized counterintuitive phenomena.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. In response to these issues, we have introduced a new cycleGAN framework based on a single, adaptive switchable generator. By incorporating adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, the baseline generator can efficiently transform a low-dose CT image into a routine-dose CT image and then easily switch to generating high-dose images from low-dose images simply by modifying the AdaIN codes. The proposed architecture achieves these conversions while minimizing the memory requirement associated with additional generators and, through careful implementation of skip connections and normalization layers, can produce highly realistic results at a relatively low computational cost. A key innovation of our approach is that the training process does not involve TGV or TGV regularization, which are typically necessary components to prevent artifact formation in the reconstructed images. Instead, our new method achieves natural-looking images without these constraints and our results demonstrate even better performance than the original cycleGAN method across various challenging CT reconstruction scenarios. Through thorough evaluation of our approach and the original cycleGAN algorithm both subjectively and objectively at public low-dose CT datasets, our method shows superior performance in terms of quantitive metrics such as PSNR, SSIM and LMHM. Moreover, our proposed architecture has the benefit of reduced parameter requirements, making it even more suitable for low-memory CT image enhancement applications. All source codes of our new cycleGAN framework based on a single, adaptive switchable generator are available online at https://github.com/ThinkDevUse/AdaIN-UNETCT. What's more, we have released our dataset preprocessing tool called CT-Prepro on the same GitHub page. What's more, we have started a related CT image enhancement challenge, which is hosted on https://www.devuseThink.com/2021/03/23/ct-challenge.html. Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-GAN, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training with a generative adversarial network to enhance dialog representation and consistency. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (GST) that unifies diverse dialog structures, and develops a novel contrastive loss function to train the model. To improve dialog representation, it employs a multi-task training approach, incorporating generative adversarial network objectives to capture realistic dialog content. The results show that SPACE-GAN achieves state-of-the-art performance on various dialog understanding tasks including closed-book question answering, paraphrasing, and recall, without deviating from the semantic tree structure. To verify the generalization ability of the model, it is tested on unsupervised data, demonstrating consistent performance across various dialog datasets. To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halos, we utilized the angular momentum projection method on wave functions derived from the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in continuum. Our self-consistent approach effectively accounts for interactions between single particle bound states and the continuum across ground and rotational states. By analyzing rotational states in isotopes of $^{42}$Mg and $^{44}$Mg, specifically excitation energy, configuration, and density distribution, our research demonstrates that deformed halo structures endure from intrinsic ground states to collective rotational states, particularly illustrating shape decoupling effects in rotating distorted halo nuclei. Our findings further reveal that the quantifiable spin extensions, extracted from wave function analysis, evolve noticeably along specific configuration paths as a function of rotation. Notably, in $^{44}$Mg, particular quantifiable spin extension patterns emerge across multiple rotational states characterized by clear energy gaps, providing valuable insights into the interplay between single particle and collective phenomena that govern the behavior of rotating distorted halo nuclei. This research is published in the journal Physical Review Letters. Specifically, the results related to $^{42}$Mg are edited and published in the European Physical Journal A for consistency with review policies. This paper introduces a comprehensive video super-resolution model that incorporates external information from recurrent videos and adapts to various input video lengths. The proposed model, known as Attention-guided Video Super-Resolution Network (AVSRN), utilizes external information from recurrent videos and adapts to various input video lengths. The AVSRN model utilizes grid propagation and deformable alignment enabled by external information to super-resolve videos. The model's key innovation lies in the incorporation of second-order grid propagation and flow-guided deformable alignment, which enhances rendering accuracy by adapting to local patches and aligning aligning non-rigid objects. Furthermore, the model leverages an outside-in approach to process videos, starting from the understanding of global patterns and progressing to the level of individual pixels. The method's comprehensive nature enables video super-resolution on multiple scales and can be expanded to address other image processing challenges. Experimental evaluations using public datasets highlight the AVSRN model's superiority over existing video super-resolution techniques. Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey is also conducted to analyze multiple 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels through weak boson fusion/scattering in both polarized and unpolarized conditions. A key contribution of this study involves the development of universal near-Wise-Line adjustments applicable to all 2-to-n particle interactions. As an example, an analysis of dijet and QCD cascade processes is presented to illustrate the applicable impact of this study. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our results highlight the advantages and disadvantages of shared
model-based methods across different scenarios. Moreover, we highlight the
challenges associated with learning multiple tasks using different context
dynamics models. To facilitate further research, we are releasing all related code

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. We further formalize a one-way direction of mathematical contemplation: starting from the fundamental theorems mentioned above, we derive Tarski's Undefinability Theorem as a consequence of the other results. This contemplation forms the basis for an informal argument that the underlying reason for these theorems, namely the inherent limitations of formal systems in mathematics, might be collectively represented by what we define as 'Formal Undecidability'. We then formally define a formal system that essentially captures the essence of these theorems and demonstrate the universality of such a definition by showing that any formal system with sufficient capabilities must be capable of replicating the proofs leading to these theorems. We term this capability as 'Formal Undecidability'. We then derive the proof for yet another, previously unknown theorem concerning such formal systems. This new theorem is actually a more comprehensive version of the first incompleteness theorem. We believe that our definition of Formal Undecidability, along with the newly derived theorem, will contribute meaningfully to the ongoing discussions in the field of the philosophy of mathematics. Additionally, we propose that our results might have implications for our comprehension of the concept of mathematical truth. We also explore connections between our work and existing research, including a previously unpublished letter by Kurt Godel. This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space. Specifically, we demonstrate that if a non-zero subharmonic function u, defined within the intersection of three balls in R^n+1, maintains a consistent growth rate, then u's product with a suitable function p, also exhibiting the same growth rate, can be analytically continued throughout the exterior of a smaller ball in R^n+1. This development is grounded in the Baouendi-Heooworth theorem, and our formulation involves the introduction of a new parametric function p, alongside an associated transformation. This transformation is analyzed within the context of bi-scalar-valued functions defined on the real line. Notably, we demonstrate that a particular rotation-like transformation is analytically continuable across what resembles a Schur stability circle, given that the rotation angle falls within a specific range. This work presents a novel algorithm that allows for sequential selection of a balanced sample. The algorithm accommodates equal and unequal inclusion probabilities and can also be applied to select spatially balanced samples when the population contains geographical coordinates. In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using estimated depth and segmentation maps to calculate the camera's position through iterative closest point alignment. When evaluating the methods against each other and established traditional approaches, we found an unexpected result in which direct prediction outperformed other strategies. Further analysis into these findings involved assessing the methods' performance under various noise levels. Ultimately, despite initial discrepancies, all evaluated methods demonstrated robustness to image sensor noise, with direct prediction emerging as a simple yet effective solution for this problem. To facilitate further research, we made the dataset and associated training codes publicly available. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. Additionally, our technique offered improved computational efficiency, beating the performance of other gan-based methods. The key innovation involved incorporating a Laplace prior into the training process, which resulted in more efficient and accurate training per iteration. We demonstrated the technique's efficacy across a variety of scenarios and thought the method's efficiency and ease of adaptation across different domains made it worthy of further research. The code is available online.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. This theoretical framework is illustrated through practical examples. The feasibility of detecting invariant sets through numerical simulation is also demonstrated. We conclude by suggesting potential directions for further research in this field. This study is intended to provide stability theorists with a valuable reference containing key definitions, theoretical frameworks, examples, numerical implementation details, and potential pathways for contributing to the field of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems. It is based on the authors' joint research over the past decade.

Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that could be achieved by utilizing Terahertz frequency bands for communication. Traditionally, THz communication is confined to short-distance applications because THz signals face high absorption in the atmosphere. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored the potential of multi-hop directional transmission techniques to extend communication range, albeit these schemes can result in prolonged beam training time using conventional methods such as exhaustive search or hierarchical approaches. To tackle this problem, a novel hierarchical beam training technique is proposed in this paper that dynamically optimizes training levels across individual single-hop links instead of applying the same technique network-wide. To validate the proposed technique's effectiveness, simulations in form of Monte Carlo are conducted under both static and mobile multi-hop Terahertz communication scenarios and the results show the new technique converges to optimal performance within a few Monte Carlo iterations and outperforms other methods by at least 50% in terms of spectral efficiency and cuts beam training time by half on average in all scenarios considered. Additionally, the impact of moving nodes on beam training and throughput is analyzed and the results indicate that the proposed technique retains its optimality even in the face of node movement, achieving full convergence within a very short period of Monte Carlo iterations. To take this research a step further, an optimization method is proposed to further minimize beam training time by taking into account the channel characteristics of all single-hop links during hierarchical training, and the results show this method can cut beam training time by another 50% or more in all scenarios considered. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. The screen at this location is positioned near the tangent point of a radial gas flow within the Bubble and may be connected to the formation of a circumstellar disk or a stellar wind wall. Furthermore, a possible alignment between the screen and the pulsar along the line of sight suggests that the screen's scatters are interacting with the pulsar's wind, potentially causing variations in its scintillation patterns over long periods. The findings provide a theoretical framework for studying the interplay between pulsars and their surrounding screens. The screen's dimensions and location within the Earth's orbit make it suitable for further analysis using data from the International Pulsar Timeline All-Sky Map. The method employed in this research can be applied to in-depth analysis of long-term data from other pulsar observations, revealing the structure of the interstellar medium along the line of sight to the pulsars and potentially uncovering the origins of scattering screens. The ultimate goal of this research is to gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between pulsars, their surrounding screens, and the interstellar medium in which they are embedded. The long-term analysis of pulsar scintillation patterns can provide valuable insights into the dynamics and properties of the screens and the interstellar medium, a significant step towards a more comprehensive understanding of the Galactic environment. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency labels by incorporating PD-DCNNs; secondly, three PD-DCNN components with increasing periods are used to tackle short-, medium-, and long-period signals. This strategy enables efficient modeling of signals with varying periods and allows the network to handle unknown pitch cases through semi-supervised learning. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of its designs, highlighting the trade-offs between data efficiency, auxiliary label efficiency, and performance. Furthermore, comparisons with prominent generative models validate the performance of QPNet across various applications. The code and model weights are available online at this link https://github.com/yushoujijin/QPNet. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first public release of a high-performance, pitch-controllable audio generation model.

This research presents a novel annotation and correction tool for Arabic texts,
namely MADARi, catering to Standard and Dialectal varieties. MADARi offers a user-
friendly interface and efficient management capabilities for annotating and handling
a considerable volume of texts. Its key features encompass a range of morphological
annotations, such as identifying the base form of words, associated clitics, part of
speech, lemma, translation, and dialect-specific markers. To facilitate productivity,
MADARi offers a set of built-in tools, including precomputed analysis to guide
annotators, access to multiple dialects via morphological analyzers, and retrieval
of prior annotations. Additionally, MADARi enables lead annotators to supervise and
coordinate the annotation process in a distributed and concurrent manner. We delve
into the rationale, design, and execution of this interface and present results from
an experiment conducted with the system. Specifically, we report on the efficiency
and quality of annotations produced by both professional and non-professional
annotators when aided by MADARi's interface. Furthermore, we outline the challenges
encountered and potential paths for enhancing the system. MADARi's design and related
approaches are now publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/fahdhi/MADARi.

Planets similar to Earth, orbiting nearby stars with reduced energy output, are being extensively studied and several are suited for further analysis. Considering that life forms may have existed on these planets, it's essential to investigate major byproducts of chemical reactions in their atmospheres. Reactions between ammonia and water vapor, influenced by methane, would break down and release hydrogen gas. This process would create hazardous conditions and ultimately lead to the disappearance of any potential life. To better understand atmospheric chemistry, we simulated various scenarios involving temperate planets with substantial ammonia levels and found the following results: when these planets have extensive storm systems, as is common on Earth, the chemistry produces little change; however, in regions with weak convection and no methane, life could potentially thrive; on the other hand, worlds with sluggish atmospheric circulation and abundant methane would lead to the destruction of any life, even if their ammonia levels are moderate. Moreover, we discovered that multi-planetary systems, with convective velocities similar to Earth's, are more likely to have atmospheres dominated by methane and ammonia. Finally, we found that extreme stellar energy can also disrupt atmospheric chemistry, leading to additional photochemical production, including hydrosines and other hazardous compounds, in gas giants and super-Earths, but also in worlds with extensive methane and ammonia levels, like our own planet during its early stages. This research highlights the intricate relationships within exoplanetary atmospheres and encourages further studies in this field. The most substantial photochemical products of ammonia, coupled with methane, are water vapor, hydrogen gas, and NH2CH2I, while intense stellar energy produces SH, SO, SO2, and CO, alongside the earlier-mentioned hydrogen compounds. The formation of these toxic compounds could provide a possible means of analyzing temperate exoplanets' bio-hazards from within their atmospheres. The most suitable approach for this would likely involve the employment of future infrared spectrographs on board observatories, with the ability to analyze multiple planets at once, such as the proposed PRISM on the JWST, which will be capable of identifying various molecular compounds, including those formed in upper atmospheric layers, and could potentially be used to assess the environmental safety of planets, in addition to identifying biological markers. This study focuses on four specific planets: Kepler-452b, Earth, Venus, and habitable exoplaner PH2c, using both 2D and 3D simulations, as well as various stellar scenarios, to simulate their atmospheric chemistry under different conditions. To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising as temperatures decrease in proportion to T^(2r-1), with r defined as the exponential product of the resistance and a universal constant divided by the Planck's constant (all values below 1/2), non-Majorana-induced zero-energy peaks fragment into two separate peaks at non-zero temperatures, displaying varying conductance in relation to temperature by way of a power law. Furthermore, tunneling associated with a Majorana mode falls within the same broad class of universal behaviors as does the case for unstable critical points with a non-Majorana mode. Additionally, our study reveals that high-resistance leads allow for more precise identification of Majorana modes over conventional methods. Finally, our findings also imply that the uniqueness of zero-energy peaks in tunneling spectroscopy could be used as a basis for constructing phase diagrams of Majorana systems. This approach would involve tracking the topology of zero-energy peaks across varying temperatures and resistance settings. This topological perspective on zero-energy peaks could provide a more robust framework for understanding the dynamics of these systems. This method is particularly vital for narrowing down the possible explanations for the zero-energy peak in superconducting carbon nanotubes, where the underlying physics remains poorly understood. This approach can also be applied beyond tunneling spectroscopy to any situation in which zero-energy peaks form. This could involve situations where a critical mode at zero energy is separated from the continuum by a significant gap, as is the case with unstable critical points with a non-Majorana mode. This separation could be attributed to either a topological reason or an imbalance in some other fundamental symmetry. This perspective on zero-energy peaks could also be applied to systems of Majorana modes located within a gap at non-zero energies. This could involve situations such as branch points, where a Majorana mode forms as a result of a collision between two other modes, or systems with multiple isolated Majorana modes, where the interplay between these modes results in zero-energy peaks in tunneling conductance, regardless of the resistance setting used. This study focuses specifically on isolated zero-energy peaks rather than topological zero-energy gaps, which are characterized by a continuous and seamless arc at zero energy in tunneling spectroscopy.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Additionally, this framework is utilized to derive computations for specific bicategories, including THH of category of finitely generated free modules over a regular local ring and derivations of such categories. Moreover, this approach enables the determination of eigenvalues of the trace map associated with THH of such categories. Lastly, this is applied to provide evidence for a conjectured relationship between THH and LHH (topological local Hochschild homology). Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. All code and models will be made publicly available as part of this research.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortion when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. The code is openly accessible on GitHub. LGCN also offers an intuitive visualization capability, making it suitable for exploring and visualizing complex graphs. Furthermore, the code enables easy experimentation with various hyperbolic graph constructions and underlying geometry configurations.
