This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. Additionally, this source term identification problem is framed as a linear quadratic optimal control problem, which can be solved using the infinite dimensional Riccati operator equation. This methodology yields an explicit expression for the optimal control, which in turn enables the construction of a nonuniform stability estimate. This new estimate, derived from the closed loop system, yields a stability estimate on a nonuniform time grid. Importantly, this new stability estimate is applicable even in the presence of external noise within the acoustic equation. When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  This choice of harmonic gauge results in a propagator that exhibits spurious modes despite being physically acceptable.  Utilizing this approach, we investigate the implications of different harmonic gauge choices on the value of the mass parameter when performing a nonlinear transformation of this model.  We find that the mass parameter can be identified consistently across all harmonic gauges, and it corresponds to the physical mass parameter as expected.  Additionally, we find that the de Sitter space can be described in a way that is gauge-invariant up to a linear approximation.  This involves introducing an effective cosmological constant Lambda, which relates to the mass parameter as well as the gauge choice.  Notably, one particular harmonic gauge leads to Lambda being equivalent to the mass parameter, i.e., Lambda = m.  We also derive a new relation involving the mass parameter, Lambda, and the speed of gravity waves, which are in accordance with the principles of the Einstein gravity theory.  We propose that this new relation be referred to as the Einstein gravity precept.  We believe that investigating linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge framework may lead to a deeper comprehension of the nonlinear gravity theory.  This understanding could offer novel perspectives on the fundamental properties of gravity.  This research is currently being expanded to encompass nonlinear solutions and higher derivative theories. Characterizing colorectal polyps pathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas.  The process of pathological assessment, which involves examining tissue samples with a microscope, is a time-consuming and labor-intensive process for specialists.  To streamline this process, implement advanced, efficient, and accurate analysis methods are being developed to support and augment specialist pathologists.  One such technique involves using artificial neural networks to analyze digital images captured during a colonoscopy procedure.  This technique, known as deep learning, can distinguish between adenomatous and non-adenomatous polyps based on visual characteristics, allowing for precedure-based treatment decisions to be made.  However, existing studies face significant limitations, as they are typically conducted in controlled, in-vitro settings using biopsy specimens which do not accurately reflect the true nature of colorectal polyps.  This research seeks to address these limitations by studying polyps that have been removed during a colonoscopy procedure and examining the relationship between their histological characteristics and location within the colon.  A publicly accessible dataset consisting of 1,107,000 digital images captured from 1,583 colorectal polyps was used for this study.  The results showed that deep learning algorithms could accurately classify adenomatous and non-adenomatous polyps (AUC: 0.8842), as well as predict the degree of adenomatous polyposis (AUC: 0.8213) and malignancy (AUC: 0.8825).  The findings also indicated that larger polyps tend to be adenomatous and located in the proximal section of the colon.  This research has significant implications as it has the potential to revolutionize the analysis of colorectal polyps and aid in the prevention and detection of colorectal cancer.  In addition, this study's large, publicly accessible dataset consisting of digital images of colorectal polyps can be utilized by other researchers to aid in the development of more effective analysis methods and deepen our understanding of the histological characteristics of these polyps.  This research was conducted in collaboration with endoscopists and pathologists at multiple institutions and involved analysis of digital images captured during colonoscopy procedures and subsequent pathologic examinations.  The researchers established an extensive dataset consisting of 1,583 colorectal polyps with varying histopathological characteristics, including degree of adenomatousness and malignancy, polyp size and location within the colon. A novel numerical approach has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered around analyzing the impact of smoothly varying material inhomogeneities on plane waves. This method's efficiency is optimal for high-frequency scenarios and is adaptable across any given frequency $\omega$. The approach operates within a time-domain framework, consisting of three main components: generating a suitable incoming plane wave with compact propagation direction, solving the time-domain scattering problem, and ultimately deriving the time-harmonic solution via Fourier transformation. Crucial to this approach is a dynamic front-tracking mesh adaptation technique which minimizes the required computational degrees of freedom, thereby enhancing performance by limiting support to the wave front's spatial extent. To complement this strategy, an alternative Fourier transformation method is developed, taking advantage of the optimized mesh dimensions for even better results. Successful applications and examples highlight the method's efficiency and adaptability with various sources, including external points and soft-scattering scenarios. However, it should be noted that trapping modes significantly reduce the method's efficiency. To address this shortcoming, an additional rescue technique is proposed, involving a more computationally expensive but highly effective resynthesis method that can be employed on an exception basis. Still, this exception-based application does not hinder the method's overall efficiency due to its limited use. Overall, this new approach remains a fast and adaptable numerical method for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering problems, especially in scenarios with complex wave fronts and limited memory constraints. As such, it remains an attractive alternative for big-data scattering problems. To facilitate further development, all numerical implementations have been openly shared as part of a new Fourier-BEM Front-Tracking (FBFT) GitHub repository. As numerical methodologies continue to evolve and improve, this novel approach is expected to provide valuable insights and contribute to the advancement of numerical algorithms tackling some of the most pressing challenges in computational science and engineering. In contrast to the water-rich Antarctic samples with terrestrial contamination, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals showed lower levels of water (around 0.018-0.087 wt.$\%$ H$_2$O) and D-poor isotopic signatures, ranging from -444 to -49. Evaluating various processes on small parent bodies, our analysis suggested minimal water loss during thermal metamorphism, and the water content in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals can be explained by a mixture of D-poor nebular hydrogen and D-rich water from mesostases. Approximately 45-95$\%$ of water with low D isotope values in the pyroxene minerals came from nebular hydrogen, and it's possible that S-type asteroids with nominally anhydrous minerals can hold significant amounts of water (254-518 ppm). This finding may imply a reduced need for additional volatile delivery to the terrestrial planets during the final stages of planetary accretion, given the water added to the nominally dry inner Solar System bodies during the accretion process. Additionally, our analysis provided a smaller estimate for the formation time of chondrite textures, based on the retention of nebular hydrogen, to as low as 10,000 to 20,000 years. The analysis of water in pyroxene and whole chondrite samples revealed an overall trend of increasing D-poor hydrogen isotopic values with more extensive magmatic reprocessing on the parent bodies, reflecting the diverse range of magmatic processes and water-rock interactions on the small bodies of the Solar System. Ultimately, this research offers a new perspective on the formation and evolution of chondrites and their parents, allowing for a re-evaluation of the Solar System's volatile element inventory. Consequently, a larger amount of volatile elements added to the inner Solar System planets during accretion is implied, consistent with other recent findings. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task. However, the large gap between speech and text, coupled with the lack of parallel data for both sources and targets, makes this a highly challenging task. We overcome these obstacles via a multi-task model that learns speech recognition and machine translation, exploiting two major strategies\---shared transformations and articulations\---and minimal pairs technique to tackle zero-shot speech-to-text. Our approach led to state-of-the-art results on the 800-hour LIG10K dataset, with a mean average error rate of 22.3%; specifically, it achieved top scores in select subsets with cleaner data. Additionally, our approach extended beyond European languages and showed the zero-shot speech-to-text's potential when aided by pre-trained speech recognition models. Our approach, code, and models are available online. We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. While the total magnetic moment remains robust across different mixing scenarios, the effective spin-orbit coupling and orbital occupation exhibit more nuanced behavior, influenced by electron-electron interactions and spin-orbit coupling. In situations with significant $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing, we find that the experimental interpretation of branching ratios can be misleading, undermining the need for microscopic theories that account for the intricate $d$-orbital physics. To facilitate future research, we provide a framework for theoretical models that incorporates the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbital states, along with relevant parameters, to model the magnetic properties and spectroscopic signatures in 4d and 5d transition metal oxides with multiple electronic configurations. This will be particularly beneficial for understanding experimental observations involving mixed $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbital occupations in these complex materials.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW. Additionally, it establishes a key computational tool for calculating quantum cohomology and demonstrates its applicability through examples of Calabi-Yau threefolds. Lastly, it identifies important properties of this calculation method. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware data generation has shown promise. In this study, we propose a method to utilize StyleGAN to create artificial chest X-rays from text descriptions. Our innovative approach involves two key components: first, we developed a system that can predict the vector parameters of a pre-trained StyleGAN model based on clinical text; this prediction model was trained using a dataset that combines clinical notes with corresponding image datasets. Secondly, we employed an editing algorithm to ensure the generated X-rays accurately represent chest scans. Evaluating our method revealed that healthcare professionals correctly identified 68% of pathologies on artificial X-rays, a figure surpassing that of existing techniques. Notably, our approach enables the creation of highly realistic artificial data without needing actual images, thereby addressing data scarcity in chest X-ray analysis. This innovative approach may also benefit other medical image processing applications. In our experiments, we demonstrated outstanding results in detecting six critical diseases and one anomaly. Our code and datasets are available for reproduction at https://github.com/ghrua/SAGOTaxo. Our work has been accepted at the 2021 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.

Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations numerically. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume integration into boundary integrals. These boundary integrals can then be computed quickly using the Helsing-Ojala method. Our new method makes expensive computations of near field interactions on an unstructured grid comparable to the time it takes for far field interactions. An essential component of our method involves using a high-order approximation to represent a function over a grid cell, which traditionally poses an ill-conditioned problem due to solving a system of equations involving Vandermonde matrices. Notably, smooth functions and a backward-stable solver for linear systems allow this approximation to be accurate over a grid cell when done correctly. In this paper, we provide a precise proof of this concept. We demonstrate our algorithm's effectiveness through several numerical experiments. These experiments involve using very fine grids to solve Poisson's equation and volume integral equations, which typically result in highly non-trivial, irregular boundary data. These experiments show our algorithm's ability to obtain highly accurate solutions on such grids. These experiments also explore the impact of using high-order approximations over grid cells on our algorithm's performance. We also explore its scalability by conducting computations with a thousand million DoFs on a single laptop.
